options.rationale: Nurses are mandated reporters, but reporting follows assessment. One behaviour alone is not yet a finding.

questions.takeaway: A caregiver controlling communication is a red flag. Assess the client privately.
questions.strategy: When someone is speaking for the patient, the answer is usually to create a private opportunity for the patient to speak.

strategies: Assessment before intervention

steps.detail: The behaviour described appears on the red flag list.
Recasts a warning sign as a positive.
Keeps the caregiver as the source of information.
Skips the assessment step.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B. Report according to requirements once you have assessed.

questions.scenario: An 84-year-old arrives at the emergency department with a caregiver who answers every question directed at the client. The client has bruising on both upper arms, is wearing soiled clothing, and flinches when the caregiver moves closer. The caregiver's account of the injury changes twice.
questions.stem: Which findings support a concern for elder mistreatment? Select all that apply.

options.text: Bruising on both upper arms
options.rationale: Unexplained injuries are a named red flag, and the bilateral pattern is consistent with being gripped.

options.text: The caregiver answering all questions
options.rationale: A caregiver controlling communication is a named red flag.

options.text: Soiled clothing
options.rationale: Poor hygiene and unmet basic needs are named red flags and point toward neglect.

options.text: The client flinching as the caregiver approaches
options.rationale: Fearfulness is a named red flag.

options.text: The client taking four prescription medications
options.rationale: Below the polypharmacy threshold and not a sign of mistreatment.

options.text: The caregiver's account changing twice
options.rationale: Inconsistent explanations are a named red flag.

options.text: The client asking the nurse to repeat a question
options.rationale: May reflect hearing or processing and is not itself a sign of mistreatment.

questions.takeaway: Red flags: unexplained injury, poor hygiene, unmet needs, fearfulness, sudden behaviour change, financial concerns, inconsistent explanations, and a caregiver controlling communication.
questions.strategy: Two options describe ordinary clinical findings. Under plus and minus scoring a wrong selection subtracts, so include only findings on the named list.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Several named red flags appear together.
Four medications is below the polypharmacy threshold and not a mistreatment sign.
Asking for repetition is an ordinary finding.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D, and F are selected. Nurses are mandated reporters: assess privately, document, and report according to requirements.

questions.stem: A nurse uses the SPICES tool to screen an older adult on admission, working through each letter in turn. She has already noted disturbed sleep, poor intake, and confusion. Which finding does the I represent?

options.text: Immobility
options.rationale: Mobility matters and is part of the 4 Ms, not the I in SPICES.

options.text: Incontinence
options.rationale: SPICES is sleep disorders, problems with eating or feeding, incontinence, confusion, evidence of falls, and skin breakdown.

options.text: Infection
options.rationale: Not one of the six.

options.text: Independence
options.rationale: A goal of care rather than a SPICES screening item.

questions.takeaway: SPICES: sleep, problems eating, incontinence, confusion, evidence of falls, skin breakdown.
questions.strategy: Distractors for acronym items are usually real concepts from the same chapter. Recall the expansion rather than judging which word fits best.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The question asks for one letter of a named tool.
Mobility belongs to the 4 Ms.
Not part of the tool.
A goal, not a screening item.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B. Incontinence is abnormal at any age and is screened for deliberately.

questions.stem: A nurse assesses fall risk for a 79-year-old admitted after tripping at home. She takes several medications, has cataracts, fell once last year, and her daughter reports she eats very little and drinks few fluids. Which factors increase an older adult's risk of falling? Select all that apply.

options.text: Decreased muscle strength and balance
options.rationale: Age-related changes named as common risk factors, along with slow reflexes.

options.text: Cataracts or other vision problems
options.rationale: Named. Poor eyesight prevents the client from seeing hazards.

options.text: A previous fall
options.rationale: A previous fall is the single strongest predictor of another one, because whatever caused the first is usually still there.

options.text: Vitamin D and calcium deficiency
options.rationale: Weakens bones and muscles and increases the risk of fracture when a fall occurs.

options.text: Adequate hydration
options.rationale: Reversed. Dehydration causes dizziness and confusion and raises risk.

options.text: Dementia or Alzheimer disease
options.rationale: Cognitive impairment affects judgment and awareness of hazards.

questions.takeaway: Falls are multifactorial: strength and balance, vision, cognition, nutrition, hydration, and previous falls.
questions.strategy: Watch for the reversal. Adequate hydration is protective; dehydration is the risk factor, and reading quickly turns one into the other.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The question asks which factors increase risk.
Adequate hydration protects. Dehydration is the risk.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D, and F remain, covering the named risk factors.

chapters.title: Concepts of Care for LGBTQ+ Patients

questions.stem: A nurse is completing an admission on a 24-year-old and must record several pieces of information accurately. The chart lists a legal name and a sex assigned at birth, the client has stated a different name and pronouns, and the nurse has not asked about relationships. She recognizes she cannot infer one of these from another. Which statement reflects correct understanding of the four concepts in this chapter?

options.text: Knowing a patient's gender identity tells the nurse their sexual orientation
options.rationale: All four concepts vary independently. Knowing one tells you nothing about the other three.

options.text: Sex assigned at birth, gender identity, gender expression, and sexual orientation vary independently
options.rationale: Sex assigned at birth is what was recorded from anatomy. Gender identity is who the person knows themselves to be. Gender expression is how they present it. Sexual orientation is who they are drawn to.

options.text: Gender expression and gender identity are the same thing
options.rationale: Identity is internal; expression is outward presentation. They can differ.

options.text: Sexual orientation is determined by sex assigned at birth
options.rationale: No such relationship exists.

questions.takeaway: Four separate concepts. Knowing one tells you nothing about the other three.
questions.strategy: Any option that infers one of the four from another is wrong by definition. That single rule answers most items on this topic.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The question tests the relationship between the four concepts.
Infers orientation from identity.
Collapses internal identity into outward expression.
Infers orientation from anatomy at birth.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B. They vary independently.

questions.scenario: A 16-year-old with a diagnosis of gender dysphoria attends clinic with a parent. The patient has recently started hormone therapy under specialist supervision and reports low mood and social isolation at school. The parent asks whether treatment can simply be stopped until the patient is older.
questions.stem: Complete the diagram by selecting from the choices below.

options.text: Explain that gender-affirming care is medically necessary and supported by strong evidence
options.rationale: Described as medically necessary and potentially life-saving care, and hormone therapy significantly reduces dysphoria, depression, anxiety, and suicidality.

options.text: Assess mood, isolation, and safety, and involve mental health services
options.rationale: Mental health is a particular concern among LGBTQ+ young people, and gender-affirming care spans mental health, medical, and social services.

options.text: Agree that treatment should pause until adulthood
options.rationale: Hormone therapy is described as safe for both youth and adults with provider supervision, and disruption is a named contributor to poor outcomes.

options.text: Advise the patient to conceal their identity at school to reduce conflict
options.rationale: Concealment is not affirmation and increases isolation.

options.text: Refer the family to a provider who does not offer gender-affirming care
options.rationale: Removes access to care that is described as medically necessary.

options.text: A patient receiving gender-affirming care with mental health needs requiring assessment
options.rationale: Combines the medical picture with the named mental health concern in LGBTQ+ young people.

options.text: An adverse reaction to hormone therapy requiring discontinuation
options.rationale: Nothing in the scenario describes an adverse physical reaction.

options.text: A patient whose treatment should be deferred pending maturity
options.rationale: Contradicts the evidence described for youth with appropriate supervision.

options.text: A routine adolescent visit requiring no additional follow-up
options.rationale: Low mood and isolation require assessment.

options.text: Mood, and screening for suicidality
options.rationale: Named as outcomes that hormone therapy improves and as a particular concern in this population.

options.text: Social support and experiences of isolation
options.rationale: Isolation and loneliness are named, and school is where this patient's difficulty is occurring.

options.text: Serum sodium
options.rationale: Not a monitoring priority described here.

options.text: Bone mineral density weekly
options.rationale: Not a parameter this chapter identifies, and weekly monitoring is not plausible.

options.text: Daily weight
options.rationale: Not relevant to the concerns described.

questions.takeaway: Gender-affirming care is medically necessary and reduces dysphoria, depression, anxiety, and suicidality. Disruption is a named harm.
questions.strategy: The parent's question is sincere and the answer is still no. Options that pause, conceal, or redirect care all appear reasonable and all cause the harms the chapter names.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Ongoing affirming care plus a named mental health concern.
Disruption in hormone therapy is a named contributor to poor outcomes.
Both reduce affirmation and access.

elimination.verdict: Actions A and B, condition A, parameters A and B.

questions.stem: A clinic finds that several LGBTQ+ clients have not returned after an initial visit, and two describe feeling judged by staff. The nurse manager reviews the evidence on why this population experiences worse health outcomes than the general population. Which factor is a named contributor?

options.text: A biological predisposition to chronic disease
options.rationale: Not a cause. The disparities are driven by how care is delivered and experienced.

options.text: Lack of LGBTQ+ affirmation in health care, which discourages people from using services
options.rationale: Named alongside bias and discrimination during care and heterocentric policies. Care avoided is care not received.

options.text: Lower rates of health insurance in all LGBTQ+ populations
options.rationale: Not one of the named drivers in this chapter.

options.text: A reluctance among providers to prescribe medication
options.rationale: Not a named factor.

questions.takeaway: The disparities come from bias, heterocentric policies, and lack of affirmation, not from anything intrinsic to patients.
questions.strategy: When a stem asks about a health disparity, look for a system or care-delivery cause rather than a patient-level one.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The question asks for a named contributor.
Locates the cause in the patient rather than the system.
Not named in this chapter.
Not named.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B. Avoidance of care is itself an outcome of non-affirming environments.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old arrives for a scheduled procedure. The chart lists a legal name and the client asks to be called Sam, which does not appear anywhere in the record. Several staff will care for the client today. Which nursing action is most appropriate?

options.text: Use the legal name in all interactions to avoid documentation errors
options.rationale: Prioritizes the record over the person and is not required for accurate documentation.

options.text: Use the patient's preferred name and pronouns, and document both
options.rationale: Practising affirming language and communication means using preferred names and pronouns. Both can be recorded so the whole team uses them.

options.text: Ask the patient which name to use only when family is not present
options.rationale: Treats the name as something to conceal, which undermines the affirmation.

options.text: Avoid using any name and address the patient as sir or ma'am
options.rationale: Gendered honorifics carry the same risk as the wrong name, with less information behind them.

questions.takeaway: Use preferred names and pronouns, and document them so the team does too.
questions.strategy: Options that hide a patient's identity to avoid awkwardness are wrong. The affirming answer is the open one.

strategies: Client-centered option

steps.detail: A mismatch between legal name and used name.
Puts the record ahead of the patient.
Makes the name conditional on who is watching.
Substitutes a gendered guess.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B. Documenting both keeps the record accurate and the care affirming.

questions.scenario: A 17-year-old arrives at a clinic for a sports physical. The intake form asks for mother's name and father's name. The patient tells the receptionist they have two mothers, and the receptionist reacts visibly. In the examination room the patient asks to be called Sam, though the chart lists a different legal name.
questions.stem: For each nursing action, indicate whether it supports or undermines an affirming environment.

rows.text: Use the name Sam and document both the preferred and legal name
rows.rationale: Affirming language means using preferred names and pronouns, recorded so the whole team uses them.

rows.text: Ask the patient to explain their family structure to the clinic staff
rows.rationale: Places the burden of educating staff on the patient during their own care.

rows.text: Revise the intake form to ask for parent or guardian names
rows.rationale: Addresses the heterocentric policy that caused the exposure in the waiting room.

rows.text: Take information without visible reaction
rows.rationale: Named directly in the case discussion. The reaction, not the information, caused the harm.

rows.text: Record only the legal name to keep documentation consistent
rows.rationale: Puts the record ahead of the patient, and both names can be documented.

rows.text: Provide staff training in affirming language and communication
rows.rationale: One of the five named domains for creating safe spaces.

questions.takeaway: Harm often happens before the clinical encounter begins. Fix the forms, the reactions, and the language.
questions.strategy: Two rows here shift work onto the patient or prioritize the record. Both patterns recur throughout this chapter and are always the wrong side.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The exposure happened at the front desk, not in the examination room.
The patient is there for care, not to train staff.
Both names can be documented.

elimination.verdict: Four rows support and two undermine.

questions.stem: A nurse takes a sexual history from a 31-year-old transgender man who had masculinizing chest reconstruction two years ago, takes testosterone, and has not had genital surgery. She needs the history to determine which screening he requires. Which approach is correct?

options.text: Base the history on the patient's gender identity
options.rationale: Identity does not tell you which anatomy is present or which screening is needed.

options.text: Base the history on anatomy and behaviour, using the words the patient uses for their body
options.rationale: Take the history from anatomy and behaviour rather than identity or label, and use the patient's own terms, since some prefer non-gendered words for their sex organs.

options.text: Base the history on the sex assigned at birth recorded in the chart
options.rationale: May not reflect current anatomy after gender-affirming care, and it ignores behaviour.

options.text: Omit the sexual history unless the patient raises it
options.rationale: Omitting it means missing screening needs, which is one of the named disparities.

questions.takeaway: History from anatomy and behaviour, in the patient's own words.
questions.strategy: Two distractors here rely on a label to predict a body. Neither label does that reliably.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The question asks what the history should be based on.
Identity does not determine anatomy.
Birth record may not reflect current anatomy.
Skipping it perpetuates overlooked needs.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B. Ask what words the patient uses, then use them.

questions.stem: A nurse reflects on her practice after a client tells her he has avoided health care for years because of how he was treated. She wants to identify what she and her unit can change. Which nursing actions support an affirming environment for LGBTQ+ clients? Select all that apply.

options.text: Use the patient's preferred name and pronouns
options.rationale: Part of practising affirming language and communication.

options.text: Participate in ongoing training about LGBTQ+ health issues
options.rationale: Educate yourself is one of the five named domains.

options.text: Ask the patient to educate the staff about their identity
options.rationale: Places the burden of education on the patient during their own care.

options.text: Reflect on personal biases and assumptions
options.rationale: Self-reflection, including accountability and commitment to growth.

options.text: Use intake forms that do not assume a heterosexual two-parent family
options.rationale: Addresses heterocentric policies, a named driver of poor experiences.

options.text: Record the patient's legal name only, to keep documentation consistent
options.rationale: Preferred name and pronouns are used and documented alongside the legal name.

questions.takeaway: Educate yourself, self-reflect, use affirming language, and fix the systems patients meet.
questions.strategy: Two wrong options here shift work onto the patient or prioritize the record over the person. Both patterns recur across this chapter.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The question asks which actions support affirmation.
Makes the patient responsible for staff education.
Puts documentation consistency ahead of the patient.

elimination.verdict: A, B, D, and E remain, covering education, self-reflection, language, and systems.

questions.stem: A nursing student caring for a client with a diagnosis of gender dysphoria asks whether gender-affirming care means surgery, and whether it is elective. The nurse explains what the term actually covers and how it is regarded clinically. Which response by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: It refers only to surgical procedures
options.rationale: It involves a wide range of services including mental health care, medical care, and social services.

options.text: It is elective care that can be delayed indefinitely without harm
options.rationale: Described as medically necessary and potentially life-saving, supported by strong evidence.

options.text: It is treatment for a diagnosis of gender dysphoria and spans mental health, medical, and social services
options.rationale: Accurate, and transitioning is private, personal, and individualized.

options.text: It follows a standard sequence that is the same for every patient
options.rationale: Transitioning is individualized. There is no single pathway.

questions.takeaway: Gender-affirming care is medically necessary, spans several services, and is individualized.
questions.strategy: Words like only, every, and standard narrow a definition that the chapter deliberately keeps broad.

strategies: Eliminate absolutes

steps.detail: The question asks for an accurate description.
Only restricts it to surgery.
Contradicts medically necessary.
Every patient contradicts individualized care.

elimination.verdict: That leaves C: accurate, and transitioning is private, personal, and individualized.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old starting hormone therapy under specialist supervision asks the nurse how quickly she will see changes and whether the medication is safe long term. She has read conflicting information online. Which statement by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: These medications reduce gender dysphoria, depression, anxiety, and suicidality
options.rationale: A named benefit, and they are safe for both youth and adults with provider supervision and appropriate management.

options.text: The effects are immediate
options.rationale: Effects may take an extended period and some are not fully realized quickly.

options.text: These medications are available over the counter
options.rationale: They are prescription medications requiring provider supervision.

options.text: They are recommended only for adults
options.rationale: Described as safe for both youth and adults with appropriate supervision.

questions.takeaway: HRT significantly reduces negative psychological outcomes and is safe with provider supervision.
questions.strategy: Timing and access distractors are common in medication items. Check whether the option adds a restriction the source does not.

strategies: Eliminate absolutes

steps.detail: The question asks for an accurate statement about HRT.
Effects are not immediate.
These are prescription medications.
Only for adults adds a restriction that is not accurate.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A: a named benefit, and they are safe for both youth and adults with provider supervision and appropriate management.

questions.scenario: A community clinic is reviewing its practice after several LGBTQ+ patients reported feeling unwelcome and two did not return for follow-up.
questions.stem: Which actions address the named domains for creating safe spaces? Select all that apply.

options.text: Provide ongoing staff training on LGBTQ+ health issues and terminology
options.rationale: Educate yourself is a named domain, and it includes participating in ongoing training.

options.text: Support staff in reflecting on personal biases and assumptions
options.rationale: Self-reflection is a named domain, including accountability and commitment to growth.

options.text: Revise forms and policies that assume a heterosexual two-parent structure
options.rationale: Heterocentric policies are a named driver of poor experiences.

options.text: Assign all LGBTQ+ patients to a single designated nurse
options.rationale: Segregates care and does not improve what other staff provide.

options.text: Adopt consistent use of preferred names and pronouns across the team
options.rationale: Practising affirming language and communication is a named domain.

options.text: Ask returning patients to disclose their identity at each visit
options.rationale: Places a repeated disclosure burden on the patient.

options.text: Review whether sexual and reproductive health needs are being addressed
options.rationale: Overlooked reproductive and sexual health needs are a named disparity.

questions.takeaway: Educate yourself, self-reflect, use affirming language, and fix the systems patients meet.
questions.strategy: Under plus and minus scoring, the two wrong options cost you. Both shift burden onto the patient or isolate them.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Patients felt unwelcome and did not return, which is avoidance of care.
Segregation is not affirmation.
Repeated disclosure burdens the patient.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, E, and G are selected.

questions.stem: A community clinic has received several complaints from LGBTQ+ clients, two of whom did not return for follow-up. Its intake forms ask for mother's name and father's name, and staff have had no training on affirming language. Which action best reflects the chapter's guidance?

options.text: Display a rainbow sticker at the reception desk
options.rationale: Visible signals help, but on their own they do not change the forms, the language, or staff knowledge.

options.text: Revise intake forms so they do not assume a heterosexual two-parent structure, and train staff in affirming language
options.rationale: Addresses heterocentric policies and affirming communication, two of the named domains, and it changes the encounter rather than its decoration.

options.text: Ask LGBTQ+ patients to disclose their identity at every visit
options.rationale: Places the burden on the patient and treats identity as a repeated disclosure requirement.

options.text: Assign all LGBTQ+ patients to one designated nurse
options.rationale: Segregates rather than affirms, and it does not improve the care others provide.

questions.takeaway: Affirming environments come from forms, language, and staff education, not from signage alone.
questions.strategy: The word best is asking you to rank. A symbolic action and a structural one are both positive; the structural one wins.

strategies: Priority key word

steps.detail: Key word best. More than one option is not harmful.
Symbolic without changing the encounter.
Shifts the burden to the patient.
Segregates care.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B. Educate yourself and change the system the patient meets.

questions.stem: A nurse prepares to care for a client scheduled for gender-affirming surgery and reviews the range of procedures that fall under that heading, recognizing that transitioning is individualized and no client has all of them. Which procedures are included in the range of gender-affirming surgeries? Select all that apply.

options.text: Masculinizing chest reconstruction, also called top surgery
options.rationale: Masculinizing chest reconstruction sits within the range of gender-affirming surgeries, and no patient has all of them since transitioning is individualized.

options.text: Breast augmentation
options.rationale: Breast augmentation is part of the feminizing range, and like every other procedure here it is elective and individual.

options.text: Facial feminization surgery
options.rationale: Facial feminization addresses features that are often the most socially visible, which is why it matters to some patients more than genital surgery does.

options.text: Genital surgical procedures, also called bottom surgery
options.rationale: Genital surgical procedures are one option in the range, and many transgender patients never have them.

options.text: Coronary artery bypass grafting
options.rationale: A cardiac procedure with no relationship to gender affirmation.

options.text: Gynecologic surgery
options.rationale: Gynecologic surgery belongs to the range, and a patient who has had it may still require screening based on remaining anatomy.

questions.takeaway: The range spans gynecologic, chest, genital, and facial procedures. Not every patient has any of them.
questions.strategy: One clearly unrelated option in a select-all is a gift. Take it out and evaluate the rest against the named list.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The question asks which procedures fall in the named range.
A cardiac procedure, unrelated to gender affirmation.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D, and F remain. Transitioning is individualized, so no patient has all of them.

questions.stem: A nurse works with a 74-year-old lesbian client in a long-term care setting who has no surviving family, rarely receives visitors, and has declined to attend group activities. Which finding is characteristic of health disparities among LGBTQ+ older adults?

options.text: Lower rates of chronic conditions than the general older population
options.rationale: Reversed. Higher rates of chronic conditions and poorer overall health are named.

options.text: Struggles with isolation and loneliness
options.rationale: Named alongside historical discrimination, lifetime exposure to stigma and violence, higher rates of chronic conditions, and overlooked reproductive and sexual health needs.

options.text: Greater likelihood of having adult children as caregivers
options.rationale: Not a named finding, and family estrangement is part of why isolation is significant.

options.text: Higher rates of participation in senior services
options.rationale: Lack of affirmation discourages people from using services.

questions.takeaway: Lifetime stigma, isolation, higher chronic disease burden, and overlooked sexual health needs.
questions.strategy: When two options state opposite directions of the same variable, one is likely the answer. Decide which direction the chapter reports.

strategies: Opposite pair, look closely

steps.detail: The question asks for a characteristic finding.
States the direction backwards.
Not named, and estrangement contributes to isolation.
Non-affirming environments reduce service use.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B: named alongside historical discrimination, lifetime exposure to stigma and violence, higher rates of chronic conditions, and overlooked reproductive and sexual health needs.

questions.scenario: A 29-year-old transgender man presents for a routine health visit. He had masculinizing chest reconstruction two years ago and takes testosterone. He has not had genital surgery.
questions.stem: Complete the sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence: The nurse should base the sexual history and screening recommendations on [[1]], using [[2]].

options.text: anatomy and behaviour
options.rationale: Identity does not tell you which organs are present or which screening applies. This patient still requires cervical screening.

options.text: gender identity
options.rationale: Identity is not a reliable guide to anatomy after or before gender-affirming care.

options.text: the sex recorded at birth in the chart
options.rationale: May not reflect current anatomy, and it ignores behaviour.

options.text: the words the patient uses for their own body
options.rationale: People with transgender or non-binary identities may prefer non-gendered terms for their sex organs.

options.text: standard clinical anatomical terms in every case
options.rationale: Ignores the guidance to use the patient's own language.

options.text: terms matching the sex assigned at birth
options.rationale: Likely to be experienced as invalidating and is not what the guidance directs.

questions.takeaway: History from anatomy and behaviour, in the patient's own words.
questions.strategy: The clinical consequence is real: basing screening on identity rather than anatomy is how a needed cervical screening gets missed.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Screening follows organs present, not labels.
Neither predicts current anatomy.
Ask what words the patient uses, then use them.

elimination.verdict: Blank 1 is A and blank 2 is A.

questions.stem: A nurse is assigned to a transgender client and notices she feels uncertain about what to say and worried about causing offence. She has had no education on this area and no colleague is free to swap assignments. Which action reflects the chapter's guidance?

options.text: Ask a colleague to take the assignment instead
options.rationale: Avoidance, and it leaves the patient with whichever nurse is available rather than with competent care.

options.text: Reflect on the personal biases and assumptions behind the discomfort, and seek education
options.rationale: Self-reflection is a named domain: examine assumptions, cultivate accountability, and commit to self-awareness and growth, alongside educating yourself.

options.text: Ask the patient to explain their identity so the nurse can learn
options.rationale: Places the burden of education on the patient during their own care.

options.text: Avoid discussing anything related to gender during the encounter
options.rationale: Omits relevant assessment and models discomfort.

questions.takeaway: Self-reflection first, then education. Not avoidance, and not asking the patient to teach you.
questions.strategy: Discomfort in a nurse is answered by self-examination and learning. Options that transfer the work to the patient or a colleague are wrong.

strategies: Client-centered option

steps.detail: The nurse's discomfort is the finding.
Avoids rather than addresses.
Makes the patient the teacher.
Omits assessment.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B, which pairs self-reflection with ongoing education.

questions.stem: A midwifery unit reviews why same-sex and transgender parents report poorer birthing experiences than other families using the same service. Staff examine the paperwork, the language used, and the care provided after birth. Which factors contribute to poor birthing experiences among LGBTQ+ parents? Select all that apply.

options.text: Bias or discrimination during care
options.rationale: Bias during care shapes whether a parent is treated as a parent, and it is a documented driver of poorer birthing outcomes.

options.text: Heterocentric policies
options.rationale: Policies written around a heterosexual two-parent structure exclude the family before anyone speaks, which is why forms and paperwork are part of clinical care.

options.text: Invalidation as parents
options.rationale: Being treated as though you are not the parent undermines the relationship at the moment it is forming.

options.text: Disruptions in hormone therapy
options.rationale: Named, and specifically relevant for transgender and non-binary parents.

options.text: Universal access to affirming postpartum care
options.rationale: Reversed. Difficulties receiving postpartum care are among the named contributors.

options.text: Birth trauma
options.rationale: Birth trauma is more likely when a parent feels unsafe or unheard, so the experience and the outcome are connected.

questions.takeaway: Poor birthing experiences and outcomes are driven by bias, policy, invalidation, and gaps in affirming care.
questions.strategy: Look for the option that describes the solution rather than the problem. It is the reversal, and it is the one to reject.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The question asks for contributing factors.
Describes access that, when absent, is itself a contributor.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D, and F remain.

questions.stem: A teenager arrives at a clinic and the intake form asks for mother's name and father's name. The receptionist reacts visibly when the teenager explains they have two mothers. Which understanding does this illustrate?

options.text: Documentation requirements must take priority over patient comfort
options.rationale: The form could be written differently without losing any information.

options.text: Harm often happens before the clinical encounter begins
options.rationale: A heterocentric form combined with a visible reaction exposed the patient in a waiting room, before any clinician was involved.

options.text: Front desk staff are not part of the care team
options.rationale: The opposite. Their interaction shaped the patient's experience of the whole visit.

options.text: The teenager should have completed the form differently
options.rationale: Places responsibility on the patient for a form that did not fit their family.

questions.takeaway: The form and the front desk are part of the care. Harm can happen before a nurse is involved.
questions.strategy: When a stem describes a non-clinical interaction, ask what it reveals about the system rather than about the individuals.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The events occur at intake, before any clinical encounter.
The form can be revised without losing data.
Reception staff shape the patient experience.
Blames the patient for the form.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B. Use forms that ask for parent or guardian names, and take information without visible reaction.

questions.stem: A nurse educator introduces the chapter on caring for LGBTQ+ clients and explains that the approach is framed by two concepts drawn from the ANA Code of Ethics, with sexuality and gender identity as interrelated concepts. Which priority concepts frame this chapter's approach?

options.text: Safety and infection control
options.rationale: Important elsewhere, not the framing concepts here.

options.text: Patient-centered care and health equity
options.rationale: The two named priority concepts, with sexuality and gender identity and expression as interrelated concepts.

options.text: Mobility and nutrition
options.rationale: Priority concepts from the older adult chapter.

options.text: Perfusion and gas exchange
options.rationale: Physiological concepts unrelated to this chapter's framing.

questions.takeaway: Patient-centered care and health equity, framed by the ANA Code of Ethics.
questions.strategy: Priority concept items reward recognizing which chapter a concept belongs to. Two of these belong to other chapters.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The question asks for this chapter's framing concepts.
Belongs elsewhere.
Belongs to the older adult chapter.
Physiological concepts.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B. The ANA Code frames it: compassion, respect for dignity, and regard for the worth of every patient.

questions.scenario: A nurse is completing an admission assessment and needs to record several pieces of information accurately.
questions.stem: A nurse is completing an admission assessment and must record several pieces of information accurately, recognizing that each describes something different and that none predicts another. For each piece of information, indicate which concept it describes.

rows.text: What was recorded based on anatomy at birth
rows.rationale: The observation made and documented at birth.

rows.text: Who the person knows themselves to be
rows.rationale: Internal and self-known, independent of anatomy or presentation.

rows.text: How the person presents outwardly through dress and manner
rows.rationale: The outward presentation, which may or may not match identity.

rows.text: Who the person is romantically or sexually drawn to
rows.rationale: Independent of the other three.

rows.text: The marker on a birth certificate
rows.rationale: A record of the observation made at birth.

rows.text: The pronouns a person asks to be used
rows.rationale: Pronouns follow from who the person knows themselves to be.

questions.takeaway: Four separate concepts. Knowing one tells you nothing about the other three.
questions.strategy: Matrix items on this topic are answered by asking whether the information is recorded, internal, outward, or directional.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Recorded at birth, internally known, outwardly shown, or directed at others.
Pronouns belong to identity, not to expression.

elimination.verdict: Each row maps to exactly one concept, and none predicts another.

questions.stem: A school nurse notices that several LGBTQ+ students have been referred for anxiety and low mood this term. She reviews what the evidence says about mental health in this population and how affirming care affects it. Which statement about mental health in LGBTQ+ populations is accurate?

options.text: Mental health concerns are unrelated to experiences of discrimination
options.rationale: Bias and discrimination during care are named drivers of poorer outcomes.

options.text: Mental health is a particular concern among LGBTQ+ young people
options.rationale: Named specifically, and it is a reason affirming care matters.

options.text: Mental health outcomes are equivalent to the general population
options.rationale: LGBTQ+ patients experience worse health outcomes overall.

options.text: Mental health screening should be deferred until the patient raises it
options.rationale: Deferring screening perpetuates the overlooked-needs pattern this chapter describes.

questions.takeaway: Mental health is a particular concern among LGBTQ+ young people, and affirming care is protective.
questions.strategy: Options claiming equivalence between a marginalized group and the general population usually contradict the disparity data being tested.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The question asks for an accurate statement.
Discrimination is a named driver.
Contradicts the disparity findings.
Waiting for the patient perpetuates overlooked needs.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B: named specifically, and it is a reason affirming care matters.

questions.stem: A patient with well-controlled multiple sclerosis tells the nurse she considers herself healthy because she teaches full time, travels, and is writing a book. Which model of health does her statement reflect?

options.text: Adaptive model
options.rationale: The adaptive model defines health as flexible adjustment to change, which is not the emphasis in her statement.

options.text: Eudaimonistic model
options.rationale: This model defines health as the fullest realization of a person's potential, which is what she is describing.

options.text: Clinical model
options.rationale: The clinical model defines health as the absence of disease. By that definition she would not be healthy.

options.text: Role performance model
options.rationale: Close, but role performance stops at fulfilling expected roles. She is describing something larger than her job.

questions.takeaway: The clinical model is the narrowest definition of health and the eudaimonistic is the broadest.
questions.strategy: Match the patient's own words to the model. Potential and self-actualization point to eudaimonistic; working and functioning point to role performance.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Polarity is positive. No priority key word, so look for the single accurate option.
The adaptive model defines health as flexible adjustment to change, which is not the emphasis in her statement.
The clinical model defines health as the absence of disease.
Close, but role performance stops at fulfilling expected roles.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B. This model defines health as the fullest realization of a person's potential, which is what she is describing.

questions.stem: A 54-year-old hospitalized for pneumonia allows staff to bathe and dress him and follows every instruction without question, though he lived alone and managed everything independently before admission. He has stopped asking about his care. This best reflects what?

options.text: Learned helplessness
options.rationale: A pattern developed over time from repeated lack of control, not a brief hospital stay.

options.text: Noncompliance with self-care
options.rationale: He is complying. He has simply accepted the patient role.

options.text: Regression requiring psychiatric evaluation
options.rationale: An overreach. Some dependency during acute illness is expected.

options.text: Assumption of the dependent client role
options.rationale: Accepting care and the authority of providers is an expected stage of illness behavior.

questions.takeaway: Some dependency during acute illness is normal. The nursing concern is whether it persists past recovery.
questions.strategy: Distinguish an expected stage of illness behavior from a pathological response.

strategies: Priority key word

steps.detail: Polarity is positive. Key word: best. More than one option may be true, so you are ranking them.
A pattern developed over time from repeated lack of control, not a brief hospital stay.
He is complying.
An overreach.

elimination.verdict: That leaves D. Accepting care and the authority of providers is an expected stage of illness behavior.

questions.stem: A patient who smokes says he has been reading about quitting and is thinking about setting a date in the next few months, but has not committed. Which stage of change is he in?

options.text: Contemplation
options.rationale: Aware of the problem and thinking seriously about change within about six months, without commitment.

options.text: Precontemplation
options.rationale: In precontemplation the person has no intention of changing and often does not see a problem.

options.text: Action
options.rationale: Action means the behavior has actually changed.

options.text: Preparation
options.rationale: In preparation the person intends to act soon and has begun taking small steps.

questions.takeaway: Contemplation is thinking about it. Preparation is planning it. Action is doing it.
questions.strategy: Look for whether a concrete step has been taken. Thinking alone is contemplation.

strategies: Negative polarity

steps.detail: Key word: next. More than one option may be true, so you are ranking them.
In precontemplation the person has no intention of changing and often does not see a problem.
Action means the behavior has actually changed.
In preparation the person intends to act soon and has begun taking small steps.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A. Aware of the problem and thinking seriously about change within about six months, without commitment.

questions.stem: A nurse counsels a 62-year-old man with a family history of myocardial infarction. He smokes fifteen cigarettes daily, has not exercised in years, eats mostly processed food, and his cholesterol is elevated. She plans teaching around what he can actually change. Which cardiovascular risk factors should the nurse target for teaching? Select all that apply.

options.text: Cigarette smoking
options.rationale: Modifiable and the highest-yield target.

options.text: Sedentary lifestyle
options.rationale: Modifiable through activity.

options.text: Family history of early myocardial infarction
options.rationale: Non-modifiable. Useful for risk assessment, not for intervention.

options.text: Untreated hypertension
options.rationale: Modifiable through medication and lifestyle.

options.text: Age 62
options.rationale: Age cannot be changed, so it is a non-modifiable risk factor. It still matters for screening decisions.

options.text: Diet high in saturated fat
options.rationale: Modifiable through nutrition teaching.

questions.takeaway: Assess all risk factors and intervene on the modifiable ones.
questions.strategy: Sort into modifiable and non-modifiable first. Age, sex, ethnicity, and family history are never the teaching target.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Polarity is positive. This is a select all that apply, so there is no single best answer. Judge each option separately.
Non-modifiable.
Non-modifiable.

elimination.verdict: Keep A, B, D, F. In a SATA, judge each option as its own true or false statement rather than picking a single best answer.

questions.stem: A 46-year-old who had a mastectomy last week turns her head away during every dressing change and has not looked at the incision. She tells the nurse she does not want to see it yet and asks her to hurry. What is the nurse's best response?

options.text: Acknowledge that many women find the first look difficult and ask what concerns her most
options.rationale: Normalizes the response without minimizing it and invites her to say what she is actually afraid of.

options.text: Tell her she will need to look at it before discharge
options.rationale: True but poorly timed, and it makes the encounter about the schedule rather than her.

options.text: Complete the dressing change quickly to spare her distress
options.rationale: Avoids the issue and removes the opportunity for her to work through it.

options.text: Reassure her that the scar will fade with time
options.rationale: False reassurance. It closes the conversation and dismisses what she is feeling now.

questions.takeaway: Body image disturbance is a human response, and the intervention is to open the conversation, not to fix the appearance.
questions.strategy: Choose the response that invites the patient to say more. Reassurance and scheduling both end the conversation.

strategies: Favour qualifiers
Priority key word

steps.detail: Polarity is positive. Key word: best. More than one option may be true, so you are ranking them.
True but poorly timed, and it makes the encounter about the schedule rather than her.
Avoids the issue and removes the opportunity for her to work through it.
False reassurance.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A. Normalizes the response without minimizing it and invites her to say what she is actually afraid of.

questions.stem: A nurse runs a cardiac rehabilitation class for clients recovering from myocardial infarction, covering activity progression, medication adherence, and how to prevent a second event. All the participants already have established disease. This is which level of prevention?

options.text: Health promotion
options.rationale: Health promotion belongs with primary prevention in a person without the disease.

options.text: Primary
options.rationale: Disease is already present, so this cannot be primary.

options.text: Secondary
options.rationale: Secondary is early detection and prompt treatment. The event has already been detected and treated.

options.text: Tertiary
options.rationale: Tertiary prevention limits disability and restores function after established disease. Rehabilitation is its clearest example.

questions.takeaway: Rehabilitation is always tertiary, even when the teaching also prevents a future event.
questions.strategy: Ask whether the disease already exists. If yes, primary is eliminated immediately.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Polarity is positive. No priority key word, so look for the single accurate option.
Health promotion belongs with primary prevention in a person without the disease.
Disease is already present, so this cannot be primary.
Secondary is early detection and prompt treatment.

elimination.verdict: That leaves D. Tertiary prevention limits disability and restores function after established disease.

questions.stem: A patient with crushing chest pain tells his wife it is indigestion and refuses to go to the hospital for two hours. Which stage of illness behavior does this represent?

options.text: Assumption of the sick role
options.rationale: He is refusing the sick role, not assuming it. Assuming it means accepting he is ill and seeking relief.

options.text: Medical care contact
options.rationale: He has not contacted care. That is what he is avoiding.

options.text: Symptom experience
options.rationale: The first stage, where the person perceives something is wrong and interprets it, often in a way that minimizes the threat.

options.text: Dependent client role
options.rationale: This stage begins after accepting treatment and the authority of the provider.

questions.takeaway: Symptom experience includes interpretation, and misinterpretation is why patients delay.
questions.strategy: Track what the patient has actually done. If he has not contacted anyone, he cannot be past the first stage.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Polarity is positive. No priority key word, so look for the single accurate option.
He is refusing the sick role, not assuming it.
He has not contacted care.
This stage begins after accepting treatment and the authority of the provider.

elimination.verdict: That leaves C. The first stage, where the person perceives something is wrong and interprets it, often in a way that minimizes the threat.

questions.stem: A client with terminal cancer receiving hospice care tells the nurse he has made peace with his diagnosis, is spending his remaining time with family, and feels more at ease than he has in years. The nurse describes him as being in a state of wellness. Which statement best explains this?

options.text: Wellness and illness exist on a continuum and a person can experience wellness while dying
options.rationale: Health is not the absence of disease. A person can find comfort, meaning, and connection while terminally ill.

options.text: The patient's disease is no longer progressing
options.rationale: Wellness does not require the disease to have stopped.

options.text: The patient no longer requires nursing care
options.rationale: Hospice patients require substantial nursing care.

options.text: The term is being used incorrectly
options.rationale: It is used correctly. This is exactly what the continuum model allows.

questions.takeaway: Health and illness are not opposites. A person can be seriously ill and still be moving toward wellness.
questions.strategy: Any option defining health as the absence of disease is using the narrowest model and is usually wrong on this topic.

strategies: Priority key word

steps.detail: Polarity is positive. Key word: best. More than one option may be true, so you are ranking them.
Wellness does not require the disease to have stopped.
Hospice patients require substantial nursing care.
It is used correctly.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A. Health is not the absence of disease.

questions.stem: A nurse cannot understand why a client who knows he is at high risk for diabetes has not changed anything about his diet. Her educator introduces a framework explaining why people act or fail to act on a health threat. Which components belong to the Health Belief Model? Select all that apply.

options.text: Perceived susceptibility
options.rationale: Could this happen to me?

options.text: Perceived severity
options.rationale: Would it be bad if it did?

options.text: Perceived benefits
options.rationale: Would acting actually help?

options.text: Perceived barriers
options.rationale: What stands in the way?

options.text: Cues to action
options.rationale: The trigger that converts belief into behavior, and the one people forget.

options.text: Stages of change
options.rationale: That is the Transtheoretical Model, a different framework.

questions.takeaway: Belief alone changes nothing. Cues to action is usually what a nursing intervention supplies.
questions.strategy: Precontemplation, contemplation, and the other stage words belong to the Transtheoretical Model, not the HBM.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Polarity is positive. This is a select all that apply, so there is no single best answer. Judge each option separately.
That is the Transtheoretical Model, a different framework.

elimination.verdict: Keep A, B, C, D, E. In a SATA, judge each option as its own true or false statement rather than picking a single best answer.

questions.stem: A nurse plans a health promotion programme for a community with a high rate of childhood obesity. She is choosing between screening at schools, treating children already diagnosed, and working with schools on physical activity and food provision. Which activity is the best example of primary prevention?

options.text: Referral of children with elevated blood glucose to endocrinology
options.rationale: Referral after an abnormal result is part of secondary prevention.

options.text: BMI screening at the school health office
options.rationale: Screening detects a problem that may already exist, which is secondary prevention.

options.text: A weight management clinic for children already diagnosed
options.rationale: Treating an existing condition to limit its effects is tertiary.

options.text: A nutrition and physical activity curriculum for all students
options.rationale: Delivered to everyone before disease exists, aimed at preventing it. That is primary prevention.

questions.takeaway: Primary prevention is delivered to people who do not have the condition.
questions.strategy: Ask who receives the intervention. Everyone means primary; those who screened positive means secondary; those already diagnosed means tertiary.

strategies: Priority key word

steps.detail: Polarity is positive. Key word: best. More than one option may be true, so you are ranking them.
Referral after an abnormal result is part of secondary prevention.
Screening detects a problem that may already exist, which is secondary prevention.
Treating an existing condition to limit its effects is tertiary.

elimination.verdict: That leaves D. Delivered to everyone before disease exists, aimed at preventing it.

questions.stem: A patient with a family history of colon cancer has repeatedly declined screening colonoscopy, saying he feels fine. His brother is then diagnosed with colon cancer and he schedules the procedure the same week. Which component of the Health Belief Model best explains the change?

options.text: Perceived barriers
options.rationale: Nothing about cost, access, or unpleasantness changed.

options.text: Perceived benefits
options.rationale: The benefit of screening was the same before and after.

options.text: Cues to action
options.rationale: His brother's diagnosis is the trigger that converted a belief he already held into behavior.

options.text: Self-efficacy
options.rationale: His confidence in his ability to have the procedure was never the obstacle.

questions.takeaway: Cues to action is the component people forget, and it is usually what a nursing intervention supplies.
questions.strategy: Ask what changed between the two moments in the stem. Whatever changed is the component being tested.

strategies: Priority key word

steps.detail: Polarity is positive. Key word: best. More than one option may be true, so you are ranking them.
Nothing about cost, access, or unpleasantness changed.
The benefit of screening was the same before and after.
His confidence in his ability to have the procedure was never the obstacle.

elimination.verdict: That leaves C. His brother's diagnosis is the trigger that converted a belief he already held into behavior.

questions.stem: A nurse works with clients who already have established disease and whose care aims to limit further damage and restore function rather than prevent onset or detect it early. Which activities are examples of tertiary prevention? Select all that apply.

options.text: Cardiac rehabilitation after myocardial infarction
options.rationale: Rehabilitation after established disease is the clearest example.

options.text: Teaching a patient with a new stroke to use a walker
options.rationale: Restoring function and limiting disability.

options.text: Mammography screening in an asymptomatic woman
options.rationale: Early detection, which is secondary prevention.

options.text: Influenza vaccination
options.rationale: Preventing disease before it exists, which is primary.

options.text: A support group for patients managing chronic pain
options.rationale: Limits the effect of an established condition on daily life.

options.text: Teaching a diabetic patient foot care to prevent ulceration
options.rationale: The disease already exists and this limits its complications.

questions.takeaway: Once the disease exists, primary is off the table. Detection is secondary; limiting damage is tertiary.
questions.strategy: Ask first whether the person already has the condition. That single question eliminates half the options.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Polarity is positive. This is a select all that apply, so there is no single best answer. Judge each option separately.
Early detection, which is secondary prevention.
Preventing disease before it exists, which is primary.

elimination.verdict: Keep A, B, E, F. In a SATA, judge each option as its own true or false statement rather than picking a single best answer.

questions.stem: A man with a new diagnosis of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis will need increasing assistance. His wife tells the nurse she is exhausted and does not know how she will manage. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Assess her specific concerns and current supports
options.rationale: Assessment comes before intervention. What she needs is not knowable until you ask.

options.text: Provide a list of community respite programs
options.rationale: A reasonable later step, but offered before assessment it may not fit her situation at all.

options.text: Reassure her that home health can take over most of the care
options.rationale: A promise the nurse cannot guarantee, and it skips assessing what she actually needs.

options.text: Suggest she consider long-term placement for her husband
options.rationale: Premature and presumes a conclusion she has not reached.

questions.takeaway: Illness happens to a family, not only to a patient, and the caregiver is also someone you assess.
questions.strategy: When an option jumps to a solution and another gathers information, gather information first.

strategies: Assessment before intervention
Negative polarity
Priority key word

steps.detail: Key word: first. More than one option may be true, so you are ranking them.
A reasonable later step, but offered before assessment it may not fit her situation at all.
A promise the nurse cannot guarantee, and it skips assessing what she actually needs.
Premature and presumes a conclusion she has not reached.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A. Assessment comes before intervention.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with a family history of cardiovascular disease attends a wellness clinic. He smokes, has a sedentary job, is overweight, and his father died of a heart attack at 60. The nurse plans teaching around what he can realistically influence. Which factor should she target?

options.text: Male sex
options.rationale: Sex cannot be changed, so it is non-modifiable. Teaching targets the factors the patient can act on.

options.text: Age 62
options.rationale: Non-modifiable. Teaching cannot change it.

options.text: Father died of myocardial infarction at 55
options.rationale: Family history is non-modifiable and useful for risk assessment, not intervention.

options.text: Smokes one pack daily
options.rationale: Modifiable, and the highest-yield target for teaching among these.

questions.takeaway: Assess all risk factors, but intervene on the modifiable ones.
questions.strategy: Sort the options into modifiable and non-modifiable first. The answer is almost always in the modifiable group.

Non-modifiable.
Non-modifiable.
Family history is non-modifiable and useful for risk assessment, not intervention.

questions.stem: A nurse cares for a client admitted with an exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. He asks when he will be back to normal, and the nurse explains how his condition differs from the pneumonia he had two years ago. Which statement about chronic illness is accurate?

options.text: It persists and often requires the patient to alter roles and self-concept
options.rationale: Chronic illness lasts longer than six months, is usually irreversible, and reshapes roles, identity, and daily life.

options.text: It always progresses steadily without periods of improvement
options.rationale: Chronic illness commonly has remissions and exacerbations.

options.text: It has a rapid onset and a short duration
options.rationale: That describes acute illness.

options.text: It resolves fully once treatment is complete
options.rationale: Resolution with treatment describes acute illness.

questions.takeaway: Chronic illness is measured by its effect on the person's life, not only by its duration.
questions.strategy: Look for the option that names the human response rather than only the disease course.

strategies: Eliminate absolutes
Favour qualifiers

steps.detail: Polarity is positive. No priority key word, so look for the single accurate option.
Chronic illness commonly has remissions and exacerbations.
That describes acute illness.
Resolution with treatment describes acute illness.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A. Chronic illness lasts longer than six months, is usually irreversible, and reshapes roles, identity, and daily life.

questions.stem: A nurse cares for a client from a cultural background she is unfamiliar with. Throughout the admission interview he answers fully and cooperatively but does not make eye contact, looking down or to the side when she speaks. She is unsure whether this signals distress. What is the best interpretation?

options.text: Eye contact norms vary and the nurse should learn this patient's preferences
options.rationale: Cultural knowledge tells you what to ask about, never what this patient does. Individual assessment follows.

options.text: The nurse should maintain steady eye contact to build trust
options.rationale: Imposing her own norm may be experienced as threatening or disrespectful.

options.text: The patient is likely being deceptive
options.rationale: A stereotype applied to a behavior with many meanings.

options.text: The patient is depressed and should be screened
options.rationale: Possible, but concluding it from a single culturally variable behavior is an assumption, not an assessment.

questions.takeaway: Not all people from a culture communicate the same way. Group knowledge is a prompt to ask, not a conclusion.
questions.strategy: Any option that applies a group generalization to an individual is wrong, even when the generalization is accurate on average.

strategies: Negative polarity
Priority key word

steps.detail: Key word: best. More than one option may be true, so you are ranking them.
Imposing her own norm may be experienced as threatening or disrespectful.
A stereotype applied to a behavior with many meanings.
Possible, but concluding it from a single culturally variable behavior is an assumption, not an assessment.

questions.stem: Two nurses care for the same client on alternating days. One has cared for him throughout the admission and notices on day four that he is quieter than usual and eating less, before any vital sign has changed. Which factor most improves a nurse's ability to detect subtle changes in a client's condition?

options.text: Access to more frequent laboratory values
options.rationale: Useful data, but subtle change often appears before laboratory values shift.

options.text: Using a standardized early warning score
options.rationale: Helpful and it triggers on measurable change. Knowing the patient catches change before the score does.

options.text: Caring for the same patient across multiple shifts
options.rationale: Knowing the patient produces a heightened awareness of what is different for this person, which is what detects early change.

options.text: Reviewing the medical history in greater depth
options.rationale: History gives context but not a baseline for how this patient looks when well.

questions.takeaway: Knowing the patient drives clinical judgment. A finding is abnormal relative to this person, not only to a textbook range.
questions.strategy: When options offer more data versus more familiarity, familiarity wins on questions about subtle change.

Useful data, but subtle change often appears before laboratory values shift.
Helpful and it triggers on measurable change.
History gives context but not a baseline for how this patient looks when well.

questions.stem: A client with advanced cancer begins describing his fear of dying and what he has not yet said to his family. The nurse's shift ends in ten minutes, she has not finished charting, and the oncoming nurse has not arrived. What is the best action?

options.text: Ask him to hold the thought until she returns tomorrow
options.rationale: Postponing an expression of fear about dying dismisses it.

options.text: Sit down and listen, then chart after
options.rationale: The patient has opened a difficult topic. Charting can wait ten minutes; the opening may not reappear.

options.text: Offer to call the chaplain
options.rationale: A reasonable later referral, but offering it immediately hands the conversation to someone else.

options.text: Tell him the night nurse will be in shortly and can talk with him
options.rationale: Deflects to someone else at the moment he chose to speak, which teaches him not to bring it up again.

questions.takeaway: When a patient opens a difficult subject, that moment is the intervention. Tasks reschedule; disclosures often do not.
questions.strategy: Options that hand the patient to another person or another time are avoidance dressed as efficiency.

Priority key word

steps.detail: Key word: best. More than one option may be true, so you are ranking them.
Postponing an expression of fear about dying dismisses it.
A reasonable later referral, but offering it immediately hands the conversation to someone else.
Deflects to someone else at the moment he chose to speak, which teaches him not to bring it up again.

questions.stem: A patient declines a blood transfusion for religious reasons. The nurse disagrees with the decision but ensures the patient's wishes are documented and communicated to the team. This best reflects which concept?

options.text: Justice
options.rationale: Justice concerns fair distribution of resources rather than an individual's refusal.

options.text: Beneficence
options.rationale: Beneficence is acting for the patient's good, which the nurse might argue points the other way here.

options.text: Paternalism
options.rationale: Paternalism would mean overriding his decision for his own good, which is the opposite of what she did.

options.text: An ethic of care expressed through advocacy for the patient's values
options.rationale: The nurse protects the patient's choice and relationship to his own values rather than substituting her judgment.

questions.takeaway: Advocacy protects the choice, not the outcome. You defend the patient's right to decide even when you disagree.
questions.strategy: If the nurse disagrees and still protects the decision, the answer names advocacy or autonomy, never paternalism.

strategies: Priority key word

steps.detail: Polarity is positive. Key word: best. More than one option may be true, so you are ranking them.
Justice concerns fair distribution of resources rather than an individual's refusal.
Beneficence is acting for the patient's good, which the nurse might argue points the other way here.
Paternalism would mean overriding his decision for his own good, which is the opposite of what she did.

elimination.verdict: That leaves D. The nurse protects the patient's choice and relationship to his own values rather than substituting her judgment.

questions.stem: A nurse reflects on how she cared for a client through a difficult diagnosis: staying with her, listening to what the illness meant to her, and helping her manage what came next. Her educator names the framework that describes these actions. Which are Swanson's caring processes? Select all that apply.

options.text: Knowing
options.rationale: Striving to understand the event as it has meaning in the patient's life.

options.text: Being with
options.rationale: Emotional presence and conveying availability.

options.text: Doing for
options.rationale: Performing what the patient would do for themselves if able.

options.text: Enabling
options.rationale: Facilitating the patient's passage through transitions.

options.text: Maintaining belief
options.rationale: Sustaining faith in the patient's capacity to get through it.

options.text: Advocating
options.rationale: Central to nursing and not one of Swanson's five processes.

questions.takeaway: Knowing, being with, doing for, enabling, maintaining belief.
questions.strategy: The distractor here is always a real nursing concept from a neighbouring framework.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Polarity is positive. This is a select all that apply, so there is no single best answer. Judge each option separately.
Central to nursing and not one of Swanson's five processes.

elimination.verdict: Keep A, B, C, D, E. In a SATA, judge each option as its own true or false statement rather than picking a single best answer.

questions.stem: A 51-year-old has just been told her cancer has metastasized. When the nurse enters she is crying and does not answer questions. The nurse has three other clients and a medication round due. What is the nurse's best action?

options.text: Leave the room to give her privacy and return in an hour
options.rationale: Leaving reads as abandonment at the moment connection matters most.

options.text: Explain the treatment options her provider mentioned
options.rationale: Information she cannot absorb right now. High distress blocks the ability to take in explanations.

options.text: Tell her that many patients do well with further treatment
options.rationale: False reassurance, which shuts down expression of feeling.

options.text: Sit with her quietly and remain available
options.rationale: Presence is being with rather than doing for. Silence gives her time and signals that she is not alone.

questions.takeaway: Presence is an intervention. Sitting quietly is doing something, not doing nothing.
questions.strategy: When a patient is overwhelmed, the correct answer is usually the one that stays and says least.

strategies: Negative polarity
Priority key word

steps.detail: Key word: best. More than one option may be true, so you are ranking them.
Leaving reads as abandonment at the moment connection matters most.
Information she cannot absorb right now.
False reassurance, which shuts down expression of feeling.

elimination.verdict: That leaves D. Presence is being with rather than doing for.

questions.stem: A nurse prepares to perform perineal care for a 68-year-old man who has been incontinent overnight. His roommate is behind a curtain and a visitor has just arrived. He appears embarrassed and says very little. Which action best demonstrates caring?

options.text: Explain what she will do and why before touching, and ask permission
options.rationale: The perineum is in the intimate touch zone, which requires permission and great sensitivity.

options.text: Ask a family member to remain to reassure the patient
options.rationale: Presumes the patient wants family present for intimate care.

options.text: Delegate the care to assistive personnel to preserve the therapeutic relationship
options.rationale: Delegable, but avoiding intimate care does not protect the relationship and abandons an opportunity for caring.

options.text: Work quickly and quietly to minimize embarrassment
options.rationale: Silence during intimate care can increase rather than reduce vulnerability.

questions.takeaway: The four touch zones are social, consent, vulnerable, and intimate. The intimate zone requires permission and great sensitivity.
questions.strategy: Announce what you are about to touch and why, every time. Any option that skips the explanation is wrong.

strategies: Priority key word

steps.detail: Polarity is positive. Key word: best. More than one option may be true, so you are ranking them.
Presumes the patient wants family present for intimate care.
Delegable, but avoiding intimate care does not protect the relationship and abandons an opportunity for caring.
Silence during intimate care can increase rather than reduce vulnerability.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A. The perineum is in the intimate touch zone, which requires permission and great sensitivity.

questions.stem: A nurse is preparing to assess and provide care for a newly admitted client and considers which parts of the examination require her to ask first, rather than proceeding as part of routine care. Which areas require the nurse to obtain permission before touching? Select all that apply.

options.text: Mouth
options.rationale: Consent zone. Permission needed.

options.text: Wrists
options.rationale: Consent zone, and the one students assume is free.

options.text: Feet
options.rationale: Consent zone. Permission needed.

options.text: Genitalia
options.rationale: Intimate zone. Permission and great sensitivity needed.

options.text: Hands
options.rationale: Social zone. Permission not needed.

options.text: Shoulders
options.rationale: Social zone. Permission not needed.

questions.takeaway: Social zone needs no permission. Consent zone does. Vulnerable needs special care, intimate needs permission and sensitivity.
questions.strategy: The consent zone is wider than it feels. Wrists and feet catch people out.

steps.detail: Polarity is positive. This is a select all that apply, so there is no single best answer. Judge each option separately.
Social zone.
Social zone.

questions.stem: A nurse tells a patient who is frightened before surgery that she will be with her in the operating room until she is asleep, and she is. Which caring process does this demonstrate?

options.text: Maintaining belief

options.text: Doing for

options.text: Being with
options.rationale: Being with is emotional presence and conveying availability, which is what she promised and delivered.

options.text: Knowing
options.rationale: Knowing is striving to understand the event as it has meaning in the patient's life.

questions.strategy: Being with is presence. Doing for is action. Enabling is teaching and supporting. Match the verb in the stem.

Maintaining belief is sustaining faith in the patient's capacity to get through the event.

questions.stem: The adult daughter of a critically ill client asks to stay overnight at the bedside. The unit does not usually allow this, the client is stable, and no other family are present. The daughter has travelled a long distance. What is the nurse's best action?

options.text: Explore what staying would mean for her and advocate for an exception if appropriate

options.rationale: Redirects her without addressing what she is asking for.

questions.stem: A client in the last hours of life is unresponsive and breathing irregularly. His wife has been sitting silently at the bedside and asks the nurse whether he can still hear her. What is the nurse's best response?

options.rationale: Dismissive, implying it benefits only her.

questions.stem: A hospital reviews patient satisfaction comments to understand what clients value most in their nursing care. questions.stem: A client the nurse has cared for over several weeks is being discharged. As she prepares his paperwork he asks for her personal phone number so they can stay in touch, saying she has been the only person who really listened. What is the best response?

options.rationale: Maintaining boundaries is part of the therapeutic relationship, and it can be done without rejecting the person.

questions.stem: A nurse who has worked in oncology for eight years tells her manager she feels emotionally numb with clients, dreads her shifts, and has begun avoiding the families she once supported. options.text: Increase her caseload to rebuild engagement

options.rationale: Deepens the detachment rather than treating it.

options.text: Dreading the start of a shift
