chapters.title: Caring for Patients with Chronic Illness

questions.stem: A 71-year-old has cared for her husband with Alzheimer disease in their shared home for three years. She manages his eight medications alone, has missed her own last two clinic appointments, and tells the nurse she rarely sleeps through the night. She says she is managing and does not want to be a burden. Which nursing conclusion is most appropriate?

options.text: The caregiver's needs fall outside the scope of the patient's care plan
options.rationale: Family caregivers should be considered in nursing care planning.

options.text: This caregiver has several risk factors for poor health and should be assessed
options.rationale: She meets four of the five named risk factors: caring for more than one year, being 65 or older, caring for someone with dementia, and living with the care recipient.

options.text: Caregiving at home protects against depression through a sense of purpose
options.rationale: Family caregivers are at risk for poor health, not protected by the role.

options.text: The caregiver should be encouraged to continue without additional support
options.rationale: Ignores the accumulated risk.

questions.takeaway: Five caregiver risk factors: over a year, age 65 or older, significant needs, dementia, and living together.
questions.strategy: Count the risk factors present in the stem. When several stack, the answer is almost always to assess the caregiver.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Three years, age 71, dementia, shared home.
Caregivers are included in care planning.
Reverses the risk.
Ignores four stacked risk factors.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B: she meets four of the five named risk factors: caring for more than one year, being 65 or older, caring for someone with dementia, and living with the care recipient.

questions.scenario: Two clients on the same unit have rheumatoid arthritis diagnosed the same year. One works full time and manages independently. The other requires assistance with dressing and has stopped driving.
questions.stem: Which nursing conclusions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Physical effects may vary between patients with the same chronic illness
options.rationale: Stated directly, along with the point that functional limitations vary.

options.text: Individual assessment is essential because no two patients are the same
options.rationale: The reason care is patient-centered rather than disease-centered.

options.text: The second client is likely not adhering to the treatment plan
options.rationale: Blames the client for a difference the chapter attributes to variation in disease effect.

options.text: Care should be patient-centered rather than disease-centered
options.rationale: Patient-centered care follows from the fact that the same diagnosis produces different effects in different people, so the plan starts from the person rather than the disease.

options.text: Both clients should follow the same care plan for consistency
options.rationale: Disease-centered care, which is what this objective argues against.

options.text: Psychosocial needs including depression and isolation should be assessed in both
options.rationale: Named psychosocial needs, and the second client's loss of driving raises isolation risk.

options.text: The first client requires no further assessment because she is functioning well
options.rationale: Current function does not remove the need for assessment, and chronic illness is experienced privately.

questions.takeaway: Same diagnosis, different lives. Assess the person, not the label.
questions.strategy: Three wrong options here standardize care, blame the client, or skip assessment. All three recur across this chapter.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Identical diagnosis, very different function.
Blames the client without evidence.
Disease-centered rather than patient-centered.
Good function does not remove assessment need.

elimination.verdict: A, B, D, and F are selected.

questions.stem: A 79-year-old with heart failure and arthritis attends clinic reporting fatigue that has worsened over six weeks. Her weight is up 3 kg since her last visit and she has stopped walking to the corner shop. Her daughter says this is just getting older. Which nursing response is most appropriate?

options.text: Agree, since fatigue is expected at this age
options.rationale: Age-related changes can mask signs of chronic illness, which is the reason not to accept this explanation.

options.text: Assess for causes including medication side effects and changes in the chronic conditions
options.rationale: Overlapping symptoms are a named challenge, and medication side effects are specifically confused with normal aging.

options.text: Reassure the family that fatigue is unrelated to heart failure
options.rationale: Factually wrong and closes off assessment.

options.text: Recommend increased rest and reassess in a month
options.rationale: Delays assessment of a new symptom in a client with two chronic conditions.

questions.takeaway: Age-related changes can mask chronic illness. New symptoms get assessed, not attributed.
questions.strategy: This is the same principle as chapter 4's age is not a diagnosis, appearing in a chronic illness context. Threads like this recur across the course.

strategies: Assessment before intervention

steps.detail: A new symptom with two chronic conditions present.
Attributes a new symptom to age.
Fatigue is a recognized feature of heart failure.
Delays assessment.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B: overlapping symptoms are a named challenge, and medication side effects are specifically confused with normal aging.

questions.stem: A clinic is redesigning how it cares for clients with long-term conditions, having found that most problems arise between visits rather than during them. The team reviews the framework built around planned rather than reactive chronic care. Which are components of the Chronic Care Model? Select all that apply.

options.text: Community
options.rationale: Community resources extend care beyond the clinic, which matters because chronic illness is lived mostly outside health care settings.

options.text: Self-management support
options.rationale: Self-management support builds the patient's capability, since they manage the condition between visits and that is where most of it happens.

options.text: Health system
options.rationale: The health system component addresses how the organization is set up to support chronic care rather than episodic care.

options.text: Delivery system design
options.rationale: Delivery system design determines how visits, follow-up, and team roles are arranged so chronic care is planned rather than reactive.

options.text: Acute rehabilitation
options.rationale: Not one of the six.

options.text: Clinical information systems
options.rationale: Clinical information systems make the data visible over time, which is what allows anyone to see a trend rather than a snapshot.

questions.takeaway: Community, self-management support, health system, delivery system design, decision support, clinical information systems.
questions.strategy: Five of the six are offered. Recognize the one that is not on the list rather than trying to rank importance.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The question asks which options belong to the model.
Not among the six components.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D, and F remain. Decision support is the sixth.

questions.stem: A community health nurse notices that several clients with asthma live in the same poorly maintained housing complex and that local air quality data show elevated pollutant levels. She considers what falls within her professional role beyond treating each client. Which action reflects the nurse's role in relation to public policy and chronic disease?

options.text: Recognizing environmental factors that influence health and using reputable information sources
options.rationale: Named alongside awareness of policies affecting chronic disease prevention, providing health education, and encouraging screening and prevention.

options.text: Avoiding discussion of policy with patients under all circumstances
options.rationale: Health education about prevention and screening is explicitly part of the role.

options.text: Endorsing specific political candidates to patients
options.rationale: Outside the professional role and not what policy awareness means.

options.text: Limiting practice to individual patient care only
options.rationale: Excludes prevention and population-level awareness.

questions.takeaway: Know the policies, recognize environmental influences, use reputable sources, teach, and encourage screening.
questions.strategy: Policy items reward the option describing professional awareness and education rather than advocacy for a position.

strategies: Eliminate absolutes

steps.detail: The question asks about the nurse's role.
All circumstances is absolute and contradicts health education.
Outside the professional role.
Only excludes prevention work.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A: named alongside awareness of policies affecting chronic disease prevention, providing health education, and encouraging screening and prevention.

questions.stem: A client newly diagnosed with type 2 diabetes tells the nurse that his father had it too, so there was nothing he could have done. He works twelve-hour shifts, eats mostly takeaway food, and has not exercised in years. Which factors are described as contributing to chronic disease?

options.text: Genetic factors only
options.rationale: Genetics is one of three named categories.

options.text: Genetic, environmental, and lifestyle factors including tobacco, alcohol, and nutrition
options.rationale: The three named categories, and genetics interacts with the others rather than acting alone.

options.text: Lifestyle factors only
options.rationale: Excludes genetics and environment.

options.text: Infectious exposure in early childhood
options.rationale: Not one of the named categories.

questions.takeaway: Genetic, environmental, and lifestyle factors, interacting rather than acting separately.
questions.strategy: Options containing only are almost always wrong when a chapter describes something as multifactorial.

strategies: Eliminate absolutes

steps.detail: The question asks what contributes to chronic disease.
Only excludes two named categories.
Only excludes two named categories.
Not among the named factors.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B: the three named categories, and genetics interacts with the others rather than acting alone.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old with rheumatoid arthritis has stopped attending her book club, declines visits, and tells the nurse she no longer feels like herself. Her joint symptoms are well controlled on her current regimen. Which psychosocial needs are specifically named for clients with chronic illness?

options.text: Depression, social isolation, and loneliness
options.rationale: The three named psychosocial needs, alongside growth and developmental considerations.

options.text: Delirium, dementia, and depression
options.rationale: The three Ds from the older adult chapter.

options.text: Anxiety, mania, and psychosis
options.rationale: Not the named set.

options.text: Grief, denial, and bargaining
options.rationale: Stages associated with loss, not the named psychosocial needs here.

questions.takeaway: Depression, social isolation, and loneliness, with age-specific developmental needs.
questions.strategy: Two distractors here are real frameworks from other chapters. Match the set to the chapter being tested.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The question asks for the named psychosocial needs.
Belongs to the older adult chapter.
Not the named set.
Loss stages rather than psychosocial needs.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A: the three named psychosocial needs, alongside growth and developmental considerations.

questions.scenario: A 77-year-old with heart failure, arthritis, and type 2 diabetes attends clinic monthly. The family attributes recent changes to getting older.
questions.stem: A 77-year-old with heart failure, arthritis, and type 2 diabetes attends clinic monthly. The nurse reviews three months of records showing weight, reported fatigue, ankle swelling, and walking distance. The family attributes the changes to getting older. Which conclusion does the nurse draw?

options.text: The changes are consistent with normal aging in a client of this age
options.rationale: Age-related changes can mask signs of chronic illness, which is exactly why this explanation is rejected.

options.text: The pattern suggests worsening heart failure and requires assessment and provider notification
options.rationale: Rising weight, increasing fatigue, new ankle swelling, and falling exercise tolerance together indicate fluid retention.

options.text: The weight gain reflects improved nutritional intake
options.rationale: Weight gain with edema and reduced tolerance is fluid, not nutrition.

options.text: The reduced walking distance is explained by arthritis alone
options.rationale: Arthritis does not explain the weight gain or the edema. Attributing everything to one condition is the multimorbidity trap.

questions.takeaway: Overlapping conditions mask each other. Read the measures together rather than assigning each to a diagnosis.
questions.strategy: In multimorbidity, the temptation is to explain each finding with a different existing condition. Ask instead what single process explains all of them.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Weight, fatigue, edema, and tolerance all move together across three months.
Age does not explain a three-month progressive change.
Weight with edema is fluid.
Arthritis explains one row, not four.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B. Fluid retention explains every row at once.

questions.stem: A nurse manager reviewing the case mix on a medical unit notes that almost every older client is being treated for more than one long-term condition at once. She uses the figure to argue for a chronic care approach rather than a single-disease one. Approximately what proportion of seniors manage two or more concurrent chronic conditions?

options.text: Around 20%
options.rationale: Far below the figure.

options.text: Around 40%
options.rationale: 40% understates it considerably, and the true figure is what makes multimorbidity the normal case rather than the exception in older adults.

options.text: Nearly 80%
options.rationale: Nearly 80% of seniors manage two or more concurrent chronic conditions, which is why care in this population is rarely about one disease.

options.text: Fewer than 10%
options.rationale: Far below the figure.

questions.takeaway: Nearly 80% of seniors live with two or more chronic conditions.
questions.strategy: The figure matters because it changes the default assumption: multimorbidity is the norm in older adults, not the exception.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A single prevalence figure is being asked for.
Too low.
Too low.
Far too low.

elimination.verdict: That leaves C. Overlapping symptoms across conditions are why assessment is complex.

questions.stem: A community nurse assesses a family caregiver during a home visit. She is 68, has cared for her husband with dementia for two years, lives with him, and manages his personal care alone. Which factors place a family caregiver at risk for poor health? Select all that apply.

options.text: Providing care for more than one year
options.rationale: Caregiving past a year moves the demand from a temporary effort to a sustained one, and the health effects accumulate with duration.

options.text: Being 65 years of age or older
options.rationale: An older caregiver is managing their own age-related changes and often their own chronic conditions while providing care.

options.text: Caring for someone with Alzheimer disease or dementia
options.rationale: Dementia care carries constant supervision and behavioural demands, which is why it is singled out from other caregiving.

options.text: Living with the care recipient
options.rationale: Living together removes any boundary between caregiving and rest, so there is no point in the day when the role stops.

options.text: Having respite care available weekly
options.rationale: Respite reduces caregiver burden rather than creating risk.

options.text: Providing care for a family member with significant needs
options.rationale: Significant needs mean the physical and time demands are high, which limits the caregiver's own sleep, activity, and health care.

questions.takeaway: Five caregiver risk factors, and they stack. Consider the caregiver in the care plan.
questions.strategy: One option in this set describes support rather than burden. That is the exclusion.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The question asks which factors create risk.
Respite relieves burden rather than adding to it.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D, and F remain, which is the full named set.

questions.stem: Two clients on the same unit were diagnosed with rheumatoid arthritis in the same year. One works full time and manages independently; the other needs assistance with dressing and has stopped driving. Both are on similar regimens. Which nursing conclusion is correct?

options.text: One patient is not adhering to the treatment plan
options.rationale: Assumes a cause the stem does not support and blames the patient for a difference in disease effect.

options.text: Physical effects and functional limitations vary between patients with the same condition, so individual assessment is essential
options.rationale: No two patients are the same, which is why care is patient-centered rather than disease-centered.

options.text: The second patient's condition is more advanced and needs no further assessment
options.rationale: May be true or not, and either way it substitutes assumption for assessment.

options.text: Both patients should follow the same care plan for consistency
options.rationale: Disease-centered care, which is what the chapter argues against.

questions.takeaway: Same diagnosis, different lives. Assess the person, not the label.
questions.strategy: Options that blame the patient or standardize care are usually wrong in chronic illness items.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Same condition, different function.
Blames the patient without evidence.
Assumes rather than assesses.
Disease-centered rather than patient-centered.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B: no two patients are the same, which is why care is patient-centered rather than disease-centered.

questions.scenario: A 68-year-old has cared for her husband with Alzheimer disease in their shared home for two years. She reports sleeping poorly, has missed her own two follow-up appointments, and says she has stopped seeing friends. She manages his eight medications alone.
questions.stem: For each factor, indicate whether it increases this caregiver's risk for poor health.

rows.text: Providing care for more than one year
rows.rationale: A named caregiver risk factor.

rows.text: Being 65 years of age or older
rows.rationale: A named caregiver risk factor.

rows.text: Caring for someone with Alzheimer disease or dementia
rows.rationale: A named caregiver risk factor.

rows.text: Living with the care recipient
rows.rationale: A named caregiver risk factor.

rows.text: Attending a weekly caregiver support group
rows.rationale: Support reduces burden rather than adding to it.

rows.text: Missing her own health appointments
rows.rationale: Caregivers are at risk for poor health, and neglecting their own care is how that risk is realized.

questions.takeaway: Five named caregiver risk factors, and they stack. Consider the caregiver in the care plan.
questions.strategy: Count the stacked factors rather than weighing them. When four or more are present, the answer is always to assess the caregiver.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Four named risk factors are present at once.
A support group relieves burden.

elimination.verdict: Five rows increase risk; the support group does not.

questions.stem: A nurse educator asks a group of students which elements belong to the framework used to organize care for long-term conditions, as opposed to the systems used for acute or emergency care. Which is a component of the Chronic Care Model?

options.text: Self-management support
options.rationale: One of the six components, alongside community, health system, delivery system design, decision support, and clinical information systems.

options.text: Acute care triage
options.rationale: Not a component of the model.

options.text: Emergency preparedness
options.rationale: Emergency preparedness is an organizational function and is not one of the six components, which all concern ongoing chronic care.

options.text: Infection surveillance
options.rationale: Infection surveillance belongs to infection control rather than to a model built around long-term condition management.

questions.takeaway: Six components: community, self-management support, health system, delivery system design, decision support, clinical information systems.
questions.strategy: The model is built around supporting the patient between visits, so components that sound acute or episodic are wrong.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: One component of a named model.
Acute rather than chronic.
Not part of the model.
Not part of the model.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A: one of the six components, alongside community, health system, delivery system design, decision support, and clinical information systems.

questions.scenario: A 44-year-old with multiple sclerosis tells the nurse she has stopped attending her book club because she is embarrassed by her tremor, and that she feels she is no longer the person her friends knew.
questions.stem: Complete the sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence: The tremor is an example of [[1]], and her withdrawal from the book club is an example of [[2]].

options.text: chronic disease
options.rationale: The medical focus: the clinical process occurring in the body.

options.text: chronic illness
options.rationale: Illness is the personal experience, not the physical sign.

options.text: multimorbidity
options.rationale: Only one condition is described.

options.text: chronic illness
options.rationale: The personal focus: the emotional and social experience of living with the condition.

options.text: chronic disease
options.rationale: The disease is the neurological process, not the social withdrawal.

options.text: non-adherence
options.rationale: Nothing in the scenario describes a treatment she is not following.

questions.takeaway: Disease is the clinical process. Illness is how the person lives it.
questions.strategy: The same distinction appears in the cultural care chapter. When an idea recurs across chapters it is being flagged as central.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The tremor is a physical manifestation of the disease process.
Withdrawal and lost identity are the lived experience.

elimination.verdict: Blank 1 is A and blank 2 is A.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is being discharged after his third admission this year. He lives with his wife, will need home oxygen, and has been referred for pulmonary rehabilitation. He struggles to manage his inhalers. Which nursing action best reflects the chapter's approach to care?

options.text: Provide written discharge instructions to the patient
options.rationale: Necessary but insufficient. Chronic illness care extends past the individual and past a single handout.

options.text: Coordinate with the patient, family, caregivers, and the health care team including therapy services
options.rationale: Care often includes patients, families, caregivers, and a team spanning physical, occupational, and speech therapy and specialty physicians.

options.text: Refer the patient to a single specialist for ongoing management
options.rationale: Narrows care to one discipline.

options.text: Schedule a follow-up appointment and end nursing involvement
options.rationale: Ends coordination at the moment self-management begins.

questions.takeaway: Chronic illness care is a team effort that includes the family and caregivers.
questions.strategy: Key word best. All four options are things someone might do; the answer is the one that matches the model of care.

strategies: Priority key word

steps.detail: Discharge planning for a chronic condition.
A handout alone does not coordinate care.
Narrows to one discipline.
Withdraws coordination too early.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B: care often includes patients, families, caregivers, and a team spanning physical, occupational, and speech therapy and specialty physicians.

questions.stem: A 59-year-old with type 2 diabetes tells the nurse he never knows what his glucose readings mean or what to do when one is high, so he mostly ignores them. He takes his medication when he remembers. Which nursing action best supports chronic disease self-management?

options.text: Providing a detailed schedule the patient must follow exactly
options.rationale: Directive rather than supportive, and it does not build the patient's capacity to manage.

options.text: Teaching the patient to recognize and respond to changes in their own symptoms
options.rationale: Self-management education builds the patient's ability to manage the condition between visits, which is where most chronic illness is lived.

options.text: Arranging daily nursing visits indefinitely
options.rationale: Creates dependence rather than capability.

options.text: Asking the family to take over medication administration
options.rationale: Removes the patient from their own care without an assessed need.

questions.takeaway: Self-management education builds the patient's capability, because they manage the condition between visits.
questions.strategy: In chronic illness items, the answer usually increases the patient's capacity rather than doing the task for them.

strategies: Client-centered option

steps.detail: Key word best, with self-management as the goal.
Directive, not capacity-building.
Creates dependence.
Removes the patient from their own care.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B: self-management education builds the patient's ability to manage the condition between visits, which is where most chronic illness is lived.

questions.stem: A practice nurse is planning the year's work for clients with long-term conditions and wants to focus on preventing complications rather than responding to them. She reviews which activities fall within the nursing role. Which nursing actions support health promotion and prevention for clients with chronic illness? Select all that apply.

options.text: Screening for diseases
options.rationale: Screening finds disease before symptoms appear, which is when intervention changes the trajectory rather than managing damage.

options.text: Patient education and chronic disease self-management
options.rationale: Education is what makes self-management possible, since a patient cannot manage a condition they do not understand.

options.text: Promoting adherence
options.rationale: Adherence determines whether a plan has any effect, and promoting it means finding the barrier rather than repeating the instruction.

options.text: Discouraging patients from asking questions about their condition
options.rationale: Undermines self-management, which depends on the patient understanding their condition.

options.text: Self-management education
options.rationale: Self-management education targets the skills used between visits, such as recognizing a change and knowing what to do about it.

options.text: Encouraging appropriate screening and prevention efforts
options.rationale: Encouraging screening extends the nurse's role beyond the individual visit into prevention at a population level.

questions.takeaway: Screening, education, adherence, and self-management education.
questions.strategy: A distractor that reduces the patient's understanding is always wrong in a chapter built on self-management.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The question asks which actions support prevention.
Reduces the understanding self-management requires.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, E, and F remain.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old with multiple sclerosis tells the nurse she has stopped attending the book club she has belonged to for years because she is embarrassed by her tremor, and that she no longer feels like the person her friends knew. Her tremor is unchanged on her current treatment. Which concept does this best illustrate?

options.text: Chronic disease
options.rationale: Chronic disease is the medical focus: the clinical process in the body, diagnosed and lasting a year or longer.

options.text: Chronic illness
options.rationale: Chronic illness is the personal focus, meaning the emotional and social experience. Withdrawing from a social group because of how the condition feels is illness, not disease.

options.text: Multimorbidity
options.rationale: Multimorbidity is managing two or more concurrent chronic conditions.

options.text: Comorbidity
options.rationale: Refers to an additional condition alongside a primary one.

questions.takeaway: Disease is the clinical process. Illness is how the person lives it.
questions.strategy: When a stem describes what a condition does to someone's life rather than to their body, the answer is illness.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The finding is social withdrawal driven by embarrassment.
Disease is the biological process.
Only one condition is described.
No second condition is mentioned.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B. The tremor is disease; the empty chair at the book club is illness.

questions.stem: A nurse admits a 61-year-old with poorly controlled hypertension who smokes, has missed several appointments, and takes his medication irregularly. She plans an assessment that will identify what is actually driving his poor control. Which areas does the chapter identify as assessment priorities?

options.text: Adherence, symptom management, tobacco use, alcohol consumption, and lifestyle
options.rationale: The named assessment priorities for patients with chronic illness.

options.text: Range of motion, reflexes, and gait only
options.rationale: A physical subset that omits the behavioural and lifestyle areas named.

options.text: Immunization status and travel history
options.rationale: Relevant elsewhere, not the named priorities.

options.text: Surgical history and anesthesia tolerance
options.rationale: Perioperative concerns rather than chronic illness assessment.

questions.takeaway: Adherence, symptoms, tobacco, alcohol, and lifestyle.
questions.strategy: The named list mixes clinical and behavioural areas. An option containing only physical findings is too narrow.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The question asks for the named assessment priorities.
Only narrows to physical findings.
Not the named set.
Perioperative rather than chronic.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A: the named assessment priorities for patients with chronic illness.

questions.scenario: A 59-year-old with type 2 diabetes and hypertension has missed two clinic appointments, reports taking medications only when he remembers, smokes 15 cigarettes daily, and says he does not understand what his blood pressure readings mean. He lives alone and works two jobs.
questions.stem: Complete the diagram by selecting from the choices below.

options.text: Assess adherence, symptom management, tobacco use, and lifestyle
options.rationale: The named assessment priorities for patients with chronic illness.

options.text: Provide self-management education, including what his readings mean and how to respond
options.rationale: Self-management education builds the capability he uses between visits, which is where chronic illness is lived.

options.text: Arrange daily home nursing visits indefinitely
options.rationale: Creates dependence rather than capability, and does not address understanding.

options.text: Tell him non-adherence will lead to complications and document the warning
options.rationale: Warning is not education, and blame does not build self-management.

options.text: Ask his family to take over his medications
options.rationale: He lives alone, and removing him from his own care is not indicated.

options.text: A client with chronic disease requiring self-management support and health promotion
options.rationale: Combines the adherence, tobacco, and health literacy findings with the model's self-management focus.

options.text: A client in acute hypertensive crisis
options.rationale: Nothing in the scenario describes acute decompensation.

options.text: A client requiring immediate hospitalization
options.rationale: No acute indication is present.

options.text: A client who has declined all treatment
options.rationale: He is taking medications inconsistently, which is not refusal.

options.text: Blood pressure and glycemic control over time
options.rationale: The measures that show whether self-management is improving.

options.text: Understanding, checked through teach-back
options.rationale: He states he does not understand his readings, so confirmed understanding is the parameter that matters.

options.text: Serum amylase
options.rationale: Not relevant to these conditions.

options.text: Daily temperature
options.rationale: Not a monitoring priority here.

options.text: Visual acuity weekly
options.rationale: Eye examinations are important in diabetes but not as a weekly monitoring parameter.

questions.takeaway: Chronic illness care builds capability. Assess adherence and lifestyle, then teach for self-management.
questions.strategy: Two action options treat the client as the problem rather than the partner. Warning and taking over both fail for the same reason.

strategies: Client-centered option

steps.detail: Inconsistent adherence plus low health literacy in chronic disease.
Creates dependence instead of capability.
Neither builds self-management.

elimination.verdict: Actions A and B, condition A, parameters A and B.

questions.stem: A nurse cares for two clients from the same country of origin who hold very different beliefs about diet, family involvement, and treatment. She recognizes that what she learned about the group does not predict either individual. Which statement best describes culturally congruent care?

options.text: Care delivered according to the nurse's understanding of the patient's cultural group
options.rationale: Bases care on group knowledge rather than on this individual, which is how stereotyping enters.

options.text: Care based on the individual patient's beliefs, practices, and values
options.rationale: Culturally congruent care fits the person in front of you, which is why assessment rather than assumption is the method.

options.text: Care that treats every patient identically to ensure fairness
options.rationale: Identical care ignores the differences that culturally congruent care exists to address.

options.text: Care that follows the practices most common in the patient's country of origin
options.rationale: Country of origin does not determine an individual's beliefs or practices.

questions.takeaway: Culturally congruent care fits the individual, not the group.
questions.strategy: Any option that predicts a patient's beliefs from a group membership is wrong. Cultural knowledge tells you what to ask about, never what to conclude.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The question asks for the definition.
Substitutes group knowledge for the individual.
Identical care is not equitable care.
Infers practices from origin.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B. Culture is learned, shared, and constantly evolving, so it varies within any group.

questions.stem: A community health nurse maps why clients in one neighbourhood have worse outcomes than those a few miles away, despite using the same clinic. She considers the non-medical conditions in which they live, learn, work, and age. Which are Healthy People 2030 social determinant of health domains? Select all that apply.

options.text: Economic stability
options.rationale: Economic stability determines whether someone can afford medication, food, and time away from work, which shapes health before any clinical care begins.

options.text: Education
options.rationale: Education affects health literacy, employment, and income, so its effects on health run through several pathways at once.

options.text: Health care access
options.rationale: Access covers whether care exists nearby, whether it can be reached, and whether it can be afforded, which are three separate barriers.

options.text: Genetic predisposition
options.rationale: A biological factor, not a social determinant.

options.text: Neighborhood and built environment
options.rationale: Where someone lives determines their exposure to hazards and their access to food, transport, and safe places to be active.

options.text: Social and community context
options.rationale: Social and community context covers connection, discrimination, and support, all of which affect both health behaviour and outcomes.

questions.takeaway: Five domains: economic stability, education, health care access, neighborhood and built environment, social and community context.
questions.strategy: The exclusion in a social determinants item is usually the biological or clinical option.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The question asks which options are named domains.
Genetics is biological, not social.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, E, and F remain, which is the full set of five.

questions.stem: Two clients have the same diagnosis of rheumatoid arthritis. One continues working and describes it as an inconvenience; the other has withdrawn from her family and says she feels she has lost herself. The nurse recognizes that the biological process and the lived experience are different things. Which statement correctly distinguishes disease from illness?

options.text: Disease is the biological or psychological malfunction; illness is the individual and family reaction to it
options.rationale: Illness is shaped by cultural stigma and socially constructed meaning, which is why two people with the same disease experience it differently.

options.text: Disease is temporary and illness is permanent
options.rationale: Duration does not distinguish them.

options.text: Disease affects the body and illness affects only the mind
options.rationale: Illness is the reaction to disease, not a separate mental condition.

options.text: The two terms are interchangeable
options.rationale: The distinction is the point of the objective.

questions.takeaway: Disease is malfunction. Illness is the individual and family reaction, shaped by culture.
questions.strategy: This same distinction appears in the chronic illness chapter. When an idea recurs across chapters, it is being flagged as central.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The question asks how the two differ.
Duration is not the distinction.
Mischaracterizes illness.
The terms are distinct.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A: illness is shaped by cultural stigma and socially constructed meaning, which is why two people with the same disease experience it differently.

questions.scenario: A 62-year-old who recently immigrated attends clinic with a new diagnosis of hypertension. She speaks limited English. Her adult daughter offers to interpret. The client mentions she uses a herbal tea her mother made for high blood pressure.
questions.stem: For each nursing action, indicate whether it demonstrates cultural skill.

rows.text: Arrange a qualified medical interpreter rather than using the daughter
rows.rationale: Family members may lack medical vocabulary, may be uncomfortable with sensitive content, and may unintentionally alter the message.

rows.text: Ask what the client believes has caused her high blood pressure
rows.rationale: Listening to the patient's perception is the L in LEARN, and it is the starting point.

rows.text: Tell the client to stop the herbal tea immediately
rows.rationale: Beliefs are incorporated when safe and feasible. The action is to check for interactions, not to forbid.

rows.text: Check the herbal tea for interactions with the prescribed medication
rows.rationale: Incorporates the practice when it is safe to do so.

rows.text: Assume her health beliefs based on her country of origin
rows.rationale: Stereotyping. Cultural knowledge tells you what to ask about, never what to conclude.

rows.text: Use teach-back and plain language to confirm understanding
rows.rationale: Named strategies, with plain language meaning everyday words instead of clinical terms.

questions.takeaway: Ask, do not assume. Incorporate beliefs when safe and feasible, and confirm understanding with teach-back.
questions.strategy: The two wrong rows either forbid a practice without assessing it or predict beliefs from origin. Both patterns recur across cultural items.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Language barrier plus a traditional practice.
Check for interactions instead.
That is stereotyping.

elimination.verdict: Four rows demonstrate cultural skill and two do not.

questions.stem: A hospital reports its rates of falls, infections, and readmissions against nationally defined benchmarks, and the quality committee reviews where the organization sits relative to others. A staff nurse asks what these benchmarks actually are. Which statement describes core measures?

options.text: Evidence-based standards of care set by CMS and The Joint Commission
options.rationale: Scientifically researched standards aimed at reducing disparities and standardizing care.

options.text: Cultural practices that patients are expected to follow
options.rationale: Core measures apply to care delivery, not to patients' cultural practices.

options.text: The five constructs of cultural competence
options.rationale: Those belong to Campinha-Bacote's model.

options.text: A tool for measuring a nurse's implicit bias
options.rationale: Not what core measures are.

questions.takeaway: Core measures are evidence-based standards from CMS and The Joint Commission, aimed at reducing disparities.
questions.strategy: The purpose stated in the option matters. Core measures standardize care to reduce variation between groups.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The question asks what core measures are.
They govern care, not patients.
Belongs to a different model.
Not a bias measurement tool.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A: scientifically researched standards aimed at reducing disparities and standardizing care.

questions.stem: A nurse admits a client who recently arrived from another country, speaks limited English, and has brought a traditional preparation her sister sends her. The nurse wants the assessment to fit this client rather than assumptions about her background. Which strategies demonstrate cultural skill in practice? Select all that apply.

options.text: Self-exploration before the encounter
options.rationale: Named strategy, and it reflects awareness as the foundation.

options.text: Asking preferred name, background, and goals for the visit
options.rationale: Asking for the preferred name and the patient's goals starts the encounter from their perspective rather than from the chart's.

options.text: Assuming the patient's health beliefs from their country of origin
options.rationale: Stereotyping. Cultural knowledge tells you what to ask, never what to conclude.

options.text: Assessing health literacy
options.rationale: Named strategy, meaning the ability to find, understand, and use health information.

options.text: Using teach-back and plain language
options.rationale: Named strategies, with plain language meaning everyday words instead of clinical terms.

options.text: Storytelling
options.rationale: Named strategy for eliciting the patient's own account.

questions.takeaway: Self-exploration, ask preferred name and goals, storytelling, history, health literacy, culturally based assessment, teach-back and plain language.
questions.strategy: The wrong option in any cultural item is the one that predicts rather than asks.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The question asks which strategies demonstrate cultural skill.
Assumes beliefs from origin, which is stereotyping.

elimination.verdict: A, B, D, E, and F remain.

questions.stem: A client who immigrated twenty years ago tells the nurse her family celebrates holidays from both her birth country and her current one, cooks food from both traditions, and speaks two languages at home. Which term describes this?

options.text: Assimilation
options.rationale: Assimilation means the original culture is replaced by the new one. Hers is retained.

options.text: Acculturation
options.rationale: Adapting to a new culture while retaining the original.

options.text: Intersectionality
options.rationale: Describes how overlapping social identities interact with privilege and oppression.

options.text: Cultural desire
options.rationale: One of Campinha-Bacote's constructs, describing the provider's motivation.

questions.takeaway: Acculturation retains the original culture. Assimilation replaces it.
questions.strategy: The word retaining is the discriminator. If both cultures are present it is acculturation.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Both cultures are being observed.
Assimilation means replacement.
Describes overlapping identities, not cultural adaptation.
A provider construct.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B: adapting to a new culture while retaining the original.

questions.stem: A nurse finds herself frustrated by a client who declines a recommended treatment for reasons she does not share. Her preceptor points out that the client's view of health and the nurse's were each formed by different families, communities, and institutions. Which statement about worldview is accurate?

options.text: Worldview is fixed at birth and does not change
options.rationale: It is shaped over time by family, peers, community, media, and institutions.

options.text: The worldview of providers and patients may differ, and recognizing that gap is part of assessment
options.rationale: Named directly. The gap between worldviews is something the nurse assesses rather than assumes away.

options.text: Providers do not have a worldview when acting professionally
options.rationale: Everyone has one, which is why self-reflection is the foundation.

options.text: Worldview and religion are the same thing
options.rationale: Religion may contribute to worldview but does not define it.

questions.takeaway: Worldview is learned from family, peers, community, media, and institutions, and yours may differ from the patient's.
questions.strategy: Options claiming a professional is neutral or without perspective are wrong throughout this chapter.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The question asks for an accurate statement.
Worldview develops over time.
Providers have worldviews too.
Conflates two different things.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B: named directly.

questions.stem: A 67-year-old with limited English proficiency needs teaching about a newly prescribed medication before discharge. Her adult daughter offers to interpret, a qualified interpreter is available, and written material exists only in English. Which action best demonstrates cultural skill?

options.text: Ask the patient's adult daughter to interpret so the teaching can start immediately
options.rationale: Family members may lack medical vocabulary, may be uncomfortable with sensitive content, and may unintentionally alter the message.

options.text: Use a qualified interpreter, plain language, and teach-back to confirm understanding
options.rationale: Three named strategies: assessing health literacy, teach-back, and plain language, meaning everyday words instead of clinical terms.

options.text: Provide written instructions in English and ask the patient to read them later
options.rationale: Assumes reading ability and does not confirm understanding.

options.text: Speak more slowly and loudly in English
options.rationale: Volume does not address a language barrier.

questions.takeaway: Qualified interpreter, plain language, and teach-back. Never a family member, especially a child.
questions.strategy: Key word best. All four options might get information across; only one confirms it was understood.

strategies: Priority key word

steps.detail: Limited English proficiency and new medication teaching.
Family interpreters risk vocabulary gaps and altered messages.
Assumes literacy and confirms nothing.
Does not address the barrier.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B. Teach-back is what turns teaching into confirmed understanding.

questions.scenario: A community health nurse reviews outcome data for two neighbourhoods served by the same clinic. Neighbourhood A has limited public transport, no grocery store selling fresh produce, and higher unemployment.

rows: Households within 1 km of fresh produce

questions.stem: Which conclusion does the nurse draw?

options.text: Residents of neighbourhood A are less motivated to manage their health
options.rationale: Locates the cause in individuals and ignores the structural differences shown in the final row.

options.text: The data show a health disparity linked to social determinants of health
options.rationale: A measurable difference between population groups, tied to neighbourhood and built environment, economic stability, and health care access.

options.text: The differences reflect genetic variation between the two populations
options.rationale: Nothing in the data supports a genetic explanation, and the access measures explain the pattern.

options.text: The clinic should reduce services to neighbourhood A given the low uptake
options.rationale: Would widen the disparity rather than address it.

questions.takeaway: A health disparity is measurable, between groups, and tied to the conditions in which people live, learn, work, and age.
questions.strategy: The last row is the key. It converts an outcome difference into an access explanation, which is what makes this a disparity rather than a choice.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Three outcome measures and one access measure move together.
Blames individuals for structural conditions.
No genetic evidence, and access explains the pattern.
Reducing services widens the gap.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B. Core measures exist partly to reduce differences like these.

questions.stem: A nurse reviews why a client with diabetes has repeatedly run out of medication. He works two jobs, has no car, and the nearest pharmacy is a bus ride away. She considers which of his circumstances are non-medical conditions shaping his health. Which is a social determinant of health?

options.text: Serum cholesterol level
options.rationale: A clinical measure, not a non-medical condition shaping health.

options.text: Neighborhood and built environment
options.rationale: One of the five Healthy People 2030 domains, alongside economic stability, education, health care access, and social and community context.

options.text: Family history of diabetes
options.rationale: A genetic and clinical factor rather than a social determinant.

options.text: Body mass index
options.rationale: A clinical measure.

questions.takeaway: Social determinants are the non-medical conditions where people live, learn, work, and age.
questions.strategy: If the option is something you would measure in a lab or on a scale, it is not a social determinant.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The question asks for a social determinant.
A laboratory value.
Genetic and clinical.
A clinical measurement.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B. The five domains are economic stability, education, health care access, neighborhood and built environment, and social and community context.

questions.scenario: A client with newly diagnosed diabetes tells the nurse he believes the illness was caused by a period of intense stress at work, and that the medication will not help until the stress resolves. The nurse has explained the role of insulin resistance.
questions.stem: Complete the sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence: The nurse's next step in the LEARN model is to [[1]], which means [[2]].

options.text: acknowledge
options.rationale: After listening and explaining, the A comes next.

options.text: listen
options.rationale: Listening has already happened; the client has described his perception.

options.text: negotiate
options.rationale: Negotiation comes after acknowledging and recommending.

options.text: recognize the differences between the two perceptions but build on the similarities
options.rationale: The instruction is specific: name both, and use the shared ground as the foundation.

options.text: correct the client's understanding before continuing
options.rationale: Correction is not acknowledgment, and it discards the common ground.

options.text: document the disagreement and involve the provider
options.rationale: Neither is what the A step directs.

questions.takeaway: LEARN: Listen, Explain, Acknowledge, Recommend, Negotiate. Acknowledge names similarities as well as differences.
questions.strategy: The step people drop is building on the similarities. Here stress genuinely does affect glucose, so there is real common ground to work from.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Listening and explaining have both occurred.
Acknowledge covers differences and similarities.
Correcting is not acknowledging.

elimination.verdict: Blank 1 is A and blank 2 is A.

questions.stem: A nurse cares for a client who is an older immigrant woman living on a low income with limited English. Her preceptor notes that no single one of these characteristics explains her outcomes, and that they act together. Which statement describes intersectionality?

options.text: Social identities such as race, gender, and class overlap, with privilege and oppression acting as interlocking systems
options.rationale: Multiple overlapping identities shape health outcomes together rather than separately.

options.text: Patients should be assessed for one primary cultural identity
options.rationale: Reduces a person to a single identity, which is what the framework argues against.

options.text: Cultural groups can be ranked by health risk
options.rationale: Not what the framework describes, and it would reinforce stereotyping.

options.text: Health outcomes are determined primarily by genetics
options.rationale: Contradicts the social determinants framing.

questions.takeaway: Overlapping identities interact. You cannot understand outcomes by looking at one alone.
questions.strategy: When a framework is about complexity, options that simplify to a single factor are wrong.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The question asks for the description of a named framework.
Reduces the person to one identity.
Ranking groups reinforces stereotyping.
Contradicts social determinants.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A: multiple overlapping identities shape health outcomes together rather than separately.

questions.stem: A public health nurse compares two districts served by the same hospital. In one, adults are diagnosed with diabetes years later and at a more advanced stage, and fewer attend screening. That district also has less transport and fewer places to buy fresh food. Which situation best illustrates a health disparity?

options.text: Two patients with the same diagnosis choose different treatments
options.rationale: Different choices reflect autonomy, not a disparity.

options.text: A measurable difference in health outcomes between population groups linked to social disadvantage
options.rationale: A health disparity is a measurable difference, and it is tied to the conditions in which people live, learn, work, and age.

options.text: A patient declines a recommended screening
options.rationale: An individual decision, not a population-level difference.

options.text: A hospital reports higher costs than a neighbouring facility
options.rationale: An economic comparison between institutions, not a health outcome between populations.

questions.takeaway: A health disparity is measurable, between groups, and tied to social disadvantage.
questions.strategy: Disparity items are answered at the population level. Options describing one patient's choice are the wrong scale.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The question asks which situation illustrates a disparity.
Individual autonomy.
An individual decision.
An institutional cost comparison.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B. Core measures exist partly to reduce these differences.

questions.scenario: A client who speaks limited English is admitted for surgery tomorrow. His teenage son offers to interpret, saying he does this for his father at every appointment. The consent discussion, preoperative teaching, and a medication history all need to be completed.
questions.stem: Which nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Arrange a qualified medical interpreter for all three conversations
options.rationale: Required wherever there is a language barrier, and consent especially depends on accurate understanding.

options.text: Explain to the son and father why a professional interpreter is used
options.rationale: Declining the offer without explanation may be experienced as rejection of the family.

options.text: Allow the son to interpret the medication history only, since it is straightforward
options.rationale: The concerns apply regardless of topic: vocabulary gaps, discomfort, and unintentional alteration.

options.text: Use plain language and teach-back through the interpreter
options.rationale: Plain language avoids clinical terms the interpreter may render inconsistently, and teach-back confirms understanding rather than assuming it.

options.text: Ask the son to interpret if no interpreter is available within the hour
options.rationale: Convenience does not change the standard, and consent is the conversation least suited to it.

options.text: Document that an interpreter was used and how understanding was confirmed
options.rationale: Records both the accommodation and the confirmation of understanding.

options.text: Assess the client's health literacy through the interpreter
options.rationale: A named cultural skill strategy, meaning the ability to find, understand, and use health information.

questions.takeaway: Never a family member, especially a child, and never for part of a conversation because it seems simple.
questions.strategy: Both wrong options carve out an exception based on convenience or topic. Neither exception exists.

strategies: Eliminate absolutes

steps.detail: A minor is offering to interpret for consent and teaching.
The concerns apply to every topic.
Availability does not lower the standard.

elimination.verdict: A, B, D, F, and G are selected.

questions.stem: A client with newly diagnosed diabetes tells the nurse he believes the illness was caused by a period of intense stress at work and will resolve when the stress does. The nurse has listened to his account and explained the role of insulin resistance. Which action reflects the A in LEARN?

options.text: Listening without judgment to the patient's perception
options.rationale: That is L, listen, using encouraging comments such as tell me more.

options.text: Explaining the nurse's perception of the problem
options.rationale: That is E, explain.

options.text: Acknowledging both the differences and the similarities between the two perceptions
options.rationale: The A is acknowledge, and the instruction is specific: recognize the differences, but build on the similarities.

options.text: Negotiating a plan the patient can accept
options.rationale: That is N, negotiate.

questions.takeaway: LEARN: Listen, Explain, Acknowledge, Recommend, Negotiate. Acknowledge means naming similarities as well as differences.
questions.strategy: The step people drop is building on the similarities. Acknowledging only the differences leaves nothing to negotiate from.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The question asks for one specific letter.
That is L.
That is E.
That is N.

elimination.verdict: That leaves C: the A is acknowledge, and the instruction is specific: recognize the differences, but build on the similarities.

questions.stem: A nurse educator explains why culturally congruent care is described as a growing rather than a specialist competency, showing population projections for the coming decades. Which changes are expected by 2060? Select all that apply.

options.text: The racial and ethnic minority population reaches 32%
options.rationale: Reaching 32% means culturally congruent care stops being a specialist skill and becomes ordinary practice.

options.text: The multiracial population grows by 200%
options.rationale: A 200% increase means more patients whose identity does not fit a single category, which is exactly why you ask rather than assume.

options.text: The Asian population doubles
options.rationale: A doubling of any population group changes who is in front of you, and the projection is the reason this competency is described as growing.

options.text: The population aged 65 and over declines
options.rationale: Reversed. It grows from 49 million in 2016 to 95 million in 2060.

options.text: The population aged 65 and over roughly doubles
options.rationale: From 49 million to 95 million.

questions.takeaway: By 2060: minority population 32%, multiracial up 200%, Asian population doubles, and those over 65 nearly double.
questions.strategy: When two options state opposite directions for the same population, one of them is the answer and the other is the trap.

strategies: Opposite pair, look closely

steps.detail: The question asks which projections are expected.
States the direction of the over-65 change backwards.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, and E remain. These demographics are why culturally congruent care is a growing competency.

questions.stem: A nurse notices she consistently spends less time with clients who remind her of a difficult family member, though she has never made a conscious decision to do so. Her preceptor explains that everyone carries such patterns and that the responsibility lies in recognizing them. Which statement about implicit bias is accurate?

options.text: It is a conscious choice that a nurse can simply decide to stop
options.rationale: Implicit bias is unconscious and outside our direct control, which is precisely why it needs deliberate management.

options.text: It is unconscious and shaped by background and experience, and we are responsible for recognizing and managing it
options.rationale: Outside our control in its formation, and within our responsibility in its management. It drives quick judgments.

options.text: It affects only providers who hold prejudiced views
options.rationale: Everyone has implicit bias, which is why self-reflection is universal rather than remedial.

options.text: It has no measurable effect on clinical decisions
options.rationale: Providers can unintentionally act on stereotypes, leading to biased diagnoses or treatment.

questions.takeaway: Implicit bias is unconscious in origin and your responsibility in management.
questions.strategy: The distinction being tested is between something you cause and something you are accountable for. Options collapsing the two are wrong.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The question asks for an accurate statement.
Implicit bias is not a conscious choice.
Only limits it to prejudiced providers.
Contradicts the effect on diagnosis and treatment.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B. Standardized tools and self-reflection are how it is managed.

questions.stem: A nursing school teaches a model in which developing cultural competence is described as an ongoing process rather than an achievement, beginning with the provider examining her own assumptions. Which are the five constructs of Campinha-Bacote's model of cultural competence?

options.text: Awareness, knowledge, skill, encounters, and desire
options.rationale: The five constructs, with awareness as the foundation and desire as the motivation that drives the rest.

options.text: Listen, explain, acknowledge, recommend, negotiate
options.rationale: That is the LEARN model.

options.text: Assessment, diagnosis, planning, implementation, evaluation
options.rationale: The nursing process.

options.text: Economic stability, education, health care access, environment, social context
options.rationale: The five Healthy People 2030 social determinant domains.

questions.takeaway: Cultural awareness, knowledge, skill, encounters, and desire.
questions.strategy: Every distractor here is a real five-part framework from this course. Match the set to the name in the stem.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The question names a specific model.
LEARN.
The nursing process.
Social determinant domains.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A: the five constructs, with awareness as the foundation and desire as the motivation that drives the rest.

questions.scenario: A 58-year-old admitted with pneumonia declines the prescribed diet, saying it conflicts with a religious observance she keeps. She has eaten little in two days. Her family asks whether a relative may bring food from home. The nurse notices a colleague charted that the client is non-compliant.
questions.stem: Complete the diagram by selecting from the choices below.

options.text: Assess the client's dietary requirements and arrange food that meets them
options.rationale: Incorporating beliefs when safe and feasible is what culturally congruent care means in practice.

options.text: Correct the documentation to describe the client's stated reason factually
options.rationale: Non-compliant is a judgment. Documentation records what the client declined and the reason she gave.

options.text: Explain that hospital diets cannot be altered
options.rationale: Inaccurate, and it treats the system as fixed rather than the care as individualized.

options.text: Ask the family to persuade the client to eat what is provided
options.rationale: Recruits the family to apply pressure the nurse may not apply herself.

options.text: Document the refusal and take no further action
options.rationale: Leaves a client eating little for a third day.

options.text: A client with unmet nutritional needs due to care that does not fit her beliefs and practices
options.rationale: The problem is the fit between the care and the client, not the client's cooperation.

options.text: A client who is refusing all treatment
options.rationale: She is declining one diet for a stated reason, not refusing care.

options.text: A client with a swallowing disorder
options.rationale: Nothing describes a swallowing problem.

options.text: A client with a diagnosed eating disorder
options.rationale: Not supported by any finding.

options.text: Nutritional intake and weight
options.rationale: The measures that show whether the adjusted plan is working.

options.text: The client's report of whether the plan fits her practices
options.rationale: Culturally congruent care is judged by fit with the individual, so the client is the source.

options.text: Serum potassium every hour
options.rationale: Not indicated by anything in the scenario.

options.text: Family satisfaction scores
options.rationale: Not a clinical monitoring parameter.

options.text: Room temperature
options.rationale: Unrelated.

questions.takeaway: Culturally congruent care fits the individual. When care does not fit, change the care, not the client.
questions.strategy: The word non-compliant in a stem is almost always a signal that the care, not the client, is the problem. It is also a documentation error.

strategies: Client-centered option

steps.detail: Care that conflicts with the client's practices, producing poor intake.

steps.action: Cut persuasion and refusal to adapt
steps.detail: Both push the client toward care that does not fit.
Poor intake continues.

elimination.verdict: Actions A and B, condition A, parameters A and B.

questions.stem: A nurse is assigned four older adults on a medical unit. One runs a business and drove himself in, one requires assistance with all activities of daily living, and two fall between. All are over 80. Which principle should guide her approach?

options.text: Most findings in an older adult represent disease requiring treatment
options.rationale: Reverses the guidance. You should not assume older adults have signs, symptoms, or behaviors representing disease.

options.text: Older adults vary widely in physiological, cognitive, and psychosocial health and in functional ability
options.rationale: Variability is the organizing idea of the chapter, and chronic conditions add to the complexity of assessment and care.

options.text: Care can be standardized because age-related changes are predictable
options.rationale: Ignores the wide range of functional ability among people of the same age.

options.text: Independence should be limited to reduce the risk of injury
options.rationale: Opposite of the guidance to identify strengths and abilities and encourage independence.

questions.takeaway: Identify an older adult's strengths and abilities and encourage independence.
questions.strategy: Options that standardize care for a group are almost always wrong in a chapter built on variability.

strategies: Eliminate absolutes

steps.detail: The question asks for the organizing principle.
Assumes findings mean disease.
Standardization contradicts variability.
Restricting independence contradicts the goal.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B: variability is the organizing idea of the chapter, and chronic conditions add to the complexity of assessment and care.

questions.topic: Acute change in an older adult
questions.scenario: An 84-year-old admitted three days ago for a hip fracture is newly confused and pulling at her intravenous line. She was oriented on admission. Temperature 37.0 C, heart rate 104, blood pressure 102/58, oxygen saturation 91% on room air. Urine in the catheter bag is dark and cloudy. She has received two doses of an opioid analgesic in the past six hours.
questions.stem: Complete the diagram by selecting from the choices below.

options.text: Assess vital signs, oxygen saturation, and level of consciousness
options.rationale: A sudden change is a red flag and the cause must be established. Poor oxygenation is already visible at 91%.

options.text: Review recently administered medications with the provider
options.rationale: Medications are a named contributor to delirium, and two recent opioid doses are a plausible cause.

options.text: Apply wrist restraints to protect the intravenous line
options.rationale: Restraints worsen delirium and agitation and are a last resort after least restrictive measures.

options.text: Reorient her once and document that she remains confused
options.rationale: Records the problem without investigating a reversible cause.

options.text: Request a sedative to settle her for the night
options.rationale: Adds to the medication burden that may be producing the confusion.

options.text: Delirium from a potentially reversible cause
options.rationale: Acute onset with fluctuation in a hospitalized older adult, with hypoxia, possible infection, and opioids all present.

options.text: Progression of dementia
options.rationale: Dementia is chronic and progressive over years. She was oriented three days ago.

options.text: An expected change of aging
options.rationale: Age is not a diagnosis, and a change from baseline is clinically significant.

options.text: Depression
options.rationale: Presents with mood change, withdrawal, and loss of interest rather than acute inattention.

options.text: Level of consciousness and orientation
options.rationale: The features that define delirium and show whether it is resolving.

options.text: Oxygen saturation and vital signs
options.rationale: Hypoxia is already present at 91% and is a named contributor.

options.text: Serum cholesterol
options.rationale: Unrelated to acute confusion.

options.text: Hair and nail condition
options.rationale: Not a monitoring parameter here.

options.text: Weekly weight
options.rationale: Too slow to track an acute change.

questions.takeaway: Sudden confusion in an older adult is delirium until proven otherwise, and it has a cause.
questions.strategy: Two options in the action pool make the problem worse while looking like management. Sedation and restraint both increase delirium.

strategies: Assessment before intervention

steps.detail: Oriented three days ago, confused now. Acute means delirium.
Both worsen delirium.
Does not investigate the cause.

elimination.verdict: Actions A and B, condition A, parameters A and B.

questions.stem: A nurse tells a colleague there is no point teaching an 88-year-old client about her new medication because of her age, though the client is alert, manages her own finances, and has asked about the drug twice. This statement is an example of which concept?

options.text: Ageism
options.rationale: Discrimination against people due to increasing age, and it is banned by current laws. Here it removes a patient's right to education based on age alone.

options.text: Reality orientation
options.rationale: A communication technique that restates time, place, and person.

options.text: Functional decline
options.rationale: A measurable change in the ability to perform daily activities.

options.text: Reminiscence
options.rationale: A technique using recall of past events.

questions.takeaway: Ageism is discrimination by age, and nurses must first assess their own attitudes toward older adults and toward their own aging.
questions.strategy: Statements that withhold care, teaching, or choice on the basis of age alone are ageism, however practical they sound.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Teaching is withheld because of age, not because of any assessed barrier.
All are techniques or findings, not attitudes.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A: discrimination against people due to increasing age, and it is banned by current laws.

questions.stem: A nurse cares for four older adults: one confused after surgery who can be reoriented, one with advanced dementia who believes she must collect her children from school, one who enjoys describing his years working on the railway, and one frightened before a procedure. Match each nursing approach with the technique it BEST demonstrates. Each term is used only once.

items.text: A nurse gently restates the day, the location, and who she is for a patient with post-operative confusion
items.rationale: Restates time, place, and person, and it fits acute, reversible confusion where the patient can be reoriented.

items.text: A nurse responds to the feeling behind a statement rather than correcting a patient with advanced dementia who believes she must collect her children
items.rationale: Acknowledges the emotion rather than the fact, and it fits chronic irreversible confusion where reorientation causes distress.

items.text: A nurse encourages a patient to talk about the years he spent working on the railway
items.rationale: Uses recall of past events to support identity and self-worth.

items.text: A nurse rests a hand on the forearm of a patient who is frightened before a procedure
items.rationale: A named psychosocial intervention, used deliberately and with attention to the patient's response.

questions.takeaway: Reality orientation for acute reversible confusion. Validation therapy for chronic irreversible confusion.
questions.strategy: The pair students confuse is orientation and validation, and reversibility is what separates them. Reorienting a patient with advanced dementia repeatedly is distressing and ineffective.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Post-operative confusion can be reoriented.
Advanced dementia calls for validation.
Recall of the past is reminiscence; physical contact is touch.

questions.note: Two of these techniques address confusion. Decide whether the confusion is reversible before choosing between them.

questions.stem: An older adult admitted three days ago for pneumonia is now inattentive, with symptoms that fluctuate through the day and periods of altered consciousness. Which condition does the nurse suspect?

options.text: Delirium
options.rationale: An acute confusional state. Acute onset, fluctuation, inattention, and altered consciousness together.

options.text: Dementia
options.rationale: Generalized impairment of intellectual functioning that interferes with social and occupational functioning, and it develops over years.

options.text: Depression
options.rationale: Presents with mood changes, withdrawal, and loss of interest.

options.text: An expected change of aging
options.rationale: Age is not a diagnosis and this is a change from baseline.

questions.takeaway: Delirium is acute and fluctuating. Dementia is progressive and chronic. Depression is mood and withdrawal.
questions.strategy: Sort the three Ds by time course before symptom lists. Onset separates them faster than anything else.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Three days, fluctuating, inattentive.
Dementia is chronic and progressive.
No mood or interest change described.
A change from baseline is significant.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A. Look for the cause: infection, oxygenation, medications, acute illness.

questions.scenario: The nurse reviews assessment findings for three older adults on the unit.
questions.stem: For each finding, click to specify whether it is consistent with delirium, dementia, or depression. Each finding may support more than one condition.

rows.text: Acute onset over hours to days
rows.rationale: Only delirium develops acutely. Dementia is progressive over years and depression develops over weeks to months.

rows.text: Impaired memory
rows.rationale: All three affect memory, which is why memory alone never distinguishes them.

rows.text: Symptoms that fluctuate through the day
rows.rationale: Fluctuation is the signature of delirium.

rows.text: Withdrawal and loss of interest in usual activities
rows.rationale: The named presentation of depression in older adults.

rows.text: Altered level of consciousness
rows.rationale: Consciousness is clear in dementia and in depression.

rows.text: Gradual decline in the ability to manage finances and medications
rows.rationale: Progressive loss of instrumental activities is the dementia pattern.
