rows.text: Potentially reversible when the underlying cause is treated
rows.rationale: Delirium resolves when the cause is corrected and depression responds to treatment. Dementia does not reverse.

questions.constraint: Each column must have at least one response selected.
questions.takeaway: Onset and consciousness separate the three Ds. Memory does not.
questions.strategy: The row that catches people is impaired memory, because it belongs to all three. Look for the rows that belong to only one.
questions.note: Each column must have at least one response selected, and one finding belongs to all three.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Acute onset, fluctuation, and altered consciousness are delirium alone.
Memory impairment appears in all three.
Two of the three can improve with treatment.

elimination.verdict: Delirium claims four rows, dementia two, depression two, with overlap on memory and reversibility.

questions.stem: An 82-year-old has become withdrawn since her husband's death six months ago, eats little, and has stopped attending activities she previously enjoyed. Her cognition is intact and her onset was gradual. Which tool does the nurse use to screen her?

options.text: The Geriatric Depression Scale
options.rationale: An easy-to-use screening tool used in conjunction with an interview with the older adult.

options.text: The Glasgow Coma Scale
options.rationale: Assesses level of consciousness.

options.text: The Braden Scale
options.rationale: Assesses pressure injury risk.

options.text: The Morse Fall Scale
options.rationale: Assesses fall risk.

questions.takeaway: The Geriatric Depression Scale, used alongside an interview rather than instead of one.
questions.strategy: Distractors for tool items are usually real instruments measuring something else. Match the tool to what it measures.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Screening for depression specifically.
Consciousness, skin risk, and fall risk.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A: an easy-to-use screening tool used in conjunction with an interview with the older adult.

questions.scenario: An 86-year-old is admitted for observation after a fall at home. The nurse completes a head-to-toe assessment.
questions.stem: For each finding, indicate whether it is an EXPECTED change of aging or a finding that REQUIRES further assessment.

rows.text: Skin has lost resilience and moisture
rows.rationale: A named integumentary change of aging.

rows.text: Reduced bowel sounds on auscultation
rows.rationale: Peristalsis slows with age, producing reduced sounds. Absent sounds would be a different matter.

rows.text: New urinary incontinence
rows.rationale: Incontinence is abnormal and typically embarrassing, and it is more common in women but occurs in men too. Common is not the same as expected.

rows.text: Slower voluntary reflexes and less ability to respond to multiple stimuli
rows.rationale: A named neurological change.

rows.text: Confusion beginning this morning
rows.rationale: Sudden confusion is a red flag, and delirium is a named risk in acute care.

rows.text: Increased anteroposterior diameter of the thorax
rows.rationale: A named change alongside decreased respiratory muscle strength.

questions.takeaway: Expected changes are gradual. Sudden change is investigated, and incontinence is abnormal at any age.
questions.strategy: Read each row for the words new or sudden. Those move a finding out of the expected column regardless of what it describes.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Gradual changes are expected.
Frequently dismissed as aging and named as abnormal.
Onset this morning is acute.

elimination.verdict: Four rows expected, two require assessment.

questions.stem: A nurse assesses an 80-year-old who managed independently until a recent admission and now needs help dressing and bathing. She considers what functional status covers and what a decline in it signals. Which understanding guides this assessment?

options.text: Functional status refers only to physical ability to walk
options.rationale: Too narrow. It includes physical, psychological, cognitive, and social domains.

options.text: A decline in function is usually linked to illness or to disease and degree of chronicity
options.rationale: Which is why a decline prompts a search for a cause rather than acceptance as aging.

options.text: Functional decline in an older adult is expected and does not require intervention
options.rationale: Interventions focus on maintaining, restoring, and maximizing functional status.

options.text: Functional status is assessed only at discharge
options.rationale: Baseline function is needed on admission to recognize any change.

questions.takeaway: Function spans physical, psychological, cognitive, and social domains, and decline points at illness rather than age.
questions.strategy: The goal named is to maintain independence while preserving safety and dignity. Options that accept decline are wrong.

strategies: Eliminate absolutes

steps.detail: The question asks what guides functional assessment.
Only walking is too narrow.
Contradicts the intervention goal.
Only at discharge loses the baseline.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B: which is why a decline prompts a search for a cause rather than acceptance as aging.

questions.stem: A nurse works with older adults in a community setting and finds that many are managing significant transitions at the same time: leaving work, moving home, losing a partner, and renegotiating relationships with grown children. Which situations represent developmental tasks associated with older adulthood? Select all that apply.

options.text: Adjusting to retirement
options.rationale: Retirement removes a role, a routine, and often a sense of usefulness at the same time, which is why it is a developmental task rather than an event.

options.text: Coping with a change of residence
options.rationale: Moving means losing familiar surroundings and established routines, and the loss of control is what makes it a task to work through.

options.text: Coping with the death of a spouse
options.rationale: Losing a spouse removes a partner, a support system, and often the household income together.

options.text: Establishing a career identity
options.rationale: A task of young adulthood, not older adulthood.

options.text: Adjusting to changing relationships with adult children
options.rationale: The relationship shifts as adult children take on decisions the parent used to make, which changes both roles.

questions.takeaway: These tasks involve varying degrees of change and loss in health, relationships, usefulness, socialization, income, and independent living.
questions.strategy: One option in a developmental task item usually belongs to a different life stage. Identify the outlier.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Tasks of older adulthood specifically.
Career identity belongs to young adulthood.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, and E are selected.

questions.stem: A nursing student assumes she will encounter older adults mainly on hospital units. Her instructor points out that most older adults live and receive care elsewhere, and lists the range of places a nurse may meet them. In which settings does the nurse encounter older adult clients?

options.text: Acute care hospitals only
options.rationale: Limiting the answer to hospitals excludes the community settings where most older adults actually live and receive care.

options.text: Private homes, apartments, retirement communities, adult day care centers, assisted-living facilities, and senior living communities
options.rationale: The named range, and nurses and social workers help older adults and families review care options.

options.text: Long-term care facilities only
options.rationale: Excludes the community settings where most older adults live.

options.text: Only settings where skilled nursing is provided
options.rationale: Excludes independent and community living.

questions.takeaway: Older adults are cared for across a wide range of community and institutional settings.
questions.strategy: Three options here contain only. In a chapter emphasizing breadth, that word is the tell.

strategies: Eliminate absolutes

steps.detail: Where nurses encounter older adults.
Each restricts the range with only.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B: the named range, and nurses and social workers help older adults and families review care options.

questions.stem: An 84-year-old admitted two days ago becomes acutely confused during the evening shift. She was oriented on admission. Place the nurse's actions in the correct order, from FIRST to LAST.

options.text: Assess the patient, including vital signs, oxygen saturation, and level of consciousness
options.rationale: You establish what is happening before deciding what it means. Poor oxygenation and infection are named contributors.

options.text: Review the medication record for recently administered or newly started agents
options.rationale: Medications are a named contributing factor and are among the fastest reversible causes to identify.

options.text: Notify the health care provider of the change from baseline and the assessment findings
options.rationale: The provider needs the findings in order to prescribe investigation or treatment.

options.text: Implement safety measures using the least restrictive interventions available
options.rationale: Safety is managed while the cause is being investigated, and restraints are a last resort.

options.text: Document the change, the assessment, the notification, and the interventions
options.rationale: The record closes the sequence so the next nurse knows what changed and what was done.

questions.takeaway: Assess, look for reversible causes, notify, keep her safe with the least restrictive measure, document.
questions.strategy: Sudden confusion items are answered by remembering that delirium has a cause. The sequence is find it, report it, then manage safety.

strategies: Assessment before intervention

steps.detail: Assessment precedes every other action.
Documentation closes the sequence.
Medications, then notification, then safety measures.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D, E.

questions.note: Safety matters throughout, but consider which action must come FIRST when the cause is unknown.

questions.stem: An 81-year-old is transferred to a restorative care setting after hospitalization for pneumonia. She walked independently before admission and now requires assistance, but is expected to regain her previous level of function. What is the goal of this care?

options.text: To regain or improve the prior level of independence in activities of daily living and instrumental activities of daily living
options.rationale: Restorative care covers continuation of recovery from acute illness and support of chronic conditions, with the focus on remaining functional and safe within the living environment.

options.text: To provide care for a need that is not expected to improve
options.rationale: Describes continuing care. The distinction is whether improvement is expected.

options.text: To provide short-term relief for the family caregiver
options.rationale: Describes respite care.

options.text: To manage an acute episode of illness
options.rationale: Describes acute care.

questions.takeaway: Restorative care expects improvement. Continuing care supports a need that will not end.
questions.strategy: The distinction between restorative and continuing care is decided by whether improvement is expected, not by the setting.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Recovery after an acute illness.
That is continuing care.
That is respite.
That is acute care.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A: restorative care covers continuation of recovery from acute illness and support of chronic conditions, with the focus on remaining functional and safe within the living environment.

questions.stem: A nurse plans care for an older adult who has become withdrawn since her husband's death, is frightened by procedures, and has lost confidence in her appearance since losing weight. The nurse reviews which areas fall under psychosocial concerns. Which topics does the chapter identify? Select all that apply.

options.text: Elder mistreatment
options.rationale: Elder mistreatment is psychosocial because the harm operates through the relationship, and the nurse may be the only person who sees it.

options.text: Therapeutic communication and touch
options.rationale: Communication and touch are how the nurse reaches an older adult whose hearing, vision, or cognition has changed.

options.text: Reality orientation and validation therapy
options.rationale: Both named, and they apply to different kinds of confusion.

options.text: Osteoporosis screening
options.rationale: A physiological concern under Healthy People 2030, not a psychosocial one.

options.text: Reminiscence
options.rationale: Named, using recall of past events.

options.text: Body image interventions
options.rationale: Body image interventions matter because aging changes appearance and function, and the response to that is psychosocial rather than physical.

questions.takeaway: Psychosocial concerns include mistreatment, communication, touch, orientation, validation, reminiscence, and body image.
questions.strategy: One option here is a real concern from the same chapter placed in the wrong category. Check which heading it belongs under.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Psychosocial concerns specifically.
Osteoporosis is a physiological concern.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, E, and F are selected.

questions.stem: A nursing student says she finds it difficult to work with older adults because they remind her of her own aging. Which response by the nurse BEST reflects the chapter's guidance?

options.text: "You should request assignments on a different unit."
options.rationale: Avoidance, and it leaves the attitude unexamined.

options.text: "Nurses must assess their own attitudes toward older adults and toward their own aging, and forming positive attitudes is a priority."
options.rationale: Attitudes come from personal experiences, education, employment experiences, and the attitudes of coworkers and institutions, so they can be examined and changed.

options.text: "Most nurses feel that way and it passes with experience."
options.rationale: Normalizes without addressing, and experience alone does not change an unexamined attitude.

options.text: "Focus on the tasks and try not to think about it."
options.rationale: Suppression rather than reflection, and it models the avoidance the chapter warns against.

questions.takeaway: Forming positive attitudes toward older adults and gaining specialized knowledge about aging are priorities for all nurses.
questions.strategy: Options that avoid, normalize, or suppress a professional attitude problem are wrong. The answer names the reflective work.

strategies: Client-centered option

steps.detail: A student naming her own discomfort.
Avoidance.
Normalizes without addressing.
Suppression.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B: attitudes come from personal experiences, education, employment experiences, and the attitudes of coworkers and institutions, so they can be examined and changed.

questions.stem: A nurse manager reviews harm data for older adults admitted to her medical unit over the past year, looking at what happened to them during hospitalization rather than what brought them in. Which adverse events pose increased risk for older adults in acute care settings? Select all that apply.

options.text: Delirium
options.rationale: Named, and common two to three days after admission.

options.text: Dehydration
options.rationale: Dehydration develops readily because thirst is blunted, bladder capacity is reduced, and access to fluids in hospital depends on staff.

options.text: Malnutrition
options.rationale: Malnutrition follows from missed meals, held diets, unfamiliar food, and reduced taste and smell.

options.text: Health care-associated infections
options.rationale: Health care-associated infections are more likely because immune function declines and hospitalization brings invasive devices.

options.text: Improved functional independence
options.rationale: Hospitalization commonly reduces function through immobility and deconditioning, not improves it.

options.text: Falls
options.rationale: Named, alongside urinary incontinence and loss of tissue integrity.

questions.takeaway: Acute care itself creates risk: delirium, dehydration, malnutrition, infection, incontinence, skin breakdown, and falls.
questions.strategy: One option in this set describes a benefit. In a risk item, that is the exclusion.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The question asks which adverse events pose increased risk.
Improved independence is an outcome, not an adverse event.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D, and F are selected.

questions.stem: A nurse plans care for an 83-year-old admitted with pneumonia who also has arthritis, lives with her daughter, and is anxious about losing her independence. The nurse sets goals with the client and her daughter rather than for them. Which statement describes gerontological nursing assessment?

options.text: It focuses on physiological findings, since psychosocial issues are outside nursing scope
options.rationale: Assessment takes into account the interrelation between physical and psychosocial aspects of aging.

options.text: It addresses mutually established goals for the older adult, the family, and health care team members
options.rationale: Mutually established is the operative phrase, and the assessment is tailored to the older person.

options.text: It uses the same approach and parameters as for younger adults without adjustment
options.rationale: Techniques and parameters are adapted to accommodate normal changes associated with aging.

options.text: It measures disease severity as the primary outcome
options.rationale: The effects of disease and disability on current functional status are what matter.

questions.takeaway: Goals are mutually established with the older adult, the family, and the team, and assessment is tailored to the person.
questions.strategy: In this chapter the answer usually includes the patient and family as partners rather than as recipients.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The question asks what characterizes the assessment.
Psychosocial aspects are included.
Parameters are adapted.
Function matters more than disease severity.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B: mutually established is the operative phrase, and the assessment is tailored to the older person.

questions.topic: Red flags in an older adult
questions.stem: The nurse admits an 84-year-old from home following a fall. She assesses the skin, cognition, continence, senses, and mobility, and speaks with the daughter about recent changes. Highlight the findings that require further nursing assessment.

segments.text: Client is alert and oriented to person, place, and time.
segments.rationale: A normal baseline, and it is the reference point against which any later change is measured.

segments.text: Skin is thin and dry with reduced elasticity.
segments.rationale: An expected integumentary change of aging.

segments.text: Reports new difficulty controlling urine over the past two weeks.
segments.rationale: Urinary incontinence is abnormal at any age. It is common in older adults and it is not expected.

segments.text: Irregular areas of dark pigmentation noted on the backs of the hands.
segments.rationale: Lentigo senilis, an expected change.

segments.text: Daughter reports her mother has fallen twice in the past month with no identified cause.
segments.rationale: A new unexplained fall is a red flag, and a fall is always a clinical clue.

segments.text: Reports needing more light to read than she did a year ago.
segments.rationale: An expected sensory change of aging.

segments.text: Has lost 5 kg since her last clinic visit three months ago.
segments.rationale: Unintended weight loss is not an expected change and points at nutrition, illness, or a functional problem.

segments.text: Slower reaction time noted during transfer.
segments.rationale: An expected change of aging.

questions.takeaway: Expected changes are gradual. Anything new, sudden, or unexplained is assessed.
questions.strategy: Read each sentence for the words new, unexplained, or a stated time frame. Those move a finding out of the expected column.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Do not highlight as you go; several findings are deliberately normal.
Gradual is expected, recent change is not.
Both are common in older adults and neither is expected.

elimination.verdict: Highlight s3, s5, and s7.

questions.note: Several findings are expected changes of aging. Under plus and minus scoring a wrong highlight subtracts.

questions.stem: A nurse notes that a client's temperature is 37.5 degrees Celsius. The value is the same for two clients on her assignment, but she interprets it differently for each. Which additional information would most change her interpretation?

options.text: That this patient's temperature has run 37.2 for the past three days
options.rationale: A normal value can still be a change. The comparison that matters is against this patient's own baseline.

options.text: The unit's average temperature for postoperative patients
options.rationale: A population average does not tell her about this person.

options.text: The reference range for oral temperature
options.rationale: 37.5 is within the normal range, so the reference range alone tells her nothing new.

options.text: The time of the last dose of acetaminophen
options.rationale: Relevant context, and it does not change the meaning of the number as much as the patient's own trend.

questions.takeaway: A finding is abnormal relative to this patient, not only relative to a textbook range.
questions.strategy: When a value is technically normal, look for the option that supplies the patient's own baseline.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Polarity is positive. No priority key word, so look for the single accurate option.
A population average does not tell her about this person.
37.5 is within the normal range, so the reference range alone tells her nothing new.
Relevant context, and it does not change the meaning of the number as much as the patient's own trend.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A. A normal value can still be a change.

questions.stem: A nurse has determined that her patient's confusion is most likely due to hypoxia. She considers repositioning, applying oxygen per protocol, and notifying the provider. Which clinical judgment skill is she using?

options.text: Analyze cues
options.rationale: Analysis produced the working explanation, which she already has.

options.text: Prioritize hypotheses
options.rationale: She has already selected the most likely explanation.

options.text: Evaluate outcomes
options.rationale: Nothing has been implemented yet.

options.text: Generate solutions
options.rationale: Identifying possible interventions and their expected outcomes before acting.

questions.takeaway: Generate solutions is the planning step. You list what could work before choosing what to do.
questions.strategy: Considering several possible actions without performing one is generating solutions.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Polarity is positive. No priority key word, so look for the single accurate option.
Analysis produced the working explanation, which she already has.
She has already selected the most likely explanation.
Nothing has been implemented yet.

elimination.verdict: That leaves D. Identifying possible interventions and their expected outcomes before acting.

questions.stem: A nursing program teaches decision-making using a model that breaks bedside thinking into distinct steps, from noticing a finding through to judging whether the action worked. Which are steps in the Clinical Judgment Measurement Model? Select all that apply.

options.text: Recognize cues
options.rationale: Recognizing cues is noticing what is there, before any interpretation. It is the step where a finding registers as significant.

options.text: Analyze cues
options.rationale: Analyzing cues is deciding what the findings mean, which is where an isolated number becomes a pattern.

options.text: Prioritize hypotheses
options.rationale: Prioritizing hypotheses ranks the possible explanations, because you cannot investigate everything at once.

options.text: Generate solutions
options.rationale: Generating solutions produces the options, and it happens before you commit to one.

options.text: Take action
options.rationale: Taking action carries out the chosen solution, and it is a separate step from deciding on it.

options.text: Document findings
options.rationale: Essential nursing work and not one of the six CJMM skills.

questions.takeaway: Six skills: recognize cues, analyze cues, prioritize hypotheses, generate solutions, take action, evaluate outcomes.
questions.strategy: The sixth step is evaluate outcomes. Anything else offered as a step is a distractor.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Polarity is positive. This is a select all that apply, so there is no single best answer. Judge each option separately.
Essential nursing work and not one of the six CJMM skills.

elimination.verdict: Keep A, B, C, D, E. In a SATA, judge each option as its own true or false statement rather than picking a single best answer.

questions.stem: A nursing student can recite the five steps of the nursing process but freezes when a client's condition changes unexpectedly. Her preceptor explains how the framework and the thinking that uses it relate to each other. Which statement best describes the relationship between the nursing process and clinical judgment?

options.text: They are separate processes used in different situations
options.rationale: They describe the same work rather than alternating.

options.text: The nursing process is used by students and clinical judgment by experienced nurses
options.rationale: Both are used at every level of experience.

options.text: Clinical judgment replaces the nursing process in complex situations
options.rationale: Nothing replaces the nursing process. It is used with every patient.

options.text: The nursing process describes what the nurse does and clinical judgment describes the thinking behind it
options.rationale: ADPIE is the action framework; the CJMM describes the cognitive skills each step requires.

questions.takeaway: ADPIE is what nurses do. The CJMM is how nurses think.
questions.strategy: Any option that separates the two into different situations or different nurses is wrong.

strategies: Priority key word

steps.detail: Polarity is positive. Key word: best. More than one option may be true, so you are ranking them.
They describe the same work rather than alternating.
Both are used at every level of experience.
Nothing replaces the nursing process.

elimination.verdict: That leaves D. ADPIE is the action framework; the CJMM describes the cognitive skills each step requires.

questions.stem: A nurse notices that a client's respiratory rate has risen from 16 to 24 over two hours and begins considering whether it reflects pain, anxiety, developing infection, or a pulmonary problem. She has not yet acted. Which step of the clinical judgment measurement model is this?

options.text: Recognize cues
options.rationale: Noticing the rate itself is recognizing the cue.

options.text: Analyze cues
options.rationale: Interpreting what the cue means, which is the step between noticing and forming hypotheses.

options.text: Take action
options.rationale: Comes after solutions have been generated.

options.text: Evaluate outcomes
options.rationale: Judges the result after action.

questions.takeaway: Recognize, analyze, prioritize hypotheses, generate solutions, take action, evaluate outcomes.
questions.strategy: The distinction between recognizing and analyzing is noticing versus interpreting. Both happen fast and they are separate steps.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Considering what the change might mean.
Noticing has already happened.
Both come later in the model.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B: interpreting what the cue means, which is the step between noticing and forming hypotheses.

questions.stem: A nurse admits a client with shortness of breath, gathers data, identifies his problems, sets outcomes with him, carries out interventions, and later determines whether he improved. A student asks her to name the steps in order. Which sequence correctly orders the steps of the nursing process?

options.text: Assessment, diagnosis, planning, implementation, evaluation
options.rationale: The five steps, and each depends on the one before it.

options.text: Diagnosis, assessment, planning, evaluation, implementation
options.rationale: Reverses two pairs.

options.text: Planning, assessment, diagnosis, implementation, evaluation
options.rationale: Plans before gathering data.

options.text: Assessment, planning, diagnosis, implementation, evaluation
options.rationale: Plans before identifying the problem.

questions.takeaway: Assessment, diagnosis, planning, implementation, evaluation.
questions.strategy: Two distractors here plan before the problem is identified. That ordering error is the one being tested.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Assessment always opens the process.
Evaluation always closes it.
Diagnosis must precede planning.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A: the five steps, and each depends on the one before it.

questions.stem: A nurse is unsure whether she has enough information to determine that a patient met an outcome, so she asks a more experienced colleague to review her findings. Which critical thinking attitude does this show?

options.text: Risk taking
options.rationale: Risk taking is being willing to try an approach that differs from the routine.

options.text: Humility
options.rationale: Humility is recognizing the limits of your own knowledge and seeking help rather than proceeding on uncertainty.

options.text: Perseverance
options.rationale: Perseverance is continuing to seek answers when a problem resists solution.

options.text: Confidence
options.rationale: Confidence is acting decisively within your competence.

questions.takeaway: Humility is what makes asking for help a professional strength rather than an admission of failure.
questions.strategy: Match the attitude to the behavior in the stem. Asking for help is humility; sticking with a hard problem is perseverance.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Polarity is positive. No priority key word, so look for the single accurate option.
Risk taking is being willing to try an approach that differs from the routine.
Perseverance is continuing to seek answers when a problem resists solution.
Confidence is acting decisively within your competence.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B. Humility is recognizing the limits of your own knowledge and seeking help rather than proceeding on uncertainty.

questions.stem: Two students study the same content and score similarly on written tests, but one consistently makes better decisions at the bedside when a client's condition changes. Their instructor explains what that difference actually is. Which statement best describes clinical judgment?

options.text: The observed outcome of critical thinking and clinical reasoning applied to a patient situation
options.rationale: Judgment is what the reasoning produces, which is why it is assessed through decisions and actions.

options.text: Following facility policy exactly as written in every situation
options.rationale: Policy informs judgment and does not replace it.

options.text: Recalling the correct answer from previous coursework
options.rationale: Recall is knowledge, not judgment.

options.text: Deferring all decisions to the provider
options.rationale: Abandons the nurse's own scope.

questions.takeaway: Critical thinking and clinical reasoning are the process. Clinical judgment is the observable result.
questions.strategy: The three terms are tested as a set. Thinking is the disposition, reasoning is the process, judgment is what shows.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The definition of clinical judgment.
Policy informs but does not replace judgment.
Recall and deferral are neither.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A: judgment is what the reasoning produces, which is why it is assessed through decisions and actions.

questions.stem: A nurse caring for a confused older adult has identified three possible explanations: hypoxia, a newly started medication, and an evolving infection. She cannot investigate all three at once and must decide which to pursue first. This represents which clinical judgment skill?

options.text: Evaluate outcomes
options.rationale: Nothing has been implemented yet.

options.text: Recognize cues
options.rationale: The cues have already been recognized.

options.text: Generate solutions
options.rationale: Generating solutions comes after the priority problem is identified.

options.text: Prioritize hypotheses
options.rationale: Ranking possible explanations by likelihood and urgency is exactly this skill.

questions.takeaway: Prioritizing hypotheses asks which problem is most likely and most urgent, and those two do not always point the same way.
questions.strategy: Count the possible explanations. If the stem gives you several and asks which to pursue, it is testing prioritization.

strategies: Priority key word

steps.detail: Polarity is positive. Key word: first. More than one option may be true, so you are ranking them.
Nothing has been implemented yet.
The cues have already been recognized.
Generating solutions comes after the priority problem is identified.

elimination.verdict: That leaves D. Ranking possible explanations by likelihood and urgency is exactly this skill.

questions.stem: A nurse begins her shift with four clients: one reporting incisional pain rated 6, one with an oxygen saturation of 88%, one who is newly confused, and one whose intravenous site is red and swollen. Which situations require assessment before the client reporting pain? Select all that apply.

options.text: New shortness of breath with oxygen saturation of 88 percent
options.rationale: An actual airway and breathing problem outranks everything.

options.text: Sudden confusion in a previously alert patient
options.rationale: An acute change in mental status can signal hypoxia, hypoglycemia, or sepsis.

options.text: A request for help to the bathroom from a patient at risk for falls
options.rationale: A real safety concern and a potential problem, which loses to an actual one and to pain.

options.text: Chest pain rated 8 with diaphoresis
options.rationale: Circulation, and a possible cardiac event.

options.text: A family asking questions about discharge paperwork
options.rationale: Important and not urgent.

options.text: Blood glucose of 42 with the patient shaky and diaphoretic
options.rationale: A physiological emergency requiring immediate treatment.

questions.takeaway: ABCs first, then acute changes in mental status and glucose. An actual problem beats a potential one.
questions.strategy: Sort into actual and potential problems first, then apply ABCs to the actual ones.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Polarity is positive. This is a select all that apply, so there is no single best answer. Judge each option separately.
A real safety concern and a potential problem, which loses to an actual one and to pain.
Important and not urgent.

elimination.verdict: Keep A, B, D, F. In a SATA, judge each option as its own true or false statement rather than picking a single best answer.

questions.stem: A nurse caring for four clients must decide whom to see first: one requesting pain medication, one whose family has questions, one with a new oxygen requirement and rising respiratory rate, and one due for a routine dressing change. Which client should she assess first?

options.text: A patient whose family has questions about discharge
options.rationale: Important and not urgent.

options.text: A patient requesting pain medication for incisional pain rated 6
options.rationale: Pain matters and is not life-threatening. This patient is second or third.

options.text: A patient with new shortness of breath and oxygen saturation of 88 percent
options.rationale: An actual airway and breathing problem outranks everything else.

options.text: A patient who is at risk for falls and asking to get up to the bathroom
options.rationale: A real safety issue and a potential problem, which loses to an actual one.

questions.takeaway: ABCs outrank everything, and an actual problem beats a potential one.
questions.strategy: Sort the options into actual and potential problems first, then apply ABCs to the actual ones.

strategies: Apply the ABCs
Priority key word

steps.detail: Polarity is positive. Key word: first. More than one option may be true, so you are ranking them.

steps.detail: Key word: first. More than one option may be true, so you are ranking them.
Documentation does not explain why the outcome was missed.
Worth knowing later and not the first check.
Relevant and it comes after checking the outcome itself.

elimination.verdict: That leaves C. An outcome that was never achievable reads as failed care when it was failed planning.

questions.topic: Evaluation and the care plan cycle
questions.stem: A patient's outcome for pain control has not been met after three days. The nurse reassesses and finds the patient has been declining medication because he fears addiction. What should she do?

options.text: Document that the patient is noncompliant with pain management
options.rationale: A label that hides a treatable fear.

options.text: Continue the current plan and re-evaluate in another three days
options.rationale: Ignores the reason the outcome was missed.

options.text: Revise the plan to address the fear, then reassess the pain outcome
options.rationale: The new data reveals a different problem. Address the cause before repeating the intervention.

options.text: Ask the provider to change to a non-opioid analgesic
options.rationale: May be reasonable eventually and it does not address the fear driving the refusal.

questions.takeaway: When an outcome is missed, look for the new data before you repeat the intervention.
questions.strategy: An unmet outcome with a newly discovered cause means revise the plan, not repeat it.

strategies: Negative polarity

steps.detail: No priority key word, so look for the single accurate option.
A label that hides a treatable fear.
Ignores the reason the outcome was missed.
May be reasonable eventually and it does not address the fear driving the refusal.

elimination.verdict: That leaves C. The new data reveals a different problem.

questions.stem: A client has not met the outcome of maintaining an oxygen saturation above 92% on room air by day four. The nurse sits with the plan of care and works through why, rather than simply adding more interventions. Which questions should the nurse consider? Select all that apply.

options.text: Was the outcome realistic for this patient?
options.rationale: The outcome itself may have been the problem.

options.text: Was the time frame appropriate?
options.rationale: A correct outcome with too short a deadline reads as failure.

options.text: Is the nursing diagnosis still accurate?
options.rationale: The wrong problem produces the wrong plan.

options.text: Were the interventions appropriate and correctly applied?
options.rationale: Both the selection and the execution matter.

options.text: Should the patient be labeled nonadherent?
options.rationale: A label that ends inquiry rather than advancing it.

options.text: Has anything changed in the patient's condition?
options.rationale: New data may have invalidated the original plan.

questions.takeaway: Unmet triggers a full reassessment of the diagnosis, the outcome, the time frame, and the interventions.
questions.strategy: Options that label the patient are never the answer on evaluation questions.

strategies: Negative polarity

steps.detail: This is a select all that apply, so there is no single best answer. Judge each option separately.
A label that ends inquiry rather than advancing it.

elimination.verdict: Keep A, B, C, D, F. In a SATA, judge each option as its own true or false statement rather than picking a single best answer.

questions.stem: A nurse determines that a client has met the outcome for independent wound care, demonstrating the full procedure correctly twice. The care plan still lists daily nurse-performed dressing changes and teaching sessions. What must she do to prevent unnecessary continued interventions?

options.text: Document that the outcome was met and the intervention discontinued
options.rationale: Documentation is what stops other nurses continuing care that is already complete.

options.text: Wait until discharge to close it out
options.rationale: Leaves a stale intervention active in the plan.

options.text: Tell the oncoming nurse at hand-off
options.rationale: Verbal report helps and does not carry forward beyond that shift.

options.text: Remove the diagnosis from the record
options.rationale: The record preserves the history of care.

questions.takeaway: Document the discontinuation, or the team keeps delivering care the patient no longer needs.
questions.strategy: Look for the option that communicates beyond the current shift.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Polarity is positive. No priority key word, so look for the single accurate option.
Leaves a stale intervention active in the plan.
Verbal report helps and does not carry forward beyond that shift.
The record preserves the history of care.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A. Documentation is what stops other nurses continuing care that is already complete.

questions.stem: A client recovering from hip replacement has met the outcome of ambulating independently with a walker, achieved two days ahead of the target date. The plan of care still lists assisted ambulation twice daily. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Remove the diagnosis from the record entirely
options.rationale: The record shows the history of care. You discontinue the plan, not the history.

options.text: Continue the intervention unchanged for the rest of the admission
options.rationale: Continuing care that is no longer needed wastes time and the patient's energy.

options.text: Wait until discharge to close the outcome
options.rationale: Delays freeing the plan and leaves stale interventions in place.

options.text: Confirm with the patient, then discontinue that part of the plan and document it
options.rationale: Confirm, discontinue, and document so other nurses do not keep delivering finished care.

questions.takeaway: Met means confirm, then continue or discontinue, and document the discontinuation.
questions.strategy: Look for the option that tells the rest of the team. Undocumented discontinuation is invisible.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Polarity is positive. No priority key word, so look for the single accurate option.
The record shows the history of care.
Continuing care that is no longer needed wastes time and the patient's energy.
Delays freeing the plan and leaves stale interventions in place.

elimination.verdict: That leaves D. Confirm, discontinue, and document so other nurses do not keep delivering finished care.

questions.stem: A client three days after abdominal surgery still has coarse crackles at both bases despite coughing and deep breathing twice daily. He is reluctant to take deep breaths because of incisional pain and has not been out of bed. Which revision is most appropriate?

options.text: Document that the patient is nonadherent
options.rationale: Nothing in the stem suggests he refused. Labeling replaces problem solving.

options.text: Increase the frequency of coughing and deep breathing and add positioning
options.rationale: Adjusting frequency based on the patient's actual response is a standard revision.

options.text: Request an order for a sedative so he rests more
options.rationale: Sedation worsens atelectasis rather than helping it.

options.text: Discontinue the intervention as ineffective
options.rationale: The intervention is appropriate. The dose is not.

questions.takeaway: Revision often means changing the frequency rather than abandoning the intervention.
questions.strategy: Before discarding an intervention, ask whether it was simply not done often enough.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Polarity is positive. No priority key word, so look for the single accurate option.
Nothing in the stem suggests he refused.
Sedation worsens atelectasis rather than helping it.
The intervention is appropriate.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B. Adjusting frequency based on the patient's actual response is a standard revision.

questions.stem: A hospital reports outcome data that reflect the quality and quantity of nursing care specifically, rather than medical management. The quality committee reviews which measures belong in that category. Which outcomes are considered nurse-sensitive indicators of care quality? Select all that apply.

options.text: Patient falls with injury
options.rationale: A nurse-sensitive never event.

options.text: Catheter-associated urinary tract infection
options.rationale: A nurse-sensitive never event.

options.text: Hospital-acquired stage 3 pressure injury
options.rationale: A nurse-sensitive never event.

options.text: Surgical wound dehiscence from a technical error in the operating room
options.rationale: Attributable to surgical technique rather than nursing care.

options.text: Central line-associated bloodstream infection
options.rationale: A nurse-sensitive never event.

options.text: Length of stay for a complex medical diagnosis
options.rationale: Driven by disease and system factors rather than nursing care.

questions.takeaway: Nurse-sensitive means nursing care measurably changes the rate, which is why Medicare will not reimburse these four.
questions.strategy: Ask whether better nursing care would move the number. If not, it is not nurse-sensitive.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Polarity is positive. This is a select all that apply, so there is no single best answer. Judge each option separately.
Attributable to surgical technique rather than nursing care.
Driven by disease and system factors rather than nursing care.

elimination.verdict: Keep A, B, C, E. In a SATA, judge each option as its own true or false statement rather than picking a single best answer.

questions.stem: A client rates his pain 3 out of 10 thirty minutes after analgesia. He is lying still, watching television, and is not grimacing. The nurse thinks he appears comfortable enough to be at 1. What should she document?

options.text: Pain rated 3 out of 10 by patient report
options.rationale: Pain is what the patient says it is. Self-report is the measure.

options.text: Pain rating unreliable
options.rationale: There is no basis for calling it unreliable and it dismisses the patient.

options.text: Pain rated 1 out of 10 based on nursing assessment
options.rationale: Substituting your judgment for the patient's report falsifies the record.

options.text: Patient appears comfortable, denies pain
options.rationale: He did not deny pain. He reported a 3.

questions.takeaway: For pain, breathing, nausea, and grief, patient self-report is the only accurate measure there is.
questions.strategy: Any option that replaces the patient's number with the nurse's impression is wrong.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Polarity is positive. No priority key word, so look for the single accurate option.
There is no basis for calling it unreliable and it dismisses the patient.
Substituting your judgment for the patient's report falsifies the record.
He did not deny pain.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A. Pain is what the patient says it is.

questions.stem: A nursing student assumes evaluation happens at the end of a shift when she reviews whether outcomes were met. Her preceptor points out that she has been evaluating all morning without labelling it as such. Which statement about evaluation in the nursing process is accurate?

options.text: Evaluation is performed only when outcomes are not met
options.rationale: It is performed regardless of the result.

options.text: Evaluation data becomes new assessment data and the cycle continues
options.rationale: The nursing process is continuous rather than linear.

options.text: Evaluation is complete once outcomes are documented
options.rationale: Documentation records evaluation; it does not end the process.

options.text: Evaluation occurs only at discharge
options.rationale: It occurs every time you have contact with the patient.

questions.takeaway: Evaluation data becomes new assessment data, and the process starts its next loop immediately.
questions.strategy: Any option describing the nursing process as ending is wrong.

strategies: Eliminate absolutes

steps.detail: Polarity is positive. No priority key word, so look for the single accurate option.
It is performed regardless of the result.
Documentation records evaluation; it does not end the process.
It occurs every time you have contact with the patient.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B. The nursing process is continuous rather than linear.

questions.stem: A client with asthma has just finished a nebulizer treatment. The nurse could check his respiratory rate, listen to his lungs, review the pulse oximetry trend, or ask him how his breathing feels. Which source gives the most accurate information about whether his breathing feels easier?

options.text: The patient's own report
options.rationale: The patient knows best whether breathing is easier. Self-report is the measure for that experience.

options.text: The respiratory therapist's impression
options.rationale: A secondhand judgment about a subjective experience.

options.text: The oxygen saturation reading
options.rationale: Objective and useful, and it does not measure how breathing feels.

options.text: The respiratory rate
options.rationale: Objective data that may not track with the patient's experience.

questions.takeaway: Person-centered evaluation includes asking the patient whether what mattered to them improved.
questions.strategy: When the outcome is about an experience, the patient is the instrument.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Polarity is positive. No priority key word, so look for the single accurate option.
A secondhand judgment about a subjective experience.
Objective and useful, and it does not measure how breathing feels.
Objective data that may not track with the patient's experience.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A. The patient knows best whether breathing is easier.

questions.stem: A nurse manager is comparing care delivery models for her unit. She describes one in which a single RN is responsible for a client from admission through discharge, writes the plan of care, and other staff carry out that plan on her days off. Which model is this?

options.text: Team nursing
options.rationale: A group led by an RN, working together, with work divided by scope.

options.text: Primary nursing
options.rationale: One RN follows a patient the whole way through. It is rare today because it is too expensive.

options.text: Case management
options.rationale: Coordination across settings and over time rather than within a unit.

options.text: Patient- and family-centered care
options.rationale: A professional practice model treating the patient and family as partners, not a staffing structure.

questions.takeaway: Continuity across the whole admission means primary nursing.
questions.strategy: Sort staffing models by whether work is divided and whether anything survives the shift.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: One RN, whole admission, others follow her plan.
Team nursing divides work among staff.
Case management crosses settings.
A philosophy of partnership, not a staffing model.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B: one RN follows a patient the whole way through.

questions.stem: A nurse works a shift on a medical unit. She is assigned five clients, decides the order in which to see them, telephones a provider to question an order she believes is unsafe, and later answers for a task she delegated that was not completed correctly. Match each situation with the concept it BEST demonstrates. Each term is used only once.

items.text: A nurse is assigned five patients and is expected to complete their assessments and medications this shift
items.rationale: What you are supposed to do, meaning your job duties. It points at the work.

items.text: A nurse decides to ambulate a patient before completing routine charting, based on her clinical judgment
items.rationale: Freedom to make independent choices within your scope, without waiting to be told.

items.text: A nurse calls the provider to question an order she believes is unsafe
items.rationale: Legal power to act, and it explicitly includes the power to question an order.

items.text: A nurse answers for a delegated task that was not completed correctly under her supervision
items.rationale: Answering for outcomes. It does not transfer even when the task does.

questions.takeaway: Responsibility is what you have. Autonomy is deciding. Authority is the power to act. Accountability is answering for it.
questions.strategy: These four are tested as a set. Sort by direction: at the work, at the decision, at the power, or back at you.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: An assignment of patients is responsibility.
Choosing the order of care is autonomy.
Questioning an order is authority.
Answering afterward is accountability.

questions.note: These four sit inside decentralization and shared governance. Sort them by what each one points at.

questions.stem: A nurse has twice paged the provider about a client whose blood pressure has fallen through the shift and who is now increasingly drowsy. Neither page was returned. The client continues to deteriorate and the nurse must communicate differently. Which tool does the nurse use next?

options.text: SBAR
options.rationale: The right tool for the first call and the wrong one for the third. Repeating a report that has already failed changes nothing.

options.text: CUS
options.rationale: Graded escalation language: I am concerned, I am uncomfortable, this is a safety issue. Each step raises the stakes explicitly.

options.text: TeamSTEPPS
options.rationale: The broader teamwork framework CUS belongs to, with pillars of communication, team leadership, situation monitoring, and mutual support.

options.text: The five rights of delegation
options.rationale: Belongs to delegation.

questions.takeaway: SBAR reports. CUS escalates.
questions.strategy: When a stem says you already reported and nothing happened, the answer is escalate, not report again.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Two reports have already failed.
Repeating the same tool changes nothing.
A framework, not a moment-to-moment tool.
Wrong domain.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B: graded escalation language: I am concerned, I am uncomfortable, this is a safety issue.

questions.stem: A hospital is preparing an application for Magnet recognition and must demonstrate that its nursing practice environment meets the program's standards. The nurse manager reviews which areas will be assessed. Which are standards of the Magnet Recognition Program? Select all that apply.

options.text: Shared decision-making
options.rationale: Shared decision-making means the nurses who deliver care participate in the decisions that govern it, which is why protocols are followed.

options.text: Leadership
options.rationale: Leadership is assessed because the practice environment is set from the top, starting with the nurse executive's philosophy.

options.text: Safety
options.rationale: Safety is a standard rather than an outcome here, meaning the structures that produce it are what get evaluated.

options.text: Reduced staffing costs
options.rationale: Not a Magnet standard. The program addresses professional practice environment, not cost reduction.

options.text: Quality
options.rationale: Quality is measured and reported, which is what allows comparison and improvement over time.

options.text: Well-being and professional development
options.rationale: Wellbeing and development are standards because burnout and stagnation drive turnover, and turnover harms patients.

questions.takeaway: Shared decision-making, leadership, safety, quality, well-being, and professional development.
questions.strategy: One option in this set describes a financial goal. Magnet standards concern the practice environment.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Magnet standards specifically.
A cost objective, not a practice standard.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, E, and F are selected.

questions.stem: Staff nurses on a medical unit form a council that reviews the unit's fall data and writes a new prevention protocol, which the manager then adopts. The nurses who will use it wrote it. Which concept does this demonstrate?

options.text: Shared governance
options.rationale: Staff involvement runs through shared governance councils and practice committees. The people who will use the protocol write it.

options.text: Decentralization
options.rationale: Closely related and different. Decentralization is how far down decisions are made; shared governance is who sits at the table.

options.text: Delegation
options.rationale: Transferring a task to another person.

options.text: Accountability
options.rationale: Answering for outcomes.

questions.takeaway: Shared governance is about who participates. Decentralization is about how far down decisions are pushed.
questions.strategy: These two appear together often. Ask whether the stem is about participation or about the level at which a decision is made.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Staff nurses writing the protocol they will use.
Concerns the level of decision-making, not participation.
Neither describes a governance structure.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A: staff involvement runs through shared governance councils and practice committees.

questions.stem: A nurse plans to delegate vital signs on a stable client to assistive personnel so she can complete an admission assessment. She wants the delegation to be safe and defensible. Place the steps of delegation in the correct order, from FIRST to LAST.

options.text: Determine whether the task is appropriate to delegate
options.rationale: Right task. Some activities never move, including assessment, evaluation, teaching, and unstable patients.

options.text: Determine whether the patient's condition is stable and appropriate for delegation
options.rationale: Right circumstance. A stable situation with a predictable outcome is required, and this is where most delegation questions are decided.

options.text: Confirm the person is competent and qualified to perform the task
options.rationale: Right person. Having watched is not the same as being competent.

options.text: Give clear instructions, expectations, and what must be reported back
options.rationale: Right directions and communication. A delegation without a reporting threshold is incomplete.

options.text: Supervise, follow up on the outcome, and evaluate the result
options.rationale: Right supervision and evaluation, and it is the step most often skipped.

questions.takeaway: Task, circumstance, person, directions, supervision. The last one is the one people drop.
questions.strategy: Read the patient, not just the task. A delegable task on an unstable patient stays with the RN.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Whether the task can be delegated at all comes first.
Supervision and evaluation close the process.
Circumstance, then person, then directions.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D, E.

questions.note: Handing off the task feels like the end. It is the fourth of five steps.

questions.stem: A nurse manager explains that the unit's practice model treats clients and families as partners rather than as recipients of care, and that the model rests on four specific elements. A new graduate asks what they are. Which are the four elements of patient- and family-centered care?

options.text: Respect and dignity, information sharing, participation, and collaboration
options.rationale: The four named elements of this professional practice model.

options.text: Situation, background, assessment, recommendation
options.rationale: That is SBAR.

options.text: Values and ethics, roles and responsibilities, communication, and teamwork
options.rationale: Those are the four interprofessional competencies.

options.text: Communication, team leadership, situation monitoring, and mutual support
options.rationale: Those are the TeamSTEPPS pillars.

questions.takeaway: Respect and dignity, information sharing, participation, collaboration.
questions.strategy: This chapter has several four-part frameworks. Distractors are drawn from the neighbours, so match the set to the name.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: One specific model is named.
SBAR.
Interprofessional competencies.
TeamSTEPPS pillars.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A: the four named elements of this professional practice model.

questions.stem: A nurse is preparing to delegate several tasks to assistive personnel and wants to be sure she is meeting each of the conditions that make a delegation safe and defensible. Which are among the five rights of delegation? Select all that apply.

options.text: Right task
options.rationale: Is this task appropriate to delegate?

options.text: Right circumstance
options.rationale: Is the patient's condition stable and appropriate?

options.text: Right person
options.rationale: Is the person competent and qualified?

options.text: Right documentation
options.rationale: Documentation matters and is not one of the five. This is a right of medication administration, which is a different framework.

options.text: Right directions and communication
options.rationale: Clear instructions, expectations, and what to report.

options.text: Right supervision and evaluation
options.rationale: Follow up on the outcome.

questions.takeaway: Task, circumstance, person, directions and communication, supervision and evaluation.
questions.strategy: The distractor in delegation items is usually borrowed from the rights of medication administration. Two different frameworks, similar wording.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The five rights of delegation specifically.
Documentation belongs to the medication rights.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, E, and F are selected.

questions.stem: A charge nurse is assigning work to assistive personnel. Her clients include one awaiting discharge after an uncomplicated appendectomy, one whose blood pressure has fallen across three readings, one on contact precautions with a healing wound, and one receiving routine antibiotics who is afebrile. Which client's vital signs should NOT be delegated?

options.text: A patient awaiting discharge after an uncomplicated appendectomy
options.rationale: Stable with a predictable outcome.

options.text: A patient whose blood pressure has fallen across the last three readings
options.rationale: A trend is not a stable situation. You take these yourself because you need the number as it exists, along with what you notice while taking it.

options.text: A patient on contact precautions with a healing wound
options.rationale: Isolation status changes the PPE worn, not who may take a vital sign.

options.text: A patient receiving routine intravenous antibiotics who is afebrile
options.rationale: Stable and predictable.

questions.takeaway: Read the patient, not just the task. A delegable task on an unstable patient stays with the RN.
questions.strategy: Option C is the deliberate distractor. Precautions look like a reason to keep the task and are not.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Which vital signs should not be delegated.
Both stable and predictable.
Isolation changes PPE, not scope.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B. A falling trend means the situation is not stable.

questions.scenario: A charge nurse plans assignments for a team of one RN, one LPN/LVN, and one assistive personnel on a medical unit with stable and unstable patients.
questions.stem: For each task, indicate the LOWEST level of staff to whom it may appropriately be assigned.

rows.text: Performing the initial admission assessment on a new patient
rows.rationale: Initial assessment establishes the baseline others judge against and cannot be delegated.

rows.text: Obtaining vital signs on a stable patient
rows.rationale: Routine, predictable data collection on a stable patient.

rows.text: Reinforcing teaching the RN has already begun
rows.rationale: The LPN assists with implementation of defined plans. Initiating teaching remains the RN's.

rows.text: Assisting a stable patient with bathing and grooming
rows.rationale: Routine care within the assistive scope.

rows.text: Evaluating whether a patient met the goal in the plan of care
rows.rationale: Evaluation requires interpretation and is not delegated.

rows.text: Recording intake and output on a stable patient
rows.rationale: Data collection. Interpreting the trend remains the RN's.

questions.takeaway: Four things never move: initial assessment, evaluation, teaching, and unstable patients.
questions.strategy: Cross out any task involving those four and most assignment questions resolve themselves.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Initial assessment and evaluation both require interpretation.
Reinforcing established teaching, not initiating it.
Routine data collection and hygiene on stable patients.

elimination.verdict: Two RN only, one LPN/LVN, three assistive personnel.

questions.stem: A nurse manager works to build a culture of autonomy, quality, and collaboration on a unit that has had high turnover and frequent sick calls. Staff have described feeling unable to act on what they know is right. Which outcome does the evidence support?

options.text: Higher staff satisfaction and lower moral distress
options.rationale: Named directly. Empowering environments support both patient outcomes and staff wellbeing.

options.text: Reduced need for interprofessional communication
options.rationale: Collaboration increases communication rather than reducing it.

options.text: Elimination of the need for delegation
options.rationale: Delegation remains a core leadership competency.

options.text: Fewer opportunities for professional development
options.rationale: Professional development is a Magnet standard and part of an empowering environment.

questions.takeaway: A culture of autonomy, quality, and collaboration raises satisfaction and lowers moral distress.
questions.strategy: Moral distress is knowing what is right and being blocked from doing it. Environments that increase autonomy reduce the blocking.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The outcome of an empowering culture.
Each describes something being reduced or eliminated that the culture actually supports.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A: named directly.

questions.stem: The nurse is preparing to call the provider about a postoperative client whose condition has changed over the past four hours. She reviews her findings and must decide what to lead with. Highlight the three highest priority findings to emphasize to the provider.

segments.text: Blood pressure has fallen from 122/74 to 88/52 over four hours
segments.rationale: A downward trend in perfusion pressure, and trends outrank single values.

segments.text: Client reports the room is too warm
segments.rationale: A comfort issue, not a priority to report.

segments.text: Heart rate has risen from 82 to 124
segments.rationale: Compensatory tachycardia accompanying the falling pressure, and the two together suggest hypovolemia.

segments.text: Dressing has a small amount of dried drainage from this morning
segments.rationale: Old, dried, and small. Expected postoperatively.

segments.text: Client is increasingly difficult to rouse
segments.rationale: A change in level of consciousness, and altered mentation with falling pressure signals decompensation.

segments.text: Client has not had a bowel movement since surgery two days ago
segments.rationale: Worth addressing and not among the three highest priorities.

segments.text: Family asks when the client can have visitors
segments.rationale: Not a clinical finding.

questions.takeaway: Report the trend, not the isolated number, and lead with perfusion and mentation.
questions.strategy: When a stem asks for a fixed number of findings, rank rather than select. Two options may be real concerns and still not make the top three.

strategies: Apply the ABCs
Priority key word

steps.detail: Three findings describe a change over time; the rest are static.
Circulation and level of consciousness outrank elimination and comfort.
Exactly three are requested, so a fourth selection costs you.

elimination.verdict: Highlight s1, s3, and s5.

questions.note: Exactly three selections are requested. Some unselected findings are still worth addressing later.

questions.stem: A new graduate asks who decides the values and direction that shape nursing practice across an entire organization, as opposed to who manages a shift or who regulates the profession. Who sets the nursing philosophy for an organization?

options.text: The nurse executive, often the chief nursing officer
options.rationale: Named directly, and the philosophy shapes the practice environment beneath it.

options.text: The charge nurse on each unit
options.rationale: Manages the shift rather than setting organizational philosophy.

options.text: The State Board of Nursing
options.rationale: Regulates licensure and practice, not one organization's philosophy.

options.text: The Joint Commission
options.rationale: Sets accreditation standards.

questions.takeaway: The nurse executive, often the CNO, sets the nursing philosophy.
questions.strategy: Sort by scope: shift, organization, state, or accreditation. Only one operates at organizational level.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Organizational nursing philosophy.
Shift-level.
External regulators.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A: named directly, and the philosophy shapes the practice environment beneath it.

questions.scenario: A nurse is caring for four patients with an LPN/LVN and one assistive personnel. Assistive personnel reports that a patient's blood pressure is 86/50, down from 118/70 four hours ago, and that the patient seems drowsy. The nurse has already paged the provider twice about this patient's declining pressures with no response.
questions.stem: Complete the diagram by selecting from the choices below.

options.text: Assess the patient directly, including level of consciousness and perfusion
options.rationale: An unstable patient requires RN assessment. Reported numbers do not replace what you observe at the bedside.

options.text: Escalate using graded language: concerned, uncomfortable, this is a safety issue
options.rationale: Two reports have already failed. CUS escalates where repeating SBAR would change nothing.

options.text: Ask assistive personnel to recheck the blood pressure in one hour
options.rationale: Delegates monitoring of an unstable patient and delays action by an hour.

options.text: Page the provider a third time with the same information
options.rationale: Repeating a method that has already failed twice.

options.text: Assign the patient to the LPN/LVN so the RN can complete the medication round
options.rationale: An unstable patient with an unpredictable outcome stays with the RN.

options.text: An unstable patient requiring RN assessment and escalation
options.rationale: A falling trend with altered mental status is not a stable situation, and the communication pathway has failed.

options.text: A stable patient appropriate for delegated monitoring
options.rationale: A trend across four hours with drowsiness is the opposite of stable.

options.text: A staffing problem requiring reassignment
options.rationale: Reassignment does not address the patient's condition.

options.text: An expected postoperative variation
options.rationale: Nothing in the scenario supports this.

options.text: Blood pressure, heart rate, and level of consciousness
options.rationale: The parameters that show whether the patient is deteriorating further.

options.text: Urine output
options.rationale: A direct marker of perfusion, and it falls before many other signs.

options.text: Serum calcium
options.rationale: Not indicated by anything described.

options.text: Deep tendon reflexes
options.rationale: Not the parameter that tracks perfusion.

options.text: Skin turgor once daily
options.rationale: Too infrequent to track an acute change.

questions.takeaway: SBAR reports and CUS escalates. An unstable patient stays with the RN however routine the task looks.
questions.strategy: Two options here delegate or delay care for a patient whose condition is changing. Read the patient, not just the task.

strategies: Priority key word

steps.detail: A falling trend plus drowsiness means unstable.
Both treat an unstable patient as stable.
The same method has failed twice.

elimination.verdict: Actions A and B, condition A, parameters A and B.

questions.stem: A new graduate says she does not see herself as a leader because she manages no one. Her preceptor explains that leading her own patient care requires a specific set of learnable, practical skills used every shift. Which skills does the chapter identify as the ground-level leadership skills?

options.text: Budgeting, staffing, and scheduling
options.rationale: Management functions rather than the bedside leadership skills named.

options.text: Clinical judgment, priority setting, time management, delegation, and team communication
options.rationale: Named directly, with team communication delivered through SBAR, CUS, and TeamSTEPPS. Leadership skills are learnable and practical, not abstract.

options.text: Policy writing and committee chairing
options.rationale: Governance activities, not the ground-level set.

options.text: Research design and statistical analysis
options.rationale: Not the named skills.

questions.takeaway: Leadership at the bedside is clinical judgment, priorities, time, delegation, and communication.
questions.strategy: The framing matters: these are learnable and practical skills, which is why they are testable as actions rather than traits.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Ground-level skills for leading your own patient care.
Management functions.
Neither is the named set.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B: named directly, with team communication delivered through SBAR, CUS, and TeamSTEPPS.

questions.stem: A hospital is introducing interprofessional rounding, with the whole team reviewing each client together at the bedside. Staff are asked to prepare by reviewing the competencies that make team practice work. Which are the four interprofessional competencies? Select all that apply.

options.text: Values and ethics
options.rationale: Values and ethics establish that team members share a commitment to the patient rather than to their own discipline's priorities.

options.text: Roles and responsibilities
options.rationale: Knowing each discipline's roles prevents both duplication and the assumption that someone else has done it.

options.text: Communication
options.rationale: Communication is a named competency because most team failures are communication failures rather than knowledge failures.

options.text: Teamwork
options.rationale: Teamwork covers how the group functions under pressure, which is when coordination usually breaks down.

options.text: Financial stewardship
options.rationale: Not one of the four.

questions.takeaway: Values and ethics, roles and responsibilities, communication, teamwork, supported by interprofessional rounding.
questions.strategy: Four of the five are named, so identify the outlier rather than ranking importance.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The four interprofessional competencies.
Not among the four.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, and D are selected.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old is being discharged after a stroke with a rehabilitation bed arranged, home oxygen ordered, and a follow-up appointment at a specialty clinic in another town. Someone must coordinate all three across settings. Which model of care best describes this?

options.text: Team nursing
options.rationale: A staffing structure within one unit.

options.text: Primary nursing
options.rationale: One RN following a patient within the admission, not across settings.

options.text: Case management
options.rationale: Someone coordinates care across settings and over time, with attention to outcomes and resource use.

options.text: Shared governance
options.rationale: Staff participation in unit decisions, not a care delivery model.

questions.takeaway: If the stem crosses settings or agencies, think case management.
questions.strategy: Staffing models operate inside a unit. Case management is the one that reaches past discharge.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Three different settings after discharge.
Both are unit staffing structures.
A governance structure.

elimination.verdict: That leaves C: someone coordinates care across settings and over time, with attention to outcomes and resource use.

questions.scenario: A charge nurse is planning assignments for a team of one RN, one LPN/LVN, and one assistive personnel.
questions.stem: For each task, click to specify which staff members may appropriately perform it. Each task may be appropriate for more than one.

rows.text: Obtaining vital signs on a stable client
rows.rationale: Routine data collection on a stable client sits within every scope.

rows.text: Performing the initial admission assessment
rows.rationale: Establishes the baseline others judge against and cannot be delegated.

rows.text: Reinforcing teaching the RN has already begun
rows.rationale: The LPN assists with implementation of a defined plan. Initiating teaching remains the RN's.

rows.text: Evaluating whether a client met the goal in the care plan
rows.rationale: Evaluation requires interpretation.

rows.text: Assisting a stable client with bathing and grooming
rows.rationale: Within every scope, though it is usually delegated.

rows.text: Administering an intramuscular medication
