rows.rationale: Within LPN scope in many states, and medication administration varies with education and the state nurse practice act.

rows.text: Assessing a client whose condition has become unstable
rows.rationale: An unstable client with an unpredictable outcome stays with the RN.

questions.constraint: Each column must have at least one response selected.
questions.takeaway: Four things never move: initial assessment, evaluation, teaching, and unstable clients.
questions.strategy: Work down from the RN. Everything the RN may do is the widest column; the question is how far down each task travels.
questions.note: The RN column applies to every task. Decide how far down each one travels.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The RN may perform every task listed.
Initial assessment, evaluation, and the unstable client.
Reinforcing teaching yes, initiating no.

elimination.verdict: Three rows are RN only, two extend to the LPN, and two extend to all three.

questions.stem: A competent adult with newly diagnosed cancer declines chemotherapy after the oncologist explains the prognosis with and without treatment. The nurse has confirmed the patient understands the consequences. Which ethical principle does honoring this decision demonstrate?

options.text: Beneficence
options.rationale: The most dangerous distractor in ethics. Doing what you believe is good for a competent person who has refused it is not beneficence, it is a violation of autonomy.

options.text: Autonomy
options.rationale: The competent patient decides. Confirming understanding first is what makes it autonomy rather than abandonment.

options.text: Justice
options.rationale: Concerns fair distribution of resources, and no allocation question is present.

options.text: Fidelity
options.rationale: Keeping promises and commitments, which is not what is being tested here.

questions.takeaway: Beneficence never overrides autonomy for a competent patient.
questions.strategy: When a competent patient has stated a wish, autonomy usually wins. Look for the option that names the patient's authority.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Competent, informed, understanding confirmed.
Overriding an informed refusal is not doing good.
No allocation and no promise are in play.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B: the competent patient decides.

questions.stem: A nurse manager reviews four staff actions from the past week: an error reported immediately, a workstation logged out before leaving the room, a client's wishes relayed to a provider despite family objection, and a stated return time kept exactly. Match each nursing action with the ethical or legal term it BEST demonstrates. Each term is used only once.

items.text: A nurse discovers a medication error, immediately notifies the provider and manager, and completes an occurrence report
items.rationale: Accountability is answering for your own actions. Owning the error and reporting it is the definition in practice.

items.text: A nurse steps away from a shared workstation and logs out of the record before administering a medication in another room
items.rationale: Protecting information from those without a need to know. An open record under your login exposes data and attributes anything done next to you.

items.text: A nurse contacts the primary provider to relay a patient's wish for comfort care despite family objections
items.rationale: Advocacy promotes care that reflects the patient's wishes. It points outward at the patient, even when others disagree.

items.text: A nurse says, "I will be back in 20 minutes with your next dose," and returns at the stated time
items.rationale: Responsibility is following through on what you accepted. Keeping a stated commitment is the everyday form of it.

questions.takeaway: Accountability points back at you, responsibility points at the work, advocacy points at the patient, confidentiality protects the information.
questions.strategy: Matching items are answered by direction. Ask where each action points before reaching for a definition.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Backward at yourself, at the work, outward at the patient, or at the information.
Logging out is unambiguously confidentiality.
Each term is used once, so the last pairing is fixed by elimination.

questions.note: Two of these terms are frequently confused. Decide whether the action answers for the past or delivers on the present.

questions.stem: A disagreement about the goals of care for a client with advanced illness cannot be resolved between the team and the family. Both positions are defensible, no law has been broken, and the discussion has stalled after two meetings. Which resource does the nurse recommend?

options.text: The charge nurse
options.rationale: Manages the shift, not the ethical question.

options.text: The State Board of Nursing
options.rationale: Handles licensure and discipline and enforces the standard of care. Legal, not philosophical, and it is the trap worth understanding.

options.text: The multidisciplinary ethics committee
options.rationale: The body that determines an ethical course of action when a dilemma arises in patient care. Multidisciplinary matters, because the point is several perspectives on one hard case.

options.text: Risk management
options.rationale: Prevents harm and financial loss from liability, and is problem-focused rather than values-focused.

questions.takeaway: Ethical course of action means the ethics committee. Discipline or licensure means the Board.
questions.strategy: Sort by what the body does. One writes standards, one advises on a case, one disciplines licensees, one manages liability.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: An unresolved values disagreement in patient care.
A staffing role.
Discipline and licensure.
Liability prevention.

elimination.verdict: That leaves C: the body that determines an ethical course of action when a dilemma arises in patient care.

questions.stem: A family asks the nurse not to tell a patient about a new cancer diagnosis. The patient has asked the nurse three times what the tests showed. What is the nurse's BEST action?

options.text: Agree to the family's request to protect the patient
options.rationale: Abandons the patient's autonomy and makes you party to withholding information they have requested.

options.text: Tell the patient the diagnosis directly
options.rationale: Well-intentioned and outside your role. Disclosure of a diagnosis belongs to the provider.

options.text: Explore the family's concerns and notify the provider
options.rationale: Neither agrees to the deception nor steps outside your scope. Exploring usually surfaces fear, and the provider is the one who discloses.

options.text: Document the family's request and take no further action
options.rationale: Records the problem and leaves the patient exactly where they were.

questions.takeaway: When a family asks you to withhold information, the answer is rarely yes or no. It is explore, then involve the provider.
questions.strategy: Two options here are the obvious poles. The answer is almost always the one that works the problem rather than resolving it in either direction.

strategies: Priority key word

steps.detail: Key word BEST, and the patient has asked repeatedly.
Violates autonomy and veracity.
Outside nursing scope.
Documents without acting.

elimination.verdict: That leaves C: neither agrees to the deception nor steps outside your scope.

questions.note: More than one action may eventually be needed. Select the action that is both within scope and responsive to the patient.

questions.stem: A nurse reviews the chart of a client with advanced illness whose family disagrees with the plan of care. The record contains laboratory values, routine care entries, a written directive, and notes about the disagreement. Highlight the findings that indicate an ethical problem rather than a purely clinical one.

segments.text: Client has a written advance directive requesting comfort measures only
segments.rationale: A documented decision. On its own it is a clinical fact to follow, not a conflict.

segments.text: Adult daughter has asked staff to continue aggressive treatment against the directive
segments.rationale: Two defensible positions grounded in different principles, autonomy and beneficence.

segments.text: Hemoglobin is 9.2 g/dL
segments.rationale: A laboratory value requiring clinical judgment, not ethical reasoning.

segments.text: A staff nurse has told the client's family that the directive can be ignored if they insist
segments.rationale: Misinformation that undermines the client's documented autonomy.

segments.text: Client received scheduled analgesia at 0800
segments.rationale: Routine care.

segments.text: Team members disagree about whether the client's quality of life justifies further treatment
segments.rationale: Quality of life is contested because it is culturally shaped, individually defined, and largely unmeasurable.

segments.text: Client is unresponsive and cannot participate in the discussion
segments.rationale: A clinical fact that raises the stakes and is not itself the ethical problem.

questions.takeaway: Recognizing that a situation involves an ethical problem is the first step in working toward resolution.
questions.strategy: An ethical problem exists where defensible positions conflict or where someone's documented autonomy is at risk. A difficult clinical fact is not the same thing.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Two parties wanting different things on principled grounds.
Misinformation about a directive threatens the client's decision.
Laboratory values and routine care are clinical, not ethical.

elimination.verdict: Highlight s2, s4, and s6.

questions.note: Several findings are clinically significant without being ethical problems. Highlight only the ethical ones.

questions.stem: A nurse believes a patient needs unhurried discharge teaching but has six patients and no time to provide it. She knows exactly what the patient needs and cannot deliver it. Which term describes her experience?

options.text: Ethical dilemma
options.rationale: Requires that you do NOT know what is right, because two defensible options pull against each other. Here nothing is unclear.

options.text: Moral distress
options.rationale: You know what is right and something outside you prevents it. The barrier is staffing and time.

options.text: Values conflict
options.rationale: Would mean her values clash with someone else's.

options.text: Negligence
options.rationale: A legal term requiring a breach of the standard of care.

questions.takeaway: One question separates them: do you know what is right? No means dilemma. Yes, and you are blocked, means moral distress.
questions.strategy: Phrases like the nurse believes or the nurse knows signal that the right action is already clear, which points at moral distress.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: She knows what is right, so it is not a dilemma.
No competing values between people are described.
No breach of the standard of care has occurred.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B. Unaddressed moral distress drives burnout.

questions.stem: A care team is struggling to agree on a plan for a patient with a severe chronic illness because members disagree about the patient's quality of life. Which statements help explain why consensus on this term is difficult to reach? Select all that apply.

options.text: Community and cultural values shape definitions of quality, and these values shift over time
options.rationale: Quality of life is socially constructed, so the standard itself moves between groups and across decades.

options.text: A person's individual life experiences influence how they personally define quality of life
options.rationale: Two people with identical function can rate their lives very differently based on what they have lived.

options.text: Elements such as meaningful work and family relationships are difficult to measure objectively
options.rationale: The components that matter most to people resist measurement, which is why teams cannot simply check them.

options.text: Whether a person is employed is the single objective measure that should determine quality of life
options.rationale: Reduces a contested multidimensional concept to one variable, and employment status says nothing about meaning.

options.text: Outcomes that cannot be easily quantified are difficult to evaluate using standard statistical methods
options.rationale: Unmeasurable outcomes cannot be compared across patients, which is part of why evidence does not settle the disagreement.

questions.takeaway: Quality of life is contested because it is culturally shaped, individually defined, and largely unmeasurable.
questions.strategy: The wrong option in a quality-of-life item is usually the one offering a single objective substitute for the whole concept.

strategies: Eliminate absolutes

steps.detail: The question asks why consensus is hard, so correct options explain difficulty.
Single and should determine are both absolutes, and employment is not a proxy for meaning.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, and E are selected.

questions.note: One option offers a simple measurable substitute for a complex concept. That is the distractor pattern here.

questions.stem: A nurse educator teaches the framework used to reason through difficult decisions in client care, and asks students to distinguish it from the nursing process, the delegation rights, and the handoff tool they have also learned. Which set names the ethical principles in this chapter?

options.text: Autonomy, beneficence, nonmaleficence, justice, and fidelity
options.rationale: The five principles, with fidelity meaning keeping promises and commitments.

options.text: Assessment, diagnosis, planning, implementation, evaluation
options.rationale: The nursing process.

options.text: Right task, circumstance, person, directions, supervision
options.rationale: The five rights of delegation.

options.text: Situation, background, assessment, recommendation
options.rationale: SBAR is a handoff structure for communicating about a patient, not a set of ethical principles.

questions.takeaway: Autonomy, beneficence, nonmaleficence, justice, fidelity.
questions.strategy: Distractors here are drawn from the other five-part frameworks in this course. Match the set to the name in the stem.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The ethical principles specifically.
The nursing process.
Delegation.
A handoff tool.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A: the five principles, with fidelity meaning keeping promises and commitments.

questions.scenario: A nurse works a medical unit shift and takes several actions during the day.
questions.stem: A nurse works a shift on a medical unit and takes several actions: repositioning a client, withholding a medication, honouring a refusal, and allocating the last available sitter. Her educator asks her to identify the principle behind each. For each nursing action, indicate which ethical principle it BEST demonstrates.

rows.text: Repositions a patient every two hours to prevent skin breakdown
rows.rationale: An action taken to produce benefit.

rows.text: Holds a scheduled antihypertensive when the systolic pressure is 84
rows.rationale: Refraining in order to prevent foreseeable harm.

rows.text: Honors a competent patient's refusal of a bath after confirming she understands
rows.rationale: The patient decides, and understanding was confirmed.

rows.text: Assigns the last available one-to-one sitter to the patient at highest fall risk
rows.rationale: A scarce resource allocated on need rather than preference.

rows.text: Provides pain medication before a painful dressing change
rows.rationale: An action taken to produce benefit.

rows.text: Stops an infusion when the site shows signs of infiltration
rows.rationale: Stopping to prevent tissue injury.

questions.takeaway: Acting to help is beneficence. Refraining to prevent injury is nonmaleficence. The patient deciding is autonomy. Scarcity is justice.
questions.strategy: Work each row by asking whether the nurse added something, withheld something, deferred to the patient, or divided a resource.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Provides and repositions are actions; holds and stops are refraining.
One sitter for several candidates is allocation.
Honoring a refusal is the patient deciding.

elimination.verdict: Two beneficence, two nonmaleficence, one autonomy, one justice.

questions.stem: A nurse prepares to give a scheduled dose of metoprolol and finds the client's heart rate is 44, down from 62 this morning. She withholds the dose and notifies the provider before the next scheduled administration. Which principle does this action demonstrate?

options.text: Nonmaleficence
options.rationale: The nurse refrained in order to prevent harm. A rate of 44 with a drug that slows the heart is foreseeable injury.

options.text: Beneficence
options.rationale: The pair-mate and the trap. Beneficence is acting to do good; this nurse withheld an action.

options.text: Fidelity
options.rationale: Keeping promises and commitments, which is not what is being tested here.

options.text: Justice
options.rationale: Fairness in allocation.

questions.takeaway: Ask whether the nurse acted or refrained. Adding something is beneficence; withholding to prevent injury is nonmaleficence.
questions.strategy: When both principles appear as options, the verb in the stem decides it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Withholds is the key word.
Beneficence requires an action taken.
Neither truth-telling nor allocation is present.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A: the nurse refrained in order to prevent harm.

questions.stem: A care team disagrees with a family about continuing aggressive treatment for a patient with an advance directive requesting comfort measures. Place the following actions in the correct order the nurse should take to work toward resolution, from FIRST to LAST.

options.text: Gather all relevant clinical, social, and spiritual information about the situation
options.rationale: You cannot reason about a situation you have not described. Gathering comes after recognizing there is an ethical question and before values are sorted.

options.text: Recognize that the situation involves an ethical problem, not just a clinical one
options.rationale: Nothing else can happen until the problem is named as ethical. Treated as purely clinical, the disagreement gets managed rather than resolved.

options.text: Clarify the values and key ethical principles and relationships involved
options.rationale: With the facts assembled, name whose values are in play and which principles collide. Here autonomy and beneficence pull against each other.

options.text: List the possible actions that could be taken to address the disagreement
options.rationale: Options are generated only after the values are clear, otherwise you are choosing between actions without knowing what you are optimizing for.

options.text: Develop and implement a plan that addresses the identified problem
options.rationale: Acting comes last, and it addresses the problem as defined rather than the surface disagreement.

questions.takeaway: Recognize it as ethical, gather information, clarify values, list options, then act.
questions.strategy: Ordered-response items reward finding the first and last step before sorting the middle. Recognition almost always opens a process and implementation almost always closes it.

strategies: Assessment before intervention

steps.detail: Recognizing the problem as ethical must precede everything.
Implementing a plan is the only action step.
Information, then values, then options. Each depends on the one before it.

elimination.verdict: B, A, C, D, E.

questions.stem: A patient tells the nurse he does not want his daughter making decisions for him, but he is afraid to say so because she has always managed the family. Which nursing action BEST demonstrates advocacy?

options.text: Tell the daughter that her father does not want her involved
options.rationale: Speaks for the patient in a way he did not authorize and may damage the relationship he is trying to protect.

options.text: Support the patient in expressing his wishes and ensure the record reflects who he designates
options.rationale: Advocacy promotes care that reflects the patient's wishes. It amplifies his voice rather than replacing it.

options.text: Encourage the patient to accept his daughter's help since she knows him well
options.rationale: Persuasion toward someone else's preference, which is the opposite of advocacy.

options.text: Document the conversation and take no further action
options.rationale: Records the concern and leaves the situation unchanged.

questions.takeaway: Advocacy amplifies the patient's voice. It does not speak instead of them.
questions.strategy: The word BEST is asking you to rank. Options that act on the patient's behalf without their direction are not advocacy.

strategies: Client-centered option

steps.detail: The patient has a wish and is afraid to state it.
Speaks for him without authorization.
Persuades toward another person's preference.
Documents without acting.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B: advocacy promotes care that reflects the patient's wishes.

questions.stem: Two patients need the unit's only negative-pressure room. One has suspected tuberculosis and one has a wound infection. The charge nurse assigns the room based on transmission risk. Which principle is applied?

options.text: Beneficence
options.rationale: Would describe doing good for one patient, but the question is how to choose between two.

options.text: Fidelity
options.rationale: Fidelity is keeping promises and commitments, which is not what a decision about allocating a scarce room turns on.

options.text: Justice
options.rationale: Fairness in the distribution of a scarce resource, allocated on clinical risk rather than on who advocated loudest.

options.text: Autonomy
options.rationale: Would apply if a patient were making a decision, and neither is.

questions.takeaway: Justice questions almost always involve scarcity. One bed, one room, limited staff, triage.
questions.strategy: Look for two claimants and one resource. That structure names the principle before you read the options.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Two patients, one room.
The question is allocation, not care of one.
No promise and no patient decision.

elimination.verdict: That leaves C: fairness in the distribution of a scarce resource, allocated on clinical risk rather than on who advocated loudest.

questions.stem: A nurse is asked by a student which organization sets the ethical standards for the profession nationally, as opposed to the body that disciplines licensees or the committee that advises on a single case. Which body publishes the code of ethics for nurses in the United States?

options.text: The American Nurses Association
options.rationale: The ANA publishes the Code of Ethics for Nurses, alongside the ICN internationally.

options.text: The State Board of Nursing
options.rationale: Enforces licensure and discipline under the Nurse Practice Act. It is legal, not philosophical.

options.text: The organizational ethics committee
options.rationale: Works a specific patient case and is advisory rather than binding.

options.text: The Joint Commission
options.rationale: Sets accreditation standards including safety goals, not the profession's ethical code.

questions.takeaway: ANA and ICN write the codes. The Board enforces licensure. The ethics committee works a case.
questions.strategy: Three different bodies get confused here, and each has a distinct function. Sort by what each one produces.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Which body publishes the profession's ethical code.
Enforcement, not authorship.
Advisory on a single case.
Accreditation standards.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A: the ANA publishes the Code of Ethics for Nurses, alongside the ICN internationally.

questions.stem: A competent 67-year-old refuses his prescribed antihypertensive, saying it makes him dizzy and he would rather manage without it. He understands he has high blood pressure. The nurse must respond within her role. Which nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Determine the reason for the refusal
options.rationale: Often uncovers a side effect or misunderstanding that can be resolved.

options.text: Ensure the patient understands the risks of not taking it
options.rationale: A refusal is only informed if the patient knows what refusing costs.

options.text: Conceal the medication in food so the patient receives the dose
options.rationale: Removes consent entirely and is never acceptable, however compassionate the intent.

options.text: Notify the health care provider
options.rationale: So the plan can be reconsidered.

options.text: Document that the patient is noncompliant
options.rationale: Noncompliant is a judgment. Documentation must be factual: what was refused and what the patient said.

options.text: Document the refusal and the patient's stated reason
options.rationale: The factual entry that belongs in the record.

questions.takeaway: Confirm understanding, notify the provider, and document factually. Not to change the patient's mind.
questions.strategy: Two wrong options here are the compassionate violation and the judgmental charting entry. Both recur across the legal and ethics chapters.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A competent patient refusing.
Concealment removes consent.
Noncompliant is a judgment, not a fact.

elimination.verdict: A, B, D, and F are selected.

questions.stem: A nurse and a colleague disagree about whether to tell a client something his family wants withheld. One argues from her own upbringing about honesty, the other from the profession's agreed standards. Their educator explains that these are two different things. Which statement correctly distinguishes morals from ethics?

options.text: Ethics are personal judgments and morals are professional standards
options.rationale: Reverses the two terms. Morals are the personal judgments and ethics is the study of how such judgments are determined.

options.text: Morals are personal judgments about right and wrong; ethics is the study of how such judgments are determined
options.rationale: A person has morals. A profession has ethics, meaning both the reasoning and the agreed standards such as the ANA and ICN codes.

options.text: Ethics are legally enforceable statutes and morals are not
options.rationale: Ethical standards are enforced by boards and employers but they are not statutes.

options.text: Morals are universal and ethics are relative to each situation
options.rationale: States the relative-and-universal distinction backwards.

questions.takeaway: Morals are the judgments. Ethics is the reasoning behind them, and also a profession's agreed standards.
questions.strategy: Both senses of ethics appear on exams. If an option makes ethics purely legal or purely personal, it is wrong.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The question asks how the two differ.
Reversed.
Confuses ethics with law.
States the distinction backwards.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B: a person has morals.

questions.topic: Ethical conflict at end of life
questions.scenario: A patient with advanced heart failure has a written advance directive requesting comfort measures only. He is now unresponsive. His adult children insist that everything be done and have told the nurse they will hold her responsible if their father dies. The provider has written orders consistent with the directive. The nurse feels caught between the document and the family's distress.
questions.stem: Complete the diagram by selecting from the choices below.

options.text: Follow the advance directive and the current orders while supporting the family
options.rationale: The directive is the patient's own decision and it carries legal weight. Autonomy holds when the patient can no longer speak.

options.text: Request a consultation with the multidisciplinary ethics committee
options.rationale: The body that determines an ethical course of action when a dilemma arises in patient care.

options.text: Provide resuscitative measures because the family has demanded them
options.rationale: Overrides the patient's documented decision on the basis of family preference.

options.text: Tell the family the decision is not theirs to make and end the conversation
options.rationale: Factually close and it abandons a family in distress, which is itself part of nursing care.

options.text: Contact the State Board of Nursing for direction
options.rationale: The Board handles licensure and discipline. It does not advise on a patient's care decisions.

options.text: An ethical dilemma between the patient's autonomy and the family's beneficence
options.rationale: Two defensible positions, each grounded in a real principle. Nobody is behaving badly and the right action is contested.

options.text: Moral distress in the nurse
options.rationale: Would require that the nurse knows what is right and is blocked. Here the orders and the directive agree, so she is not blocked.

options.text: A legal violation by the family
options.rationale: Disagreeing with a directive is not itself unlawful.

options.text: A failure of the provider to write appropriate orders
options.rationale: The orders are consistent with the directive.

options.text: The family's understanding of the directive and their emotional response
options.rationale: The distress is real and addressable, and understanding is often what is missing.

options.text: Whether the patient's comfort needs are being met
options.rationale: Comfort measures only is an active plan, not the absence of one.

options.text: The nurse's own liability exposure
options.rationale: A concern, not a clinical monitoring parameter for this patient.

options.text: Family satisfaction survey scores
options.rationale: Not a clinical parameter.

options.text: Serum electrolytes every six hours
options.rationale: Inconsistent with a comfort-focused plan.

questions.takeaway: A written directive speaks for the patient when the patient cannot. Family preference does not override it.
questions.strategy: The family's threat is a deliberate pressure in the stem. It does not change what the patient decided, and it does not make the nurse's response colder.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Two defensible positions grounded in different principles.
Overrides the patient's own decision.

steps.action: Cut the dismissive response and the Board
steps.detail: One abandons the family, one is the wrong body.

elimination.verdict: Actions A and B, condition A, parameters A and B.

questions.stem: A conscious adult with a life-threatening gastrointestinal hemorrhage has an order for 2 units of packed red blood cells. The spouse insists the patient would refuse blood products for religious reasons, but the patient cannot communicate directly because of confusion from blood loss. What is the nurse's FIRST responsibility?

options.text: Withhold the transfusion based on the spouse's statement
options.rationale: Acts on an unverified report of the patient's wishes. A spouse does not automatically hold decision-making authority.

options.text: Administer the blood as ordered since the patient has not personally refused
options.rationale: Ignores credible evidence about the patient's values and treats silence as consent.

options.text: Gather more information, including whether the spouse holds documented health care power of attorney and whether an advance directive exists
options.rationale: Both extremes act before the facts are known. A documented advance directive or a health care power of attorney converts the spouse's claim into a legally binding one.

options.text: Contact the ethics committee before taking any further action
options.rationale: Appropriate later if a genuine conflict remains, and it is not the first step in a hemorrhage.

questions.takeaway: Verify decision-making authority before acting on a surrogate's report of what a patient would want.
questions.strategy: When two options are opposite actions, the answer is often the one that establishes the facts first. Both poles are wrong for the same reason.

strategies: Assessment before intervention

steps.detail: Key word FIRST. The patient cannot speak and the spouse is reporting.
Both act on an incomplete picture, in opposite directions.
A reasonable later step, not the first one in an emergency.

elimination.verdict: That leaves C: both extremes act before the facts are known.

questions.note: More than one action may eventually be needed. Select the correct FIRST step.

questions.stem: A nurse manager investigates several incidents on her unit over the past month, including a record accessed without a care reason, a client restrained without an order, and vital signs charted that were never taken. She must determine which carry consequences beyond employment. Which actions could result in BOTH criminal and administrative sanctions? Select all that apply.

options.text: Accessing the record of a family member on another unit out of curiosity
options.rationale: A privacy violation carrying federal penalties and board discipline. Being related to the patient grants no access.

options.text: Applying physical restraints without an order and without following agency policy
options.rationale: Restraining a person without authority can constitute false imprisonment or battery, and it breaches the standard of care.

options.text: Reporting a reasonable suspicion of child abuse to the appropriate authority
options.rationale: A legally protected and mandated action. Good-faith reporting carries immunity.

options.text: Falsifying documentation of vital signs to avoid appearing behind
options.rationale: Fraudulent record-keeping is criminal and is grounds for licensure action.

options.text: Completing a routine occurrence report after a minor fall with no injury
options.rationale: A risk management process functioning as intended, not sanctionable conduct.

questions.takeaway: Privacy breaches, unauthorized restraint, and falsified records carry both criminal and licensure consequences.
questions.strategy: Two options in this item describe protected or routine actions. Identify those first and the rest follow.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: BOTH criminal and administrative, so ordinary errors do not qualify.
Mandated reporting is protected.
Occurrence reports are routine risk management.

elimination.verdict: A, B, and D are selected.

questions.note: Two options describe legally PROTECTED or routine nursing actions, not sanctionable conduct.

questions.stem: A home health nurse notes multiple bruises in various stages of healing on the head, abdomen, and posterior legs of a nonambulatory 8-month-old infant. The caregiver states the bruises are from the infant rolling off the couch a few times. What is the nurse's FIRST priority action?

options.text: Document the findings in detail and complete a full physical assessment
options.rationale: Essential and not first. Documentation supports the report; it does not substitute for making it.

options.text: Report the reasonable suspicion of abuse to the appropriate child protective authority
options.rationale: Nurses are mandated reporters. A nonambulatory infant cannot produce bruises in varied stages across those sites, so the explanation is not plausible and the threshold for reporting is met now.

options.text: Confront the caregiver about the inconsistency in the explanation
options.rationale: Risks the child's safety by alerting a possible perpetrator, and it is not the nurse's role to investigate.

options.text: Discuss the situation with a colleague for a second opinion first
options.rationale: Delays a mandated report. The standard is reasonable suspicion, not certainty.

questions.takeaway: Mandated reporting requires reasonable suspicion, not proof, and it is not delayed for confirmation.
questions.strategy: The detail that decides this is nonambulatory. An infant who cannot move independently cannot self-inflict bruises in multiple stages across several body regions.

strategies: Priority key word

steps.detail: Key word FIRST, with a nonambulatory infant and an implausible explanation.
Documentation supports but does not replace the report.
Investigation is not the nurse's role and may endanger the child.
Reasonable suspicion is the threshold, so no second opinion is required.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B: nurses are mandated reporters.

questions.note: Documentation is essential, but consider which action is legally mandated FIRST given a nonambulatory infant with these findings.

questions.stem: A patient in skeletal traction develops pale, cold toes with decreased sensation. The nurse becomes occupied with another patient's emergency and never documents or reports the finding. Two days later the leg requires amputation. Which statements correctly describe a breach of duty in this situation? Select all that apply.

options.text: Failure to document the change in neurovascular assessment findings
options.rationale: Documentation is part of the standard of care, and an undocumented finding is invisible to everyone who follows.

options.text: Failure to notify the provider about a significant change in condition
options.rationale: The change required an order to act on, and the omission is the direct link to the harm.

options.text: Failure to provide discharge teaching about cast care
options.rationale: Not relevant to this injury. The patient is in traction and the harm occurred during the admission.

options.text: Failure to recognize and act on early signs of impaired circulation
options.rationale: A reasonably prudent nurse recognizes pale, cold, insensate toes as neurovascular compromise.

options.text: Failure to complete an occurrence report for the other patient's emergency
options.rationale: Unrelated to this patient's harm and not a breach of duty toward him.

questions.takeaway: Breach of duty means conduct fell below what a reasonably prudent nurse would do, and it must connect to the harm.
questions.strategy: Two options here describe real nursing responsibilities that are not connected to this patient's injury. Relevance to the harm is what makes an omission a breach.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The harm is amputation from unrecognized circulatory compromise.
Cast care teaching is unrelated to a patient in traction.
Concerns a different patient.

elimination.verdict: A, B, and D are selected.

questions.note: Two options describe nursing responsibilities that are real but unconnected to this patient's harm.

questions.stem: A patient scheduled for surgery is unable to describe the procedure and asks the nurse what will be done. The consent form is unsigned. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Explain the procedure so the consent can be signed
options.rationale: Generous and outside your role. Explaining the procedure belongs to the provider, and doing it yourself produces a signature on an explanation the provider never gave.

options.text: Ask another nurse to witness the signature
options.rationale: Witnesses a consent you know is not informed.

options.text: Stop the process and contact the provider
options.rationale: The nurse verifies that the patient is competent, that the signature is voluntary, and that the patient understands what the provider explained. Not understanding means the third condition has failed.

options.text: Have the patient sign and document that teaching will follow
options.rationale: Reverses the order and records a consent obtained without understanding.

questions.takeaway: Confusion or not understanding is a stop signal, not a teaching opportunity.
questions.strategy: The nurse's role in consent is verification, not explanation. Any option that has you explaining the procedure is wrong.

strategies: Assessment before intervention

steps.detail: The patient cannot describe the procedure.
Explaining is the provider's role.
Both proceed with a consent known to be uninformed.

elimination.verdict: That leaves C. The same applies at any hint of coercion.

questions.stem: A nurse completes an occurrence report after a client's minor fall with no injury. A colleague tells her she should not have filed it because it will be used against her, and asks whether it belongs in the chart. Which statement about the occurrence report is correct?

options.text: It becomes part of the patient's medical record
options.rationale: It is a risk management tool and is not part of the record, which is why it can capture system detail the chart does not.

options.text: The nurse documents in the chart that a report was completed
options.rationale: The subtle error. Chart the clinical facts only; referencing the report pulls it toward the legal record.

options.text: It is used to identify problems and take corrective action
options.rationale: Risk management is a systems process aimed at preventing recurrence, and review of these reports is its basic component.

options.text: It is completed only when a patient is injured
options.rationale: Near-misses are reported precisely so harm can be prevented.

questions.takeaway: The occurrence report is a systems tool, not part of the record, and not a disciplinary instrument.
questions.strategy: Treating these reports as punishment is what stops people filing them, which is the lesson of every high-profile medication error case.

strategies: Eliminate absolutes

steps.detail: The question asks what the report is for.
It sits outside the medical record.
Referencing it in the chart defeats its protection.
Only is absolute, and near-misses are reportable.

elimination.verdict: That leaves C: risk management is a systems process aimed at preventing recurrence, and review of these reports is its basic component.

questions.stem: A nurse is named in a malpractice claim after a client was harmed. Her attorney explains that her conduct will be compared against a defined benchmark rather than against her own view of the situation or the best nurse on the unit. Against which standard is her conduct measured?

options.text: What the most experienced nurse in the facility would have done
options.rationale: Raises the bar to an ideal that no one meets and that is not the legal test.

options.text: What a reasonably prudent nurse would do under similar circumstances in the same geographical area
options.rationale: The skill and knowledge commonly exercised by nurses currently practicing, with both qualifiers.

options.text: Whatever the facility policy manual specifies
options.rationale: Policy is one input alongside law and professional organizations, not the whole standard.

options.text: The nurse's own judgment about what was appropriate at the time
options.rationale: Would make the standard whatever each nurse believed, which is no standard at all.

questions.takeaway: Reasonably prudent, similar circumstances, same geographical area.
questions.strategy: Options that raise the standard to perfection or lower it to personal judgment are both wrong. The test is an ordinary competent nurse.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The legal test for conduct.
An ideal rather than a reasonable nurse.
Policy is one input.
No objective standard.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B: the skill and knowledge commonly exercised by nurses currently practicing, with both qualifiers.

questions.stem: A nurse manager reviews four reported events: a competent client restrained after refusing, a client discussed by name in a crowded lift where a visitor recognized her, a client threatened with an injection unless he cooperated, and a required assessment omitted with resulting harm. Match each situation with the legal term it BEST illustrates. Each term is used only once.

items.text: A nurse restrains a competent patient who has refused, without an order
items.rationale: Confining a person without authority or consent. The refusal and the absent order are what make it a tort.

items.text: A nurse discusses a patient by name in a crowded elevator and a visitor recognizes her
items.rationale: A quasi-intentional tort. Harm was not intended, and it resulted from the nature of the act.

items.text: A nurse threatens to give an injection unless a patient cooperates
items.rationale: Assault is the threat that creates fear of harmful contact. No touching has occurred yet.

items.text: A nurse omits a required assessment and the patient is harmed as a result
items.rationale: Professional negligence: duty, breach of the standard, and resulting harm.

questions.takeaway: Assault is the threat, battery is the contact, false imprisonment is confinement, invasion of privacy is disclosure.
questions.strategy: Sort by whether the act was intended, whether contact occurred, and whether harm followed from carelessness or from the act itself.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Only the omission describes carelessness rather than a chosen act.
A threat with no touching is assault.
Each term is used once.

questions.note: One of these is unintentional and three are intentional or quasi-intentional. Sort by intent first.

questions.stem: A nurse is completing annual compliance training and is asked which law governs how client information is stored, accessed, and shared, as distinct from the law defining what she may do as a nurse. Which federal statute governs the privacy and security of protected health information?

options.text: HIPAA
options.rationale: The Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act, which sets the privacy and security standards for protected health information.

options.text: The Nurse Practice Act
options.rationale: A state statute defining scope of practice.

options.text: The Good Samaritan law
options.rationale: Protects voluntary aid at an emergency scene.

options.text: The Patient Self-Determination Act
options.rationale: Requires that patients be informed of their right to make advance directives, which is a different federal statute.

questions.takeaway: HIPAA governs privacy and security of health information. The Nurse Practice Act is state law defining scope.
questions.strategy: Sort by level: federal statute, state statute, or a protection. Option D is a real federal statute addressing a different right.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Privacy and security of health information.
State law on scope.
Emergency aid protection.
Advance directives, not privacy.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A: the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act, which sets the privacy and security standards for protected health information.

questions.stem: A nurse admits a 76-year-old for elective surgery and asks whether he has documented his wishes about future care. He says his daughter will decide if anything goes wrong, but has signed nothing. Which statements about advance directives are accurate? Select all that apply.

options.text: They allow a competent adult to state wishes about future care
options.rationale: The purpose of the document.

options.text: A health care power of attorney designates a person to make decisions if the patient cannot
options.rationale: A durable power of attorney for health care names the surrogate.

options.text: They take effect only when the patient can no longer make or communicate decisions
options.rationale: A competent patient continues to decide for themselves regardless of what the document says.

options.text: A family member automatically has authority to override a written directive
options.rationale: Family standing does not override a documented directive, and this is the assumption that creates the conflicts requiring ethics committees.

options.text: The nurse should confirm whether a directive exists on admission
options.rationale: Part of admission assessment, and finding out at the point of crisis is too late.

questions.takeaway: The directive speaks for the patient when the patient cannot. Family preference does not override it.
questions.strategy: Any option granting family automatic authority over a written directive is wrong, and it appears frequently.

strategies: Eliminate absolutes

steps.detail: The question asks which statements are accurate.
Automatically is absolute, and family standing does not override the document.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, and E are selected.

questions.stem: A nurse reviews an order for a medication and believes the dose is ten times higher than expected for this client's weight and condition. The prescribing provider is unavailable and the medication is due now. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Administer the dose since the provider wrote the order
options.rationale: The most important wrong answer in this chapter. Carrying out an incorrect order makes the error yours as well; the provider's responsibility does not erase yours.

options.text: Follow the chain of command to clarify the order before administering
options.rationale: The nurse must determine that an order is complete, clear, appropriate, safe, consistent with the condition, and within scope. When it is not, you clarify before acting.

options.text: Refuse to give the medication and say nothing further
options.rationale: The patient goes untreated and no one knows why.

options.text: Ask another nurse to administer it instead
options.rationale: Transfers the risk to a colleague and changes nothing about the order.

questions.takeaway: An order is not a substitute for nursing judgment.
questions.strategy: This principle recurs in legal implications, medication administration, and delegation. It is one of the most repeated ideas in the course.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A dose that appears tenfold too high.
Following an unsafe order makes the error yours.
Refusing silently abandons the patient.
Moves the risk without resolving it.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B: the nurse must determine that an order is complete, clear, appropriate, safe, consistent with the condition, and within scope.

questions.stem: An 83-year-old admitted two days ago is confused and pulling at his intravenous line, which he has already dislodged once. He is febrile at 38.3 degrees Celsius and received an opioid two hours ago. The unit is short-staffed. Which action does the nurse take FIRST?

options.text: Apply soft wrist restraints
options.rationale: Restraints are a last resort and can worsen confusion and agitation.

options.text: Assess for the cause of the confusion and try least restrictive measures
options.rationale: Confusion has a cause, and infection, hypoxia, medications, and dehydration are all reversible. Least restrictive intervention comes first.

options.text: Raise all four side rails
options.rationale: Four raised side rails constitute a restraint, which students frequently do not realize.

options.text: Request an order for a sedative
options.rationale: Adds to the medication burden that may be causing the confusion.

questions.takeaway: Least restrictive intervention first, and four raised side rails count as a restraint.
questions.strategy: Three of these options are restraints or chemical restraint in different clothing. Only one assesses.

strategies: Assessment before intervention

steps.detail: Key word FIRST, with confusion of unknown cause.
Both are restraints.
Chemical restraint, and it may worsen the cause.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B: confusion has a cause, and infection, hypoxia, medications, and dehydration are all reversible.

questions.stem: A nurse realizes she has administered a scheduled medication to the wrong client. He is alert, asymptomatic, and the drug was not one he takes. She must respond before continuing her round. Place the following actions in the correct order, from FIRST to LAST.

options.text: Assess the patient for effects of the medication given
options.rationale: The patient comes first. Everything else follows from knowing whether harm has occurred.

options.text: Notify the health care provider of the error and the patient's status
options.rationale: The provider needs to know in order to prescribe monitoring or treatment.

options.text: Implement any prescribed monitoring or treatment
options.rationale: Acting on the orders that result from the notification.

options.text: Document the medication given, the assessment, and the provider notification in the record
options.rationale: The clinical facts belong in the record. Note that you document what happened, not that a report was filed.

options.text: Complete an occurrence report according to agency policy
options.rationale: A risk management tool, completed after the patient is safe, and it is not part of the medical record.

questions.takeaway: Patient first, provider second, treatment third, then the record, then the occurrence report.
questions.strategy: Every error-response sequence starts with assessing the patient and ends with the occurrence report. The middle is notify and treat.

strategies: Apply the ABCs
Assessment before intervention

steps.detail: Assessing the patient outranks any administrative action.
The occurrence report is a systems tool and comes last.
Notify, treat, then document the clinical facts.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D, E.

questions.note: The occurrence report is not part of the medical record, and the chart should not state that one was filed.

questions.stem: A new graduate asks her preceptor what she can do to protect herself legally, having heard that nurses are frequently named in claims. The preceptor explains that the strongest protection is something she already does every shift. Which nursing action most reduces legal risk?

options.text: Documenting care accurately, completely, and at the time it is provided
options.rationale: The record is the evidence of what was done, and contemporaneous accurate documentation is the strongest protection.

options.text: Avoiding documentation of any adverse event
options.rationale: Omission does not remove the event and undermines the record.

options.text: Carrying out every order without question
options.rationale: An order is not a substitute for nursing judgment, and following an unsafe order makes the error yours.

options.text: Relying on verbal handoff rather than written records
options.rationale: Verbal report does not survive the shift.

questions.takeaway: Accurate, complete, timely documentation is the strongest legal protection a nurse has.
questions.strategy: Three distractors here reduce the record rather than strengthen it. Anything that hides or omits raises risk.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The action that most reduces legal risk.
Omission is not protection.
Following unsafe orders creates liability.
Verbal report leaves no record.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A: the record is the evidence of what was done, and contemporaneous accurate documentation is the strongest protection.

questions.stem: A nurse administers a medication to the wrong client after omitting the armband check during a busy medication round. The client has an adverse reaction and requires treatment. Which term BEST describes this?

options.text: Negligence only
options.rationale: Not wrong so much as imprecise. Negligence is the broad category, and when a licensed professional commits it in that role the specific term is malpractice.

options.text: Malpractice
options.rationale: Negligence committed by a professional acting in that role. Duty existed, the armband check was omitted, conduct fell below the standard, and harm followed.

options.text: A quasi-intentional tort
options.rationale: Covers acts such as breaching confidentiality, where harm was not intended but resulted from the nature of the act.

options.text: An intentional tort
options.rationale: Requires intent, which is absent.

questions.takeaway: Malpractice is the professional species of negligence. Name a licensed professional in the stem and the answer is malpractice.
questions.strategy: The standard is what a reasonably prudent nurse would do under similar circumstances in the same geographical area.

strategies: Favour qualifiers

steps.detail: A licensed nurse acting in that role, with harm resulting.
Correct but not the specific term.
Neither intent nor a quasi-intentional act is present.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B: negligence committed by a professional acting in that role.

questions.scenario: A home health nurse visits a 79-year-old who has lost 6 kg since the last visit. She is wearing soiled clothing, has bruising on both upper arms, and flinches when her son enters the room. The son answers every question directed at her and says she has been refusing to eat. Her monthly pension has been withdrawn in full each month with no receipts for groceries or medications.
questions.stem: Complete the diagram by selecting from the choices below.

options.text: Interview the patient privately, away from the son
options.rationale: She cannot disclose while the possible perpetrator is answering for her, and a caregiver controlling communication is itself a red flag.

options.text: Report the reasonable suspicion to the appropriate adult protective authority
options.rationale: Nurses are mandated reporters, and reasonable suspicion is the threshold rather than proof.

options.text: Confront the son about the inconsistencies in his account
options.rationale: Investigation is not the nurse's role, and it may increase the risk to the patient after the visit ends.

options.text: Wait until the next scheduled visit to see whether the findings persist
options.rationale: Delays a mandated report and leaves her in the situation.

options.text: Advise the son on better nutrition and rebook in two weeks
options.rationale: Treats a possible neglect situation as an education gap.

options.text: Suspected elder mistreatment, including possible neglect and financial abuse
options.rationale: Weight loss, poor hygiene, unexplained bruising, fearfulness, a caregiver controlling communication, and unexplained financial withdrawals together.

options.text: Expected changes of aging
options.rationale: None of these findings is an expected change, and several are named red flags.

options.text: A patient exercising the right to refuse care
options.rationale: The refusal is reported by the son, not by the patient, and she has not been asked alone.

options.text: Early dementia affecting appetite
options.rationale: Would not explain the bruising, the fearfulness, or the missing funds.

options.text: Weight, hydration, and skin integrity
options.rationale: Objective markers of whether the neglect is ongoing.

options.text: The patient's account when interviewed alone
options.rationale: The information that has been unavailable so far, and the reason private interview is the first action.

options.text: The son's satisfaction with the care plan
options.rationale: Not a clinical parameter.

options.text: Serum amylase
options.rationale: Not indicated.

options.text: Visual acuity
options.rationale: Unrelated to the findings described.

questions.takeaway: Reasonable suspicion is the threshold for a mandated report, and the assessment happens privately.
questions.strategy: Two wrong actions here delay or investigate. Nurses report; they do not investigate, and delay leaves the patient where she is.

strategies: Assessment before intervention

steps.detail: Multiple named red flags occurring together.
Investigation is not the nurse's role and may raise the risk.
Both leave her in the situation.

elimination.verdict: Actions A and B, condition A, parameters A and B.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old scheduled for a mastectomy tomorrow tells the nurse she does not know how her husband will look at her afterward. She has been quiet all morning and has not asked about the surgery itself. What is the nurse's best response?

options.text: You are worried about how this will change how he sees you
options.rationale: Reflection. It hands the feeling back so she can look at it and keeps her talking.

options.text: Your husband loves you and that will not change
options.rationale: False reassurance, and she cannot know it. It closes the conversation.

options.text: Many women feel this way and do well afterward
options.rationale: A cliche that minimizes her specific fear.

options.text: Have you talked to him about how you feel?
options.rationale: Redirects to someone else rather than exploring what she just said.

questions.takeaway: The kindest-sounding option is usually wrong. The correct one often sounds flatter because it does not resolve anything.
questions.strategy: Ask whether the response invites more or ends the conversation.

strategies: Negative polarity
Priority key word

steps.detail: Key word: best. More than one option may be true, so you are ranking them.
False reassurance, and she cannot know it.
A cliche that minimizes her specific fear.
Redirects to someone else rather than exploring what she just said.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A. Reflection.

questions.stem: A nurse is precepting a student who has been talking with a client awaiting biopsy results. Reviewing the conversation afterward, the preceptor notes that several of the student's replies ended the exchange rather than opening it. Which nurse responses block therapeutic communication? Select all that apply.

options.text: Do not worry, everything will be fine
options.rationale: False reassurance promises an outcome nobody can guarantee, and it closes the conversation the patient just opened.

options.text: Why did you not call us sooner?
options.rationale: A why question, which produces defensiveness.

options.text: You seem worried about going home
options.rationale: Reflection, which is therapeutic.

options.text: I think you made the right decision
options.rationale: Approval is still a judgment and implies there was one acceptable answer.

options.text: Let us talk about something more pleasant
options.rationale: Changing the subject.

options.text: Tell me more about that
options.rationale: Open-ended and encourages elaboration.

questions.takeaway: Approval blocks as surely as disapproval, because it tells the patient which answer you wanted.
questions.strategy: Reassurance, advice, why, subject changes, and judgments in either direction all block.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Polarity is positive. This is a select all that apply, so there is no single best answer. Judge each option separately.
Reflection, which is therapeutic.
Open-ended and encourages elaboration.

elimination.verdict: Keep A, B, D, E. In a SATA, judge each option as its own true or false statement rather than picking a single best answer.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old admitted for chemotherapy tells the nurse she is frightened about how her family will manage if the treatment does not work. Four nurses respond differently to the same statement, and the charge nurse uses the exchange to teach about therapeutic responses. Which nurse statement is a blocking response?

options.text: Tell me more about what happened at home
options.rationale: Open-ended and encourages elaboration.

options.text: Why did you stop taking your medication?
options.rationale: A why question, which reads as accusation and produces defensiveness.

options.text: It sounds like this has been frightening for you
options.rationale: Reflection, which is therapeutic.

options.text: I will sit with you for a while
options.rationale: Offering self, which is therapeutic.

questions.takeaway: Rephrase why into what. Not why are you anxious, but you seem upset, what is on your mind.
questions.strategy: Scan for the word why. It is a blocking technique nearly every time it appears.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Polarity is positive. No priority key word, so look for the single accurate option.
Open-ended and encourages elaboration.
Reflection, which is therapeutic.
Offering self, which is therapeutic.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B. A why question, which reads as accusation and produces defensiveness.

options.text: Whether the patient is interested and ready to learn
options.rationale: Readiness determines whether anything you say will be retained.

questions.takeaway: Assess knowledge, barriers, and ability, then readiness, then learning needs.
questions.strategy: Factors about the nurse's schedule are never the answer on assessment questions.

strategies: Favour qualifiers

steps.detail: Polarity is positive. This is a select all that apply, so there is no single best answer. Judge each option separately.
A staffing constraint rather than a patient factor, and it must not drive whether teaching happens.

elimination.verdict: Keep A, B, C, E, F. In a SATA, judge each option as its own true or false statement rather than picking a single best answer.

questions.stem: A client nods through the whole of his discharge teaching, asks no questions, and says it all makes sense. The nurse notes he has missed two previous appointments and left half his registration form blank, saying he forgot his glasses. What should the nurse suspect?

options.text: Low health literacy
options.rationale: Missed appointments, incomplete forms, and no questions are recognized signs, and patients often hide it out of shame.

options.text: Disinterest in his own care
options.rationale: An assumption about motivation with no supporting data.

options.text: Cognitive impairment
options.rationale: Possible and not the most likely explanation for this pattern.

options.text: Nonadherence to the treatment plan
options.rationale: A label that hides the cause and removes the fix.

questions.takeaway: Missed appointments, blank forms, poor adherence, and no questions are cues, not character.
questions.strategy: When you are about to write nonadherent, look first for the quiet signs of low health literacy.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Polarity is positive. No priority key word, so look for the single accurate option.
An assumption about motivation with no supporting data.
Possible and not the most likely explanation for this pattern.
A label that hides the cause and removes the fix.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A. Missed appointments, incomplete forms, and no questions are recognized signs, and patients often hide it out of shame.

questions.stem: A 49-year-old newly diagnosed with type 2 diabetes tells the nurse the laboratory must have mixed up his results because he feels perfectly well, and declines to discuss glucose monitoring today. Which teaching approach is appropriate now?

options.text: Delay all teaching until he accepts the diagnosis
options.rationale: Present-tense teaching about current therapy is still appropriate and necessary.

options.text: Explain the long-term complications to motivate him
options.rationale: Attempting to convince a patient in denial produces anger or withdrawal.

options.text: Teach the full self-management plan since discharge is soon
options.rationale: He is in denial and cannot yet learn about a future he has not accepted.

options.text: Teach only about current therapy in the present tense and remain available
options.rationale: In denial, anger, and bargaining you teach in the present tense and do not argue about the illness.

questions.takeaway: Patients cannot learn while they are unable to accept the loss. Teach the present until they reach resolution.
questions.strategy: Match the teaching to the stage. Denial, anger, and bargaining all get present-tense teaching only.

strategies: Eliminate absolutes

steps.detail: Polarity is positive. No priority key word, so look for the single accurate option.
Present-tense teaching about current therapy is still appropriate and necessary.
Attempting to convince a patient in denial produces anger or withdrawal.
He is in denial and cannot yet learn about a future he has not accepted.

elimination.verdict: That leaves D. In denial, anger, and bargaining you teach in the present tense and do not argue about the illness.

questions.stem: A nurse is planning her shift and considering what she can delegate. A client needs initial teaching about a new diagnosis, another needs reinforcement of instructions already given, and a third has been taught to use a walker and now needs encouragement to practise. Which patient education task may be delegated to assistive personnel?

options.text: Evaluating whether the patient understood the teaching
options.rationale: Evaluation is never delegated.

options.text: Teaching a patient to use an incentive spirometer
options.rationale: Initial teaching is nursing process and cannot be delegated.

options.text: Reinforcing previously taught instructions on fluid intake
options.rationale: Reinforcement of teaching already provided is within AP scope.

options.text: Assessing the patient's learning needs
options.rationale: Assessment is never delegated.

questions.takeaway: Patient education is in the nurse's scope and cannot be delegated. Reinforcing is permitted; teaching is not.
questions.strategy: Assess, teach, evaluate, and plan never move. Reinforce does.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Polarity is positive. No priority key word, so look for the single accurate option.
Evaluation is never delegated.
Initial teaching is nursing process and cannot be delegated.
Assessment is never delegated.

elimination.verdict: That leaves C. Reinforcement of teaching already provided is within AP scope.

questions.stem: A nurse has taught a 62-year-old about a newly prescribed anticoagulant, covering dosing, bleeding precautions, and when to seek help. The client nodded throughout and said it made sense. The nurse must now determine whether he actually understood. Which action best evaluates learning?

options.text: Provide a written handout and confirm he received it
options.rationale: Receiving material is not learning.

options.text: Document that teaching was completed
options.rationale: Records a nursing action, not the patient's learning.

options.text: Ask whether he has any questions
options.rationale: A yes or no question that invites the answer ending the conversation.

options.text: Ask him to explain in his own words when to call the office
options.rationale: Teach-back. Understanding is confirmed only when he restates it accurately.

questions.takeaway: Replace do you understand with tell me in your own words.
questions.strategy: Any evaluation method answerable with yes or no is not evaluation.

strategies: Assessment before intervention
Priority key word

steps.detail: Polarity is positive. Key word: best. More than one option may be true, so you are ranking them.
Receiving material is not learning.
Records a nursing action, not the patient's learning.
A yes or no question that invites the answer ending the conversation.

elimination.verdict: That leaves D. Teach-back.

questions.stem: A nurse is handing over a client whose blood pressure has fallen through the shift and who now needs closer monitoring. The oncoming nurse has four other clients and has not met him. Which handoff report best supports continuity of care?

options.text: A structured report covering situation, background, assessment, and recommendation
options.rationale: SBAR gives the receiving nurse the picture and the ask in a predictable order, so nothing essential depends on memory.

options.text: A written note left at the workstation for the oncoming nurse to read
options.rationale: Removes the opportunity to ask questions.

options.text: A brief verbal summary of tasks still outstanding
options.rationale: Tasks without clinical context leave the next nurse unable to prioritize or recognize deterioration.

options.text: Directing the oncoming nurse to read the chart
options.rationale: Provides data without the interpretation that makes it usable.

questions.takeaway: SBAR reports. It exists so the receiving nurse gets context, not just a task list.
questions.strategy: Handoff items reward structure plus the chance to ask questions. Options removing dialogue are wrong.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Key word best, with continuity as the goal.
Both remove the chance to clarify.
Tasks without context.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A: sBAR gives the receiving nurse the picture and the ask in a predictable order, so nothing essential depends on memory.

questions.stem: A nurse educator introduces the systems and documentation formats used on the unit: one where providers enter orders directly, one that generates guidance during administration, one that records only deviations from a norm, and one that displays repeated measurements. Match each description with the term it BEST describes. Each term is used only once.

items.text: A system through which providers enter orders directly, reducing transcription and legibility errors
items.rationale: Computerized provider order entry. Its gain is removing handwriting and transcription from the order pathway.

items.text: An alert that analyzes patient data and delivers guidance at the point of care
items.rationale: Clinical decision support system. It supports the decision; it does not make it.

items.text: A documentation method in which only findings deviating from a defined norm are recorded
items.rationale: Efficient, and it depends entirely on the norms being clearly defined and understood.

items.text: A structured format for recording repeated measurements such as vital signs over time
items.rationale: A format for repeated data, which makes trends visible at a glance.

questions.takeaway: CPOE enters orders. CDSS supports decisions. Charting by exception and flow sheets are documentation formats.
questions.strategy: Sort by whether the item creates an order, gives guidance, or records data. That separates all four cleanly.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Only one describes entering orders.
Only one analyzes data and advises.
One records exceptions, one records repeated measures.

questions.note: Two of these are systems and two are documentation formats. Sort by function first.

questions.stem: During a system downtime a nurse reviews four handwritten provider orders before administering the medications. Some use abbreviations, and she must identify any that create a risk of misreading serious enough to require clarification. Which order contains an abbreviation on The Joint Commission's official Do Not Use list?

options.text: Furosemide 40 mg PO daily
options.rationale: Daily is written out, which is the correct form.

options.text: Potassium chloride 20 mEq PO BID
options.rationale: BID is a standard accepted abbreviation and is not on the list.

options.text: Morphine sulfate 2 mg IV q.d. for severe pain
options.rationale: Q.D. is on the official list. It is mistaken for QID or for QOD, changing a once-daily order into four times daily.

options.text: Metformin 500 mg PO with breakfast and dinner
options.rationale: Written out in full, which avoids abbreviation risk entirely.

questions.takeaway: Write daily rather than q.d., and every other day rather than q.o.d.
questions.strategy: Several options may look error-prone. The list is specific, and Q.D. and Q.O.D. are on it while BID and TID are not.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The question asks for an abbreviation on the official list.
Both are written out.
BID is accepted.

elimination.verdict: That leaves C: q.D.

questions.note: More than one option may look similar to error-prone abbreviations. Identify the one specifically on the official Do Not Use list.

questions.stem: A student asks why so much time is spent on documentation when the team already communicates verbally. The nurse explains what the record accomplishes beyond the shift, both clinically and beyond the bedside. Which are legitimate purposes of the client health record? Select all that apply.

options.text: Communication among members of the health care team
options.rationale: The primary purpose, and the reason accuracy and timeliness matter.

options.text: A legal document of the care that was provided
options.rationale: If it was not documented, it is difficult to demonstrate it was done.

options.text: Reimbursement for services
options.rationale: Billing draws on the documented record.

options.text: Education and research
options.rationale: Records support both, within privacy protections.

options.text: A place to record staffing complaints and unit concerns
options.rationale: Those belong in occurrence reports or management channels, not in a patient's record.

questions.takeaway: Communication, legal documentation, reimbursement, education, research, and auditing.
questions.strategy: One option in this item puts a workplace concern in a clinical record. That is the exclusion pattern.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The question asks for legitimate purposes.
Staffing concerns belong in management channels, not the patient record.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, and D are selected.

questions.stem: While scanning a barcoded dose of digoxin, the nurse receives an on-screen alert: verify apical pulse at least 60 beats per minute before administration. This alert is an example of which type of system?

options.text: Computerized provider order entry
options.rationale: CPOE is where the order was entered. It creates orders; it does not generate the safety prompt at administration.

options.text: Clinical decision support system
options.rationale: A CDSS analyzes data and delivers guidance at the point of care, which is exactly what an alert prompting a parameter check does.

options.text: Charting by exception
options.rationale: A documentation method recording only deviations from a defined norm.

options.text: A structured flow sheet
options.rationale: A format for recording repeated data, not a system that generates guidance.

questions.takeaway: CPOE enters the order. CDSS supports the decision at the point of care.
questions.strategy: Focus on the FUNCTION the alert is performing rather than where the underlying order came from.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: An alert providing guidance at the moment of administration.
The order already exists; this is the alert on top of it.
Both are documentation formats, not decision support.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B: a CDSS analyzes data and delivers guidance at the point of care, which is exactly what an alert prompting a parameter check does.

questions.note: This alert originates from an order already entered into the system. Focus on the FUNCTION the alert itself is performing.

questions.stem: A nurse realizes she has charted a set of vital signs on the wrong client's paper record. The entry is complete and signed, and the correct client's record has no entry for that time. Place the following actions in the correct order, from FIRST to LAST.
