options.text: Draw a single line through the entry so the original remains readable
options.rationale: The original must stay legible. Obliterating or erasing an entry suggests concealment.

options.text: Write the word error or mistaken entry above the line, per agency policy
options.rationale: Labels why the entry was struck, so anyone reading the record understands what happened.

options.text: Initial and date the correction
options.rationale: Identifies who made the correction and when, preserving the audit trail.

options.text: Enter the correct information in the appropriate patient's record
options.rationale: The clinical data still has to reach the right chart.

options.text: Notify the nurse caring for the other patient that the entry was made in error
options.rationale: Ensures no one acts on data that was never that patient's.

questions.takeaway: Single line, label it, initial and date, then correct the data and tell whoever might rely on it.
questions.strategy: Documentation correction items are answered by remembering that the record must show what was changed and by whom, never that nothing was there.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The line comes first, and it must leave the original readable.
Notifying the other nurse closes the loop.
Label, then initial and date, then enter the data correctly.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D, E.

questions.note: Never erase, black out, or use correction fluid. The original entry must remain readable.

questions.stem: A nurse transfers to a unit that uses charting by exception and finds far fewer entries in each record than she is used to. Her preceptor explains how the method works and why the unit's defined norms matter so much. Which statement describes this method?

options.text: Every assessment finding is recorded in narrative form each shift
options.rationale: Describes narrative charting, which is the opposite approach.

options.text: Only findings that deviate from a defined norm are documented
options.rationale: Reduces charting time, and it depends entirely on the norms being clearly defined and understood by everyone.

options.text: Documentation is organized by problem, intervention, and evaluation
options.rationale: Describes a problem-oriented format such as PIE.

options.text: Only the provider documents assessment findings
options.rationale: Not a documentation method.

questions.takeaway: Charting by exception records deviations from a defined standard. Its weakness is that it assumes the standard was met.
questions.strategy: The risk with this method is legal: if a finding was never charted, it can be difficult to prove it was assessed.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The question asks what the method is.
That is narrative charting.
That is a problem-oriented format.
Not a documentation method.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B: reduces charting time, and it depends entirely on the norms being clearly defined and understood by everyone.

questions.stem: A hospital is evaluating a new electronic record system and asks nursing staff what improvements they should expect and what the system will not do for them. Which outcomes are supported by well-designed nursing informatics systems? Select all that apply.

options.text: Reducing medication errors through barcode scanning at the point of care
options.rationale: Verifies the right patient and the right drug at the moment of administration.

options.text: Providing decision support alerts based on patient data
options.rationale: A CDSS delivers guidance where the decision is made.

options.text: Improving legibility compared with handwritten orders
options.rationale: One of the clearest gains, since handwriting is a documented source of error.

options.text: Eliminating the need for nursing clinical judgment
options.rationale: No system replaces judgment. Alerts inform a decision that remains the nurse's.

options.text: Supporting continuity by making the record available across settings
options.rationale: Shared access is one of the central purposes of an electronic record.

questions.takeaway: Informatics supports judgment. It never replaces it.
questions.strategy: Any option claiming a system removes the need for clinical judgment is wrong, and it appears in most technology items.

strategies: Eliminate absolutes

steps.detail: The question asks what informatics supports.
Eliminating judgment contradicts the purpose of decision support.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, and E are selected.

questions.stem: An agency uses military time for all documentation to remove the ambiguity of a.m. and p.m. A nurse administers a PRN antiemetic twenty minutes after midnight and must record the time. What is the correct military time to document?

options.rationale: That is 12:20 in the afternoon. The a.m. in the stem is the whole question.
Midnight begins at 0000, so 12:20 a.m. is twenty minutes past midnight. Four digits are always used.
There is no hour 24 in the middle of a day. The clock rolls to 0000.
That is 1:20 a.m., an hour later.

questions.takeaway: Midnight is 0000, so the 12 a.m. hour is written 00. Noon is 1200.
questions.strategy: The two hours people convert wrongly are 12 a.m. and 12 p.m. Everything between 1 p.m. and 11 p.m. is just add twelve.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 12:20 a.m. is after midnight, not after noon.
1220 is midday.
No 24 hour exists on the clock face.
One hour off.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B. Military time removes the a.m. and p.m. ambiguity that causes dosing errors.

questions.stem: A nurse manager audits practice on a unit after a client's information was found visible on an unattended screen. She reviews how staff protect access, screens, and printed material. Which are acceptable practices for maintaining security and confidentiality in an electronic health record? Select all that apply.

options.text: Changing your password regularly according to agency policy
options.rationale: A basic access control.

options.text: Logging out of a workstation any time you step away, even briefly
options.rationale: An open session under your login attributes anything done next to you.

options.text: Positioning the monitor so information is not visible to visitors or uninvolved staff
options.rationale: Screens should be kept out of public view.

options.text: Allowing a floating staff member to chart under your login to save time
options.rationale: Sharing credentials destroys the audit trail and makes you responsible for entries you did not make.

options.text: Shredding printed work lists once they are no longer needed
options.rationale: Printed patient information requires secure disposal.

questions.takeaway: Protect access, protect the screen, protect the paper, and never share credentials.
questions.strategy: The wrong option in a record security item is almost always the one that trades a safeguard for convenience.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The question asks for acceptable practices.
Sharing a login destroys accountability for every entry made under it.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, and E are selected.

questions.stem: A nurse must document her assessment of a client who declined his morning bath. She wants the entry to be usable and defensible, recording what happened rather than her impression of him. Which charting entry meets documentation standards?

options.text: Patient uncooperative and difficult this morning
options.rationale: Judgmental labels rather than facts, and they tell the next reader nothing about what happened.

options.text: Patient declined morning bath, stating "I am too tired right now." Offered again at 1100
options.rationale: Factual, specific, records the patient's own words and the nursing action taken.

options.text: Appears to be in no distress
options.rationale: Appears is a conclusion without supporting observation.

options.text: Tolerated procedure well
options.rationale: A common phrase and it records no data. Tolerated how, and by what measure?

questions.takeaway: Documentation is factual, specific, and free of judgment. Record what you observed and what the patient said.
questions.strategy: Entries containing appears, seems, tolerated well, or uncooperative are conclusions rather than data.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The question asks which entry meets standards.
A judgment, not a fact.
Conclusions with no supporting observation.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B: factual, specific, records the patient's own words and the nursing action taken.

questions.scenario: The nurse is writing a narrative note for a patient admitted with abdominal pain and nausea.
questions.stem: A nurse is writing a narrative note for a client admitted with abdominal pain and nausea. Her entries include the client's own words, measured values, observed behaviour, and a rating the client supplied. For each charting entry, indicate whether it is SUBJECTIVE or OBJECTIVE data.

rows.text: "The cramping in my stomach gets worse after I eat."
rows.rationale: The patient's own report of an experience. Only he can perceive it.

rows.text: Abdomen soft, nondistended, bowel sounds active in four quadrants
rows.rationale: Observed and verifiable by another clinician performing the same assessment.

rows.text: Temperature 100.9 F (38.3 C) tympanic
rows.rationale: A measured value.

rows.text: Ambulated 30 feet in the hallway with steady gait, no assistive device
rows.rationale: An observed behaviour, recorded as what the nurse saw.

rows.text: Rates nausea as 5 out of 10, unrelieved by the prescribed antiemetic
rows.rationale: A rating scale still records the patient's perception. The number does not make it objective.

rows.text: Skin warm and dry, no rash noted
rows.rationale: Inspected and palpated by the nurse.

questions.takeaway: Subjective is what the patient reports. Objective is what you can observe or measure.
questions.strategy: The trap is a pain or nausea rating. A number attached to a perception is still subjective, because only the patient can supply it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: If only the patient can know it, it is subjective.
5 out of 10 looks measured and is a report.
A quoted statement is always subjective.

elimination.verdict: Two rows subjective, four objective.

questions.stem: A nurse realizes at 1600 that a full respiratory assessment she performed at 1000 was never documented. The client's condition has been stable since. The record shows no entry for that time. Which action is correct?

options.text: Document it in the 1000 space so the record reads in sequence
options.rationale: Backdating an entry misrepresents when it was written and undermines the record's integrity.

options.text: Make a late entry at 1600, labeled as such, noting the time the assessment occurred
options.rationale: Preserves both truths: when the care happened and when it was recorded.

options.text: Omit the entry since too much time has passed
options.rationale: An assessment that is not documented is difficult to demonstrate was done.

options.text: Ask a colleague to document it for you
options.rationale: You document your own care; a colleague cannot attest to an assessment they did not perform.

questions.takeaway: Late entries are labeled, timed for when they were written, and reference when the care occurred.
questions.strategy: Any option that makes the record appear other than it is will be wrong, however tidy the result looks.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A six-hour gap between care and documentation.
Backdating misrepresents the record.
Omission leaves the care unevidenced.
You document your own care.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B: preserves both truths: when the care happened and when it was recorded.

questions.stem: The off-going nurse sends a personal cell phone text to the oncoming nurse stating, "Room 412 refused his 0800 lisinopril, said he felt fine." Which actions should the oncoming nurse take? Select all that apply.

options.text: Inform the nursing supervisor about the use of an unsecured personal device to transmit patient information
options.rationale: A privacy breach that needs to be addressed at the level where the practice can be changed.

options.text: Document the refused medication and the patient's stated reason in the official record
options.rationale: The clinical information is valid and belongs in the record regardless of how it arrived.

options.text: Post the information on the whiteboard at the bedside so all staff can see it
options.rationale: Compounds the breach. A bedside whiteboard is visible to every visitor.

options.text: Delete the text once the information has been verified and documented appropriately
options.rationale: The message may be evidence of a reportable privacy breach, so deleting it destroys the record of what occurred.

options.text: Forward the message to the charge nurse's personal phone for a permanent record
options.rationale: Repeats the original violation and creates a second unsecured copy.

questions.takeaway: Capture the clinical information properly, report the breach, and do not spread or destroy the message.
questions.strategy: Three wrong options either widen the exposure or eliminate evidence. Ask what each action does to the breach itself.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: There is clinical information to record and a privacy breach to report.
Both create further unsecured exposure.
Deleting removes evidence of the breach.

elimination.verdict: A and B are selected.

questions.note: Two of these actions widen the privacy exposure and one destroys evidence of it.

questions.stem: During a rapid response, a provider gives the nurse a verbal order for an intravenous medication and then leaves to attend another emergency. The unit is busy and the nurse has not worked with this provider before. Which nursing action is correct?

options.text: Write the order down, read it back to the provider, and obtain the signature within the required timeframe
options.rationale: Read-back verifies that what you heard is what was intended, and the signature closes the loop.

options.text: Enter the order and administer it without read-back to save time in the emergency
options.rationale: Skips the verification step that exists precisely because verbal orders are error-prone.

options.text: Ask another nurse to listen and administer without documenting the order
options.rationale: A second listener does not replace documentation.

options.text: Refuse all verbal orders regardless of circumstances
options.rationale: Verbal orders are permitted in emergencies with the required safeguards.

questions.takeaway: Write it, read it back, and get it signed within the required timeframe.
questions.strategy: Urgency does not remove the read-back. That is exactly when mishearing is most likely.

strategies: Eliminate absolutes

steps.detail: A verbal order during an emergency.
Skips verification.
Omits documentation.
All regardless is absolute and incorrect.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A: read-back verifies that what you heard is what was intended, and the signature closes the loop.

questions.scenario: A nurse arrives for a shift and finds the previous nurse has left a workstation logged in with a patient's record open, a printed patient list on the counter, and a text message on her own phone from the off-going nurse reading: "Room 412 refused his 0800 lisinopril, said he felt fine." The refusal does not appear anywhere in the medical record.
questions.stem: Complete the diagram by selecting from the choices below.

options.text: Log out of the open workstation and secure the printed list
options.rationale: Immediate containment. An open session attributes anything done next to the previous nurse, and printed patient information requires secure disposal.

options.text: Document the refused medication and the patient's stated reason in the record
options.rationale: The clinical information is valid and belongs in the record regardless of how it reached her.

options.text: Forward the text to the charge nurse's personal phone as a record
options.rationale: Repeats the original violation and creates a second unsecured copy.

options.text: Delete the text message immediately
options.rationale: It may be evidence of a reportable privacy breach, so deleting it removes the record of what occurred.

options.text: Write in the patient's chart that an occurrence report was filed about the text
options.rationale: The occurrence report is not part of the medical record and should not be referenced in it.

options.text: A privacy breach with clinical information missing from the record
options.rationale: Two separate problems occurring together: the exposure, and a medication refusal that was never documented.

options.text: A medication error requiring provider notification
options.rationale: No medication was given in error. The patient refused, which is his right.

options.text: A staffing issue requiring a schedule change
options.rationale: Not what the findings describe.

options.text: An expected variation in handoff practice
options.rationale: Unsecured personal messaging of patient information is not acceptable practice.

options.text: Whether the patient's blood pressure has been affected by the missed dose
options.rationale: The clinical consequence of the refusal, which is what the record exists to communicate.

options.text: Whether the record now reflects the refusal and the stated reason
options.rationale: Confirms the documentation gap has been closed.

options.text: The off-going nurse's shift assignment
options.rationale: Not a clinical parameter.

options.text: Room temperature
options.rationale: Unrelated.

options.text: The number of staff with record access
options.rationale: A systems audit question rather than a parameter for this patient.

questions.takeaway: Contain the exposure, record the clinical facts, and report the breach through the proper channel.
questions.strategy: Three wrong actions either widen the exposure, destroy evidence of it, or pull a risk management document into the legal record.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A privacy breach and a documentation gap.
One spreads it, one erases the evidence.
The occurrence report stays outside the record.

elimination.verdict: Actions A and B, condition A, parameters A and B.

questions.stem: A patient awaiting a transplant that may not come for months tells the nurse she has started a meditation practice and talks daily with a friend. Which coping approach is this?

options.text: Problem-focused coping
options.rationale: Would mean acting on the stressor itself, and the wait is not something she can change.

options.text: Emotion-focused coping
options.rationale: Managing feelings related to a stressor she cannot alter, which is the appropriate choice when the stressor is fixed.

options.text: Denial
options.rationale: She is not refusing the reality; she is managing her response to it.

options.text: Regression
options.rationale: No return to earlier developmental behaviour is described.

questions.takeaway: When the stressor cannot be changed, emotion-focused coping is the fitting strategy rather than the lesser one.
questions.strategy: Students often treat problem-focused as always better. Coping effectiveness depends on the person, the situation, and culture.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The wait itself cannot be altered.
There is no action available against the stressor.
Neither describes managing feelings.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B: managing feelings related to a stressor she cannot alter, which is the appropriate choice when the stressor is fixed.

questions.stem: A nurse cares for two clients admitted with the same diagnosis on the same day. One manages the admission calmly and the other is overwhelmed within hours. The nurse considers what differs between them beyond the diagnosis itself. Which factors influence a person's ability to cope with stress? Select all that apply.

options.text: Age and developmental stage
options.rationale: Age and developmental stage shape what a person has already faced and what resources they have built by this point in life.

options.text: Culture and beliefs
options.rationale: Culture and beliefs shape what counts as a stressor at all, and what responses are acceptable to the person.

options.text: Past experiences
options.rationale: Past experience tells the person whether they have survived something like this before, which affects appraisal directly.

options.text: Height and body build
options.rationale: Not among the named factors, and it has no bearing on coping capacity.

options.text: Support system
options.rationale: Named factor, alongside financial and personal resources.

options.text: Problem-solving skills and personal outlook
options.rationale: Problem-solving skills determine what options a person can see, and outlook determines whether they expect any of them to work.

options.text: Health and energy level
options.rationale: Named factor, and it explains why illness itself reduces coping capacity.

questions.takeaway: Eight factors: age and stage, culture and beliefs, past experiences, health and energy, support system, resources, problem-solving skills, and outlook.
questions.strategy: Health and energy level is worth remembering, because it explains why a hospitalized patient copes less well than the same person would at home.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Factors influencing coping ability.
A physical characteristic unrelated to coping.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, E, F, and G are selected.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old newly diagnosed with diabetes enrols in a self-management class, buys a glucose meter, and asks the nurse to review her injection technique before discharge. Which coping strategy is she using?

options.text: Problem-focused coping
options.rationale: Taking action to change or solve the stressor itself.

options.text: Emotion-focused coping
options.rationale: Managing feelings related to the stressor, such as talking with a friend or using relaxation.

options.text: Regression
options.rationale: A defense mechanism, returning to behaviour from an earlier stage.

options.text: Denial
options.rationale: Refusing to accept a painful reality.

questions.takeaway: Problem-focused changes the stressor. Emotion-focused manages the feeling about it.
questions.strategy: Neither is inherently better. Effectiveness depends on the person, the situation, and culture, and on whether the stressor is changeable.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: She is acting on the problem itself.
No feelings are being managed here.
Both are defense mechanisms.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A: taking action to change or solve the stressor itself.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old describing an assault tells the nurse that during it she felt as though she were watching it happen to someone else from across the room, and that parts of the evening are missing entirely. Which defense mechanism does this describe?

options.text: Dissociation
options.rationale: Detaching from thoughts, feelings, or surroundings. It commonly appears during and after trauma.

options.text: Denial
options.rationale: Refusing to accept a reality, and she is not refusing that it happened.

options.text: Projection
options.rationale: Attributing one's own feeling to another person.

options.text: Compensation
options.rationale: Excelling in one area to offset a deficit in another.

questions.takeaway: Dissociation is detachment from thoughts, feelings, or surroundings.
questions.strategy: The phrase watching it happen to someone else is the signature. It is detachment rather than refusal.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Detachment from the experience itself.
She acknowledges the event occurred.
Neither involves detachment.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A: detaching from thoughts, feelings, or surroundings.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old is admitted after a house fire destroyed her home. The nurse assesses her orientation, mood, sleep, vital signs, intake, and contact with family. Highlight the findings that require immediate nursing intervention.

segments.text: Client is alert and oriented to person, place, and time
segments.rationale: A normal finding and a useful baseline.

segments.text: States, "Nothing I do works anymore and I do not see how I get through this"
segments.rationale: Expressed hopelessness with failed coping. Safety is prioritized first in planning.

segments.text: Reports she has not slept in three days
segments.rationale: Sleep loss impairs judgment and coping capacity and is a named marker in evaluation.

segments.text: Tearful during the admission interview
segments.rationale: An expected emotional response to a catastrophic loss, and it is an objective cue rather than an emergency.

segments.text: Heart rate 104 and hands trembling
segments.rationale: Consistent with sympathetic activation in the alarm stage, and expected in this situation.

segments.text: Has declined all contact with her sister and her closest friend
segments.rationale: Withdrawal from the support system, which is a named factor influencing coping and removes a protective resource.

segments.text: Reports she ate a small meal this morning
segments.rationale: A reassuring finding.

questions.takeaway: Safety first. Expressed hopelessness, sleep loss, and withdrawal from support all require intervention.
questions.strategy: Distinguish an expected stress response from a finding that needs action. Tearfulness after losing a home is expected; hopelessness is not.

strategies: Priority key word

steps.detail: Statements about not getting through are assessed immediately.
Withdrawal removes the support system.
Tearfulness and tachycardia fit the alarm stage.

elimination.verdict: Highlight s2, s3, and s6.

questions.note: Some findings are expected stress responses. Highlight only those requiring intervention.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old has cared for her husband with advanced dementia for six years. She has developed hypertension, sleeps poorly, and a wound from last year took months to heal. The nurse documents concern about the long-term physiological effects. Which term describes cumulative wear and tear from repeated or chronic stress?

options.text: Allostatic load
options.rationale: The cumulative physiologic wear and tear caused by repeated or chronic stress.

options.text: Alarm reaction
options.rationale: The first stage of the general adaptation syndrome.

options.text: Adventitious crisis
options.rationale: An unplanned, rare, catastrophic event.

options.text: Emotion-focused coping
options.rationale: A coping strategy, not a physiological consequence.

questions.takeaway: Allostatic load is the price of staying adapted for too long.
questions.strategy: The word cumulative in a stem points at allostatic load rather than at any single stage or event.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Years of stress and long-term effects.
A single stage, not accumulation.
An event type and a coping strategy.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A: the cumulative physiologic wear and tear caused by repeated or chronic stress.

questions.stem: A 54-year-old has cared for a spouse with advanced illness for three years. She reports frequent colds, a surgical wound from last year that took months to close, and constant fatigue. The nurse considers how sustained stress may be contributing. Which effects does chronic stress have on the body? Select all that apply.

options.text: Reduces the body's immune response
options.rationale: Leaving the body less able to fight pathogens.

options.text: Increases susceptibility to infections
options.rationale: A direct consequence of the reduced immune response.

options.text: Slows the healing process
options.rationale: Which is why chronic stress appears as a risk factor in the infection chapter as well.

options.text: Improves cardiovascular efficiency over time
options.rationale: Chronic stress contributes to cardiovascular and metabolic harm, not efficiency.

options.text: Contributes to long-term physical and mental health effects
options.rationale: The accumulated result of allostatic load.

questions.takeaway: Chronic stress lowers immunity, raises infection risk, and slows wound healing.
questions.strategy: This connects two chapters. Chronic stress appears as a named risk factor for infection, and the mechanism is the same one tested here.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Effects of chronic stress.
States a benefit where the chapter describes harm.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, and E are selected.

questions.stem: A client who survived a serious motor vehicle collision six months ago reports intrusive memories, difficulty sleeping, and avoidance of driving. He was not physically injured in the crash and asks whether what he is experiencing is real. Which statement about post-traumatic stress disorder is accurate?

options.text: It develops only in people who were physically injured
options.rationale: Exposure to actual or threatened harm is sufficient, and injury is not required.

options.text: It is a stress response following exposure to actual or threatened harm
options.rationale: It sits within traumatic stress, and symptoms persist beyond the event.

options.text: It resolves without intervention within one month in all cases
options.rationale: Absolute, and untreated symptoms can persist for years.

options.text: It is the same as secondary traumatic stress
options.rationale: Secondary traumatic stress arises from repeated exposure to others' trauma rather than from one's own.

questions.takeaway: PTSD follows exposure to actual or threatened harm. Injury is not required.
questions.strategy: Options containing only, all cases, or always are usually wrong in this chapter, because stress responses vary by person.

strategies: Eliminate absolutes

steps.detail: An accurate statement about PTSD.
Only who were injured is too narrow.
All cases is absolute.
Conflates two distinct types.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B: it sits within traumatic stress, and symptoms persist beyond the event.

questions.stem: A client is admitted following a house fire and remains in hospital for several days. The nurse observes an initial surge in heart rate and blood pressure, a period where the vital signs settle while the client remains under strain, and later a decline in her physical condition. Place the stages of the general adaptation syndrome in the correct order, from FIRST to LAST.

options.text: The body recognizes a stressor and activates the fight-or-flight response
options.rationale: Alarm. The sympathetic nervous system activates, producing increased heart rate, respirations, blood pressure, and blood glucose, plus sweating, muscle tension, dilated pupils, increased alertness, and decreased digestion.

options.text: The body attempts to adapt and stabilize while the stressor continues
options.rationale: Resistance. Vital signs may return toward normal while resources are being consumed, which is why a patient can look stable and still be depleting.

options.text: Adaptive resources are depleted and physiological functioning declines
options.rationale: Exhaustion. When the stressor persists beyond the body's capacity to adapt, illness and organ effects follow.

questions.takeaway: Alarm, resistance, exhaustion. Resistance is where a patient looks fine and is spending reserves.
questions.strategy: The stage most often misread is resistance, because normalized vital signs are mistaken for recovery.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Recognition and sympathetic activation open the response.
Depletion closes it.
Adaptation while the stressor continues.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C. Alarm activates the sympathetic response, resistance adapts while the stressor continues, and exhaustion follows when adaptive resources run out.

questions.note: A patient in the resistance stage may have near-normal vital signs. Stability is not the same as recovery.

questions.stem: A 46-year-old tells the nurse that she has always coped with difficulty by working harder and staying organized, but that since her diagnosis nothing she does is working and she cannot see a way forward. The nurse recognizes this as more than ordinary stress. Which statement best describes a crisis?

options.text: Any highly stressful event
options.rationale: Not every stressful event overwhelms coping.

options.text: A turning point when previous coping methods no longer work
options.rationale: The defining feature is the failure of what used to work, not the size of the event.

options.text: A psychiatric emergency requiring hospitalization
options.rationale: Some crises require that and the term is broader.

options.text: A permanent inability to cope
options.rationale: A crisis is a turning point, not a permanent state.

questions.takeaway: What makes it a crisis is that the person's usual coping has stopped working.
questions.strategy: Two people can face the same event and only one is in crisis, which is why the definition rests on coping rather than on the event.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The definition is being asked for.
Stressful is not the same as overwhelming.
Too narrow.
A turning point implies change is possible.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B: the defining feature is the failure of what used to work, not the size of the event.

questions.stem: An emergency nurse who has worked trauma for eight months tells a colleague she no longer feels anything when patients die, dreads her shifts, and has stopped talking about work at home. Which action best reflects the chapter's guidance?

options.text: Continue working and expect the feeling to pass with experience
options.rationale: Untreated secondary traumatic stress accumulates rather than resolving.

options.text: Recognize this as a possible stress response and seek support and coping strategies
options.rationale: Emotional numbing after repeated exposure to others' trauma is consistent with secondary traumatic stress, and coping and resilience can be built.

options.text: Request transfer to a unit with no acutely ill patients
options.rationale: Avoidance may be part of a plan and does not by itself address the response.

options.text: Avoid discussing the feeling with colleagues to remain professional
options.rationale: Isolation worsens the response, and dialogue with colleagues is a named support.

questions.takeaway: Secondary traumatic stress is a recognized occupational response, and resilience is built rather than assumed.
questions.strategy: Any option that normalizes, avoids, or isolates a stress response in a nurse is wrong. The chapter treats nurse wellbeing as part of the content.

strategies: Client-centered option

steps.detail: Emotional numbing after months of trauma exposure.
Normalizes without addressing.
Avoidance alone.
Isolation worsens it.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B: emotional numbing after repeated exposure to others' trauma is consistent with secondary traumatic stress, and coping and resilience can be built.

questions.scenario: A nurse reviews several client situations during a shift.
questions.stem: A nurse reviews several client situations during a shift, each involving a different pattern and duration of stress. Some describe a single recent event, others describe strain that has continued for years, and in some the client's usual coping has stopped working. For each situation, click to specify which concepts it supports. Each situation may support more than one.

rows.text: A client feels tense before a scheduled family meeting this afternoon
rows.rationale: Short-term stress from an immediate event, and it resolves when the event passes.

rows.text: A client has managed housing instability and debt for three years
rows.rationale: Ongoing stress persisting over time, and it is what produces allostatic load.

rows.text: A client loses his job of twenty years and says his usual ways of coping no longer work
rows.rationale: The event itself is acute, and the failure of previous coping makes it a crisis. It is situational because an external event provoked it.

rows.text: A client's home is destroyed by flooding and she cannot see a way forward
rows.rationale: An external event producing an immediate stress response, with coping that has stopped working.

rows.text: A caregiver has supported a spouse with dementia for four years and now reports exhaustion
rows.rationale: Persistent over time. It becomes a crisis only if previous coping methods stop working.

rows.text: A client describes years of financial strain that recently became unmanageable after an eviction notice
rows.rationale: Long-standing stress that has reached a turning point where coping no longer works.

questions.constraint: Each column must have at least one response selected.
questions.takeaway: A crisis is defined by coping that has stopped working, not by the size of the event.
questions.strategy: The rows that map to two columns are the ones where an event and a failure of coping occur together. Look for language about coping no longer working.
questions.note: Each column must have at least one response selected, and a crisis can accompany either acute or chronic stress.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Afternoon versus years separates acute from chronic.
That phrase is what adds the crisis column.
A crisis can sit on top of either acute or chronic stress.

elimination.verdict: Two rows acute only, two chronic only, and two carrying the crisis column alongside another.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old admitted after losing her home in a flood tells the nurse she cannot see how she gets through this and has stopped answering calls from her family. She has not slept in three days. The nurse begins planning care. Which consideration comes first?

options.text: Setting realistic patient-centered outcomes
options.rationale: Part of planning and not the first consideration when hopelessness has been expressed.

options.text: Prioritizing safety
options.rationale: Safety comes first in planning, and expressed hopelessness makes it the immediate concern.

options.text: Collaborating with the support system
options.rationale: Appropriate when relevant, and it follows safety.

options.text: Setting time frames that match the setting
options.rationale: A planning detail, not the priority.

questions.takeaway: Prioritize safety first, then realistic outcomes, patient involvement, collaboration, and time frames.
questions.strategy: When a stem includes hopelessness, worthlessness, or any statement about not going on, safety moves to the front regardless of what else is in the options.

strategies: Priority key word

steps.detail: Hopelessness has been expressed.
All are legitimate planning steps that come after safety.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B: safety comes first in planning, and expressed hopelessness makes it the immediate concern.

questions.note: All four options are part of planning. Select the one that must come FIRST given what the patient has expressed.

questions.stem: A client admitted in crisis two days ago has attended relaxation sessions and met with the social worker. The nurse must now determine whether the plan has helped. She reviews the record and prepares to speak with him. Which action best reflects evaluation of a stress management plan?

options.text: Asking the patient whether stress feels reduced or more manageable
options.rationale: Stress is subjective, so the patient is the source. Evaluation also reassesses symptoms and revises the plan if coping has not improved.

options.text: Reviewing whether the interventions were documented
options.rationale: Confirms the work was recorded, not whether it worked.

options.text: Confirming the patient attended all scheduled sessions
options.rationale: Attendance is participation, not outcome.

options.text: Comparing the patient's vital signs to the unit average
options.rationale: Not a meaningful measure of an individual's coping.

questions.takeaway: Evaluation asks the patient, reassesses the symptoms, and revises the plan if coping has not improved.
questions.strategy: Coping with stress takes time. A plan that has not yet worked is revised rather than abandoned.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Evaluating a stress management plan.
Both measure process rather than outcome.
A group comparison tells you nothing about this patient.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A: stress is subjective, so the patient is the source.

questions.scenario: The nurse assesses a patient admitted for observation who appears distressed.
questions.stem: A nurse assesses a client admitted for observation who appears distressed. She records both what he reports and what she observes, and must separate the two before writing her note. For each cue, indicate whether it is SUBJECTIVE or OBJECTIVE data.

rows.text: "I have not slept properly in two weeks."
rows.rationale: The patient's own report about sleep, and only he can supply it.

rows.text: Tearful during the admission interview
rows.rationale: An observed behaviour.

rows.text: "I do not know how I am going to manage."
rows.rationale: A statement about coping.

rows.text: Heart rate 104 and hands trembling
rows.rationale: Measured and observed.

rows.text: Hair unwashed and clothing soiled
rows.rationale: Observed hygiene, a named objective cue.

rows.text: Rates his anxiety as 8 out of 10
rows.rationale: A rating scale still records the patient's perception. The number does not make it objective.

questions.takeaway: Subjective cues are what the patient says about stress, fear, coping, sleep, pain, support, and safety. Objective cues are affect, behaviour, vital signs, restlessness, crying, withdrawal, hygiene, and appetite.
questions.strategy: The trap is a rating scale. A number attached to a perception is still subjective, because only the patient can supply it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: If only the patient can know it, it is subjective.
8 out of 10 looks measured and is a report.
A quoted statement is always subjective.

elimination.verdict: Three rows subjective, three objective.

questions.stem: A nurse is teaching a class on stress and coping. A student says that stress is anything unpleasant that happens to a person. The nurse explains that the event and the body's reaction to it are two different things, and that the same event affects two people differently. Which statement best defines stress?

options.text: Any unpleasant event a person experiences
options.rationale: Describes a stressor loosely, and pleasant events such as a wedding or promotion also produce stress.

options.text: The body's response to any demand or threat to the balance of homeostasis
options.rationale: Stress is the response, not the event. Stressors are the physical, psychological, or social stimuli that produce it.

options.text: A psychological disorder requiring treatment
options.rationale: Stress is a normal physiological and psychological response, not a diagnosis.

options.text: The inability to cope with daily demands
options.rationale: Describes a failure of coping, which is a possible consequence rather than the definition.

questions.takeaway: Stress is the response. Stressors are the stimuli. Appraisal is how the person interprets them.
questions.strategy: Sort these three terms before answering anything in this chapter, because items are written to see whether you confuse the event with the response.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The question asks for the definition of stress itself.
Describes a stressor, and stress is not limited to unpleasant events.
Stress is a normal response.
Describes ineffective coping.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B: stress is the response, not the event.

questions.stem: A 39-year-old admitted after a workplace injury reports difficulty sleeping, constant worry about lost income, and that the unit noise makes it worse. He asks the nurse what can be done. Which nursing interventions support a patient managing stress? Select all that apply.

options.text: Teaching relaxation techniques
options.rationale: Relaxation techniques act on the physiological arousal itself, which is why they help even when the stressor cannot be changed.

options.text: Encouraging the patient to identify what better coping would look like
options.rationale: Including the patient in defining the outcome is named in planning.

options.text: Assessing the environment for noise, privacy, and safety
options.rationale: Environmental cues are part of the named assessment.

options.text: Advising the patient to avoid thinking about the stressor
options.rationale: Suppression is not coping, and it removes the opportunity to work the problem.

options.text: Collaborating with the health care team and support system when appropriate
options.rationale: Collaboration brings in resources the nurse does not hold alone, and the support system is a named factor in coping capacity.

options.text: Reassessing sleep, anxiety, pain, appetite, concentration, and safety
options.rationale: Named in evaluation, and each is a marker of whether coping is improving.

questions.takeaway: Interventions build coping and the environment supports it. Evaluation reassesses the markers.
questions.strategy: Any option telling a patient not to think about something is wrong. Avoidance is not a coping strategy the chapter endorses.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Interventions supporting stress management.
Suppression removes the chance to cope.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, E, and F are selected.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old is admitted with chest pain that proves non-cardiac. He tells the nurse he lost the job he held for twenty years last month, that he has always coped by working, and that nothing he does now seems to help. Which type of crisis does this represent?

options.text: Developmental crisis
options.rationale: Triggered by normal life transitions such as retirement or becoming a parent.

options.text: Situational crisis
options.rationale: Provoked by external events such as a job loss, a crash, or serious illness.

options.text: Adventitious crisis
options.rationale: An unplanned, rare, catastrophic event such as a natural disaster.

options.text: Secondary traumatic stress
options.rationale: Stress from repeated exposure to others' trauma.

questions.takeaway: Developmental follows a life transition. Situational follows an external event. Adventitious is catastrophic and rare.
questions.strategy: A crisis is a turning point where previous coping methods no longer work. Sort by what triggered it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: An external event affecting one person.
Job loss is not a normal expected transition.
Not rare or catastrophic in scale.
Not exposure to another's trauma.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B: provoked by external events such as a job loss, a crash, or serious illness.

questions.stem: Two nurses on the same unit are assigned identical patient loads on a busy shift. One describes the day as demanding but energizing; the other feels overwhelmed and says she cannot keep up. Both have similar experience. Which concept explains this difference?

options.text: Allostatic load
options.rationale: Cumulative physiologic wear and tear from repeated or chronic stress.

options.text: Appraisal
options.rationale: How a person interprets the impact of the stressor. The same stimulus produces different responses depending on interpretation.

options.text: The alarm stage
options.rationale: The first stage of the general adaptation syndrome.

options.text: Secondary traumatic stress
options.rationale: Stress from repeated exposure to others' trauma.

questions.takeaway: The stressor does not determine the response. Appraisal does.
questions.strategy: When a stem gives two people the same situation and different reactions, the answer is almost always appraisal.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Identical stressor, different responses.
Describes accumulated wear, not interpretation.
A stage and a specific stress type.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B: how a person interprets the impact of the stressor.

questions.scenario: A 46-year-old is admitted after a house fire that destroyed her home. She lost her job two months ago. She tells the nurse, "I have always handled things, but nothing I do works anymore. I do not see how I get through this." She has not slept in three days, is tearful, and has declined visits from her sister.
questions.stem: Complete the diagram by selecting from the choices below.

options.text: Assess for safety, including thoughts of self-harm
options.rationale: Safety is prioritized first in planning, and she has expressed hopelessness alongside failed coping.

options.text: Explore what has helped her cope in the past and what feels different now
options.rationale: Past experiences and problem-solving skills are named factors influencing coping, and the exploration identifies what to build on.

options.text: Reassure her that most people recover from events like this
options.rationale: False reassurance, and it closes a conversation she has just opened.

options.text: Advise her not to think about the fire until she has slept
options.rationale: Suppression is not a coping strategy, and it removes the chance to work the problem.

options.text: Encourage her to accept her sister's visit today so she is not alone
options.rationale: Support systems matter and directing her toward one is not the first action when safety has not been assessed.

options.text: A situational crisis in which previous coping methods are no longer working
options.rationale: Provoked by external events, and her own words name the failure of what used to work, which is the defining feature of a crisis.

options.text: A developmental crisis
options.rationale: Triggered by normal life transitions, not by a fire and a job loss.

options.text: Post-traumatic stress disorder
options.rationale: A stress response persisting after exposure to harm, and it is too early to apply here.

options.text: An expected grief response requiring no intervention
options.rationale: Expressed hopelessness with sleep loss and withdrawal requires assessment.

options.text: Safety, including any expression of hopelessness or self-harm
options.rationale: The first priority in planning, and it is reassessed rather than checked once.

options.text: Sleep, appetite, concentration, and level of withdrawal
options.rationale: Named markers in evaluation of whether coping is improving.

options.text: Serum electrolytes daily
options.rationale: Not indicated by anything described.

options.text: Deep tendon reflexes
options.rationale: Not a marker of coping.

options.text: Weekly weight only
options.rationale: Too infrequent, and appetite is already covered as a more immediate marker.

questions.takeaway: A crisis is defined by coping that no longer works. Safety comes first in planning.
questions.strategy: Two wrong actions are the classic communication blocks: false reassurance and telling someone not to think about it.

strategies: Priority key word

steps.detail: External events plus her own statement that nothing works.
Both are named non-therapeutic responses.

steps.action: Cut directing her to the sister
steps.detail: Support matters and safety has not yet been assessed.

elimination.verdict: Actions A and B, condition A, parameters A and B.

questions.stem: A nurse manager notices rising sick calls and turnover on a busy medical unit. Staff describe long shifts, heavy assignments, rotating nights, and repeated exposure to patient deaths. Which factors are named as sources of work-related stress in health care?

options.text: High workload, emotional demands, shift work, and exposure to suffering
options.rationale: Heavy patient loads, long hours, and understaffing; supporting patients and families through crisis; disrupted sleep cycles and circadian imbalance; and exposure to trauma.

options.text: Low patient acuity and predictable schedules
options.rationale: Describes conditions that reduce stress.

options.text: Excessive autonomy and lack of supervision
options.rationale: Autonomy is associated with lower moral distress, not higher stress.

options.text: Limited access to continuing education
options.rationale: Not among the named sources.

questions.takeaway: Workload, emotional demands, shift work and circadian disruption, and exposure to suffering.
questions.strategy: Shift work belongs here because circadian disruption is a physiological stressor, not just an inconvenience.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Named sources of work stress in health care.
Describes low-stress conditions.
Autonomy reduces moral distress.
Not named.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A: heavy patient loads, long hours, and understaffing; supporting patients and families through crisis; disrupted sleep cycles and circadian imbalance; and exposure to trauma.

questions.stem: A nurse cares for four clients on a medical unit, each responding to a difficult situation in a different way. She recognizes that these unconscious responses are protecting each person from something they cannot yet face. Match each patient behaviour with the defense mechanism it BEST illustrates. Each term is used only once.

items.text: A patient with a new cancer diagnosis says the laboratory must have mixed up the samples
items.rationale: Refusing to accept a painful reality. It protects the person from information they cannot yet absorb.

items.text: A patient angry about his own smoking history accuses the nurse of being judgmental
items.rationale: Attributing your own feeling to someone else.

items.text: A hospitalized adult begins asking a parent to make all her decisions and speak for her
items.rationale: Returning to behaviour from an earlier developmental stage under stress.

items.text: A patient who can no longer play sports after an injury devotes himself to coaching
items.rationale: Making up for a perceived deficit by excelling in another area.

questions.takeaway: Denial, projection, dissociation, regression, compensation. Defense mechanisms are unconscious and not automatically unhealthy.
questions.strategy: Match by what the mechanism does with the feeling: refuses it, relocates it, retreats from it, or redirects it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Rejecting the diagnosis outright is denial.
Assigning your own feeling to another is projection.
Adult behaving as a child is regression.
Redirecting into another area is compensation.

questions.note: Dissociation is the fifth named mechanism and does not appear here. Detaching from thoughts, feelings, or surroundings.

questions.stem: A client on bed rest after surgery tells the nurse she has been lying still for hours but feels no more rested than when she was admitted. She is anxious about her results and has not slept well. The nurse explains what rest actually requires. Which statement about rest is accurate?

options.text: Rest means physical inactivity
options.rationale: Rest is not inactivity. A person can lie still for hours and not be rested.

options.text: Rest is a state of mental, physical, and spiritual calm
options.rationale: All three dimensions, which is why an anxious patient in bed is not resting.

options.text: Rest and sleep are interchangeable terms
options.rationale: Related and distinct states.

options.text: Rest is less important than nutrition and exercise
options.rationale: Sleep and rest are as essential as nutrition and exercise to physical and emotional health.

questions.takeaway: Rest is mental, physical, and spiritual calm. Lying still is not the same thing.
questions.strategy: This distinction matters clinically: a patient on bed rest who is frightened is not getting rest, and telling her to lie quietly does not deliver it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The definition of rest.
Inactivity alone is not rest.
The two are distinct.
Sleep ranks with nutrition and exercise.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B. Illness increases the need for sleep and often makes it harder to get.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old has slept about four hours a night for three weeks since starting a new job. His surgical wound from two months ago has not fully healed, he reports more pain from it than before, and he has had two upper respiratory infections. Which consequences result from inadequate sleep? Select all that apply.

options.text: Impaired immune function
options.rationale: Named directly, and it links sleep to infection risk.

options.text: Impaired wound healing
options.rationale: Named directly, alongside the growth hormone mechanism.

options.text: Reduced pain tolerance
options.rationale: Named directly, and it explains why a poorly slept patient reports more pain from the same stimulus.

options.text: Improved concentration through increased alertness
options.rationale: Sleep deprivation impairs function, judgment, and mood rather than improving them.

options.text: Impaired judgment and mood
options.rationale: Judgment and mood decline with sleep loss, which matters clinically because a sleep-deprived patient makes poorer decisions about their own care.

questions.takeaway: Poor sleep impairs immunity, healing, pain tolerance, judgment, and mood.
questions.strategy: Reduced pain tolerance is the one worth carrying into practice. The patient who slept badly is not exaggerating the same wound the next morning.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Consequences of inadequate sleep.
States a benefit where the chapter describes impairment.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, and E are selected.

questions.stem: A provider considers prescribing a benzodiazepine for an 82-year-old admitted with insomnia. She is already unsteady walking to the bathroom, takes five other medications, and has fallen once at home this year. Which nursing concern is most important to raise?

options.text: Risk of falls and confusion in older adults, and use should be short-term only
options.rationale: Both cautions are named, and they matter more in this population than in younger adults.

options.text: Benzodiazepines suppress REM sleep permanently
options.rationale: REM suppression is associated with antidepressants, opiates, and anticonvulsants, and no effect is described as permanent.

options.text: Benzodiazepines have no effect on sleep architecture
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines do alter sleep architecture, reducing deep and REM sleep, so sleep quality suffers even when total time increases.

options.text: The medication should be taken with caffeine to prevent daytime drowsiness
options.rationale: Caffeine is a named sleep disruptor and would work against the goal.

questions.takeaway: Benzodiazepines are short-term only, with falls and confusion the specific risk in older adults.
questions.strategy: This connects directly to the older adult chapters, where sedatives are a named fall-risk class.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A benzodiazepine considered for an 82-year-old.
Neither describes the drug accurately.
Caffeine disrupts sleep.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A: both cautions are named, and they matter more in this population than in younger adults.

questions.stem: A nurse assesses sleep for a client admitted three days ago. The overnight notes record that he appeared asleep at each round, his bed partner is not present, and no sleep study has been ordered. The client says he has barely slept. Which is the primary source of information when assessing sleep?

options.text: The patient
options.rationale: Sleep is subjective, and the patient is the primary source. Bed partner and family reports supplement it.

options.text: The overnight nursing observation record
options.rationale: Useful and limited. Observation cannot capture quality, latency, or how rested the patient feels.

options.text: The Epworth Sleepiness Scale alone
options.rationale: Measures daytime sleepiness, which is one component rather than the whole picture.

options.text: The polysomnography report
options.rationale: Valuable when indicated and not the primary source for routine assessment.

questions.takeaway: Sleep is subjective, so the patient is the primary source.
questions.strategy: Ask about bedtime routine, sleep latency, nighttime awakenings, wake time, and perceived quality.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Primary source for sleep assessment.
Observation misses quality and latency.
One component only.
A diagnostic study, not routine assessment.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A: sleep is subjective, and the patient is the primary source.

questions.scenario: A 68-year-old on a medical unit reports he has not slept properly since admission four nights ago. He receives a diuretic at 2000, wakes three or four times to void, and reports the overhead light is on whenever staff enter. His pain score is 6 out of 10 at night. He is drowsy during the day, has been unsteady walking to the bathroom, and asks for a sleeping tablet.
questions.stem: Complete the diagram by selecting from the choices below.

options.text: Cluster nursing care and control light and noise during the night
options.rationale: Interruptions are the largest controllable cause of hospital sleep loss, and dimming lights supports melatonin release.

options.text: Discuss the timing of the diuretic and night-time pain control with the provider
options.rationale: Diuretic timing affects nocturia, and unrelieved pain is a named cause of disrupted sleep. Both are treatable causes.

options.text: Request a benzodiazepine at bedtime
options.rationale: Short-term use only, with a specific risk of falls and confusion in older adults, and this patient is already unsteady.

options.text: Advise him to restrict all fluids after noon
options.rationale: Risks dehydration, which causes dizziness and falls, and it does not address the medication timing.

options.text: Reassure him that poor sleep in hospital is normal and expected
options.rationale: Common is not the same as acceptable, and it dismisses a problem with treatable causes.

options.text: Sleep deprivation from treatable environmental and physiological causes
options.rationale: Nocturia from diuretic timing, unrelieved pain, and light and noise are all identified and all modifiable.

options.text: Obstructive sleep apnea
options.rationale: Would require snoring with apneic episodes, and none is described.

options.text: A parasomnia
options.rationale: Undesirable events during sleep, which is not what he reports.

options.text: An expected age-related change requiring no action
options.rationale: Older adults sleep less, and a new problem with identifiable causes is still assessed.

options.text: Sleep quality, latency, and number of night-time awakenings
options.rationale: The named assessment components, and they show whether the interventions are working.

options.text: Daytime drowsiness and steadiness when ambulating
options.rationale: Sleep deprivation impairs judgment and function, and he is already unsteady, which is a fall risk.

options.text: Serum sodium every four hours
options.rationale: Not indicated by anything described.

options.text: Pupil response
options.rationale: Not a sleep parameter.

options.text: Hair and nail growth
options.rationale: Unrelated.

questions.takeaway: Find the treatable causes before medicating. Nocturia, pain, light, and noise are all modifiable.
questions.strategy: The request for a sleeping tablet is the pull in this stem. Sedating an unsteady older adult adds fall risk while the actual causes remain.

strategies: Assessment before intervention

steps.detail: Four identified causes, all modifiable.
Falls and confusion risk in an already unsteady older adult.
One risks dehydration, one dismisses the problem.

elimination.verdict: Actions A and B, condition A, parameters A and B.

questions.stem: A 76-year-old takes a diuretic each morning and reports waking three or four times each night to void, then struggling to fall back asleep. He is becoming drowsy during the day and has stumbled twice on the way to the bathroom. Which nursing action is most appropriate?

options.text: Advise the patient to restrict all fluids after noon
options.rationale: Risks dehydration, which causes dizziness and falls in older adults and does not address the medication timing.

options.text: Discuss the timing of the diuretic with the provider
options.rationale: Diuretic timing affects nocturia and nighttime awakenings, and adjusting it addresses the cause rather than the symptom.

options.text: Suggest the patient use a bedside commode and accept the awakenings
options.rationale: Improves safety and does not address why the awakenings occur.

options.text: Request an order for a benzodiazepine at bedtime
options.rationale: Adds fall and confusion risk in an older adult and treats the wrong problem.

questions.takeaway: Diuretic timing affects nocturia. Adjusting the cause beats managing the symptom.
questions.strategy: In sleep items, look for the option that removes the reason for waking rather than the one that makes waking safer or sedates through it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Nocturia in a patient on a diuretic.
Fluid restriction risks dehydration.
Accepts the awakenings.
Adds risk and misses the cause.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B: diuretic timing affects nocturia and nighttime awakenings, and adjusting it addresses the cause rather than the symptom.

questions.scenario: A nurse reviews the home medication and substance history of an older adult reporting poor sleep.
questions.stem: A nurse reviews the home substance and medication history of an older adult reporting poor sleep. He drinks coffee with dinner, has a nightly whisky, smokes, and takes an opioid and an antidepressant. For each item, indicate its effect on sleep.

rows.text: Caffeine
rows.rationale: A common and underreported disruptor, alongside nicotine and alcohol.

rows.text: Alcohol
rows.rationale: It shortens sleep latency and then fragments the night, so patients often believe it helps.

rows.text: Benzodiazepines
rows.rationale: With a specific risk of falls and confusion in older adults.

rows.text: Opiates
rows.rationale: Named alongside antidepressants and anticonvulsants.

rows.text: Antidepressants
rows.rationale: And they cause daytime drowsiness, which compounds the problem.

rows.text: Nicotine
rows.rationale: A stimulant, and it is the most commonly overlooked of the three.

questions.takeaway: Caffeine, nicotine, and alcohol disrupt. Antidepressants, opiates, and anticonvulsants suppress REM. Benzodiazepines are short-term only.
questions.strategy: Alcohol is the one patients defend most, because it does shorten sleep latency. The fragmentation later in the night is the part they do not attribute to it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Caffeine, nicotine, alcohol.
Antidepressants, opiates, anticonvulsants.
Benzodiazepines carry the short-term and falls caution.

elimination.verdict: Three rows disrupt, two suppress REM, one is short-term only.

questions.stem: A nurse assesses sleep for a client admitted three days ago who reports lying awake for a long time before sleep comes. She asks how long it usually takes him to fall asleep after getting into bed. Which component of the sleep assessment is this?

options.text: Sleep latency
options.rationale: The time from getting into bed to falling asleep, and it is a named assessment component.

options.text: Sleep efficiency
options.rationale: The proportion of time in bed actually spent asleep.

options.text: Perceived sleep quality
options.rationale: How rested the patient feels, which is asked separately.

options.text: Nighttime awakenings
options.rationale: How often the patient wakes after falling asleep.

questions.takeaway: Assessment covers bedtime routine, sleep latency, nighttime awakenings, wake time, and perceived quality.
questions.strategy: Latency and awakenings point at different problems. Difficulty falling asleep suggests one pattern; repeated waking suggests another, such as nocturia or pain.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Time taken to fall asleep.
A ratio, not a duration.
Quality and frequency of waking.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A: the time from getting into bed to falling asleep, and it is a named assessment component.

questions.stem: A nurse plans to protect a patient's sleep overnight on a busy medical unit. Place the following actions in the correct order across the evening and night, from FIRST to LAST.

options.text: Assess the patient's usual bedtime routine and what has helped at home
options.rationale: Sleep is subjective and individual, so the plan starts with what already works for this person.

options.text: Dim the lights during evening hours to support melatonin release
options.rationale: Light suppresses melatonin, so lowering it in the evening supports the natural onset of sleep.

options.text: Cluster nursing care so assessments and medications are grouped rather than scattered
options.rationale: Reduces the number of separate interruptions, which is the largest controllable cause of hospital sleep loss.

options.text: Control noise by closing doors, lowering alarm volumes, and keeping night conversations quiet
options.rationale: Named directly, and alarm volume is the part staff most often overlook.

options.text: Position the patient for comfort and airway safety
options.rationale: The final step before sleep, and airway safety is why positioning is not purely a comfort measure.

questions.takeaway: Assess the routine, dim the lights, cluster care, control noise, position for comfort and airway safety.
questions.strategy: Sleep bundles work because they combine these rather than relying on any one. Clustering care is the highest-yield single action.

strategies: Assessment before intervention

steps.detail: Assessment of the usual routine precedes any intervention.
Positioning immediately precedes sleep.
Light, then interruptions, then noise.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D, E.

questions.note: All five are appropriate interventions. Consider which one must come FIRST if the plan is to fit this patient.

questions.stem: A student asks the nurse how the body knows when to sleep and when to wake, given that patients on the unit sleep poorly regardless of how tired they are. The nurse explains the structure that governs the 24-hour cycle. Which structure is central to the regulation of the sleep-wake cycle?

options.text: The hypothalamus
options.rationale: Sleep regulation involves the hypothalamus, along with hypocretins for wakefulness and REM, prostaglandin, L-tryptophan, and growth factors.

options.text: The cerebellum
options.rationale: Coordinates movement and balance.

options.text: The medulla oblongata
options.rationale: Controls autonomic functions including respiration and heart rate.

options.text: The pituitary gland
options.rationale: Releases growth hormone during sleep and does not govern the circadian cycle.

questions.takeaway: The hypothalamus governs the 24-hour sleep-wake cycle, with hypocretins driving wakefulness and REM.
questions.strategy: Option D is the near-miss worth noting: the pituitary is involved in sleep through growth hormone, but it does not regulate the cycle.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Regulation of the sleep-wake cycle.
Movement and autonomic control.
Involved in sleep, not in regulating the cycle.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A: sleep regulation involves the hypothalamus, along with hypocretins for wakefulness and REM, prostaglandin, L-tryptophan, and growth factors.

questions.stem: A nurse reviews four clients on a medical unit, each with a different sleep complaint: one cannot fall asleep despite ample opportunity, one snores with witnessed pauses in breathing, one is simply not getting enough sleep in hospital, and one has been found walking at night. Match each description with the sleep disorder it BEST describes. Each term is used only once.

items.text: Difficulty falling asleep or staying asleep despite adequate opportunity
items.rationale: The most common complaint, and the opportunity for sleep is present while the sleep is not.

items.text: Repeated airway obstruction during sleep producing snoring, apneic episodes, and daytime sleepiness
items.rationale: Physical obstruction, and it is strongly associated with cardiovascular consequences.

items.text: Insufficient quantity or quality of sleep producing impaired function, judgment, and mood
items.rationale: It impairs immune function, wound healing, and pain tolerance, and it is common in hospitalized patients.

items.text: Undesirable physical events during sleep such as sleepwalking or night terrors
items.rationale: Behaviours occurring during sleep rather than a failure to obtain it.

questions.takeaway: Four named disorders: insomnia, obstructive sleep apnea, sleep deprivation, and parasomnias.
questions.strategy: Sort by whether the problem is getting to sleep, breathing during sleep, getting enough sleep, or doing something during sleep.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Airway obstruction is apnea.
Events during sleep are parasomnias.
Difficulty obtaining sleep versus insufficient sleep obtained.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease reports he cannot sleep in hospital. He explains that lying flat leaves him breathless, and he has been sitting upright in the chair for most of the night. Which factor most likely contributes to his difficulty sleeping?

options.text: Positioning needs and breathlessness disrupt sleep
options.rationale: Breathlessness worsens lying flat, so the position that allows sleep and the position that allows breathing work against each other.

options.text: Increased REM sleep in respiratory disease
options.rationale: Not a described feature.

options.text: Reduced need for sleep with chronic illness
options.rationale: Illness increases the need for sleep while making it harder to get.

options.text: Elevated melatonin production
options.rationale: Not a described feature of respiratory disease.

questions.takeaway: Illness increases the need for sleep and often makes it harder to get.
questions.strategy: Each disease group disrupts sleep by a specific mechanism. Respiratory is positioning and breathlessness; cardiac is nocturnal angina and apnea; gastrointestinal is nocturnal symptoms.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: COPD and difficulty sleeping.
Neither is described.
Reverses the relationship between illness and sleep need.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A: named directly for respiratory disease including COPD and asthma.

questions.stem: A 51-year-old with difficulty falling asleep tells the nurse she watches television in bed until she feels drowsy, has coffee after dinner, and exercises at 2200 because it is the only time she has. Which instructions does the nurse include when teaching sleep hygiene? Select all that apply.

options.text: Keep a consistent bedtime and wake time daily, including weekends
options.rationale: Consistency supports the circadian rhythm, and weekend variation undoes it.

options.text: Avoid caffeine, alcohol, and heavy meals close to bedtime
options.rationale: All three are named.

options.text: Limit screen time for 30 minutes before bed
options.rationale: Screens delay sleep onset through light exposure and through mental stimulation, so the instruction addresses both.

options.text: Stay in bed reading or watching television until sleep comes
options.rationale: The bed is reserved for sleep only. Using it for other activities weakens the association.

options.text: Exercise during the day, but not within 1 to 2 hours of bedtime
options.rationale: Daytime activity helps; activity too close to sleep does not.

options.text: Use relaxation techniques before bed
options.rationale: Relaxation techniques lower the arousal that keeps a person awake, which is the barrier when sleep hygiene alone has not worked.

questions.takeaway: Consistent timing, no caffeine or alcohol late, screens off 30 minutes before, bed for sleep only, daytime exercise, relaxation.
questions.strategy: The wrong option here is the one patients most commonly do. Reading in bed until sleep arrives feels productive and weakens the bed-sleep association.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Sleep hygiene instructions.
The bed is reserved for sleep only.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, E, and F are selected.

questions.stem: A client reports falling asleep during meetings and while waiting at traffic lights, though he believes he sleeps adequately at night. The nurse wants to quantify how sleepy he is during the day rather than how well he sleeps overall. Which tool measures daytime sleepiness?

options.text: The Epworth Sleepiness Scale
options.rationale: Measures daytime sleepiness specifically, in contrast to overall sleep quality.

options.text: The Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index
options.rationale: Assesses overall sleep quality rather than daytime sleepiness.

options.text: The Geriatric Depression Scale
options.rationale: Screens for depression.

options.text: The Braden Scale
options.rationale: Assesses pressure injury risk.

questions.takeaway: Epworth measures daytime sleepiness. Pittsburgh measures overall sleep quality.
questions.strategy: These two are the named pair and they measure different things, which is exactly why both exist.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Daytime sleepiness specifically.
Overall quality.
Depression and skin risk.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A: measures daytime sleepiness specifically, in contrast to overall sleep quality.

questions.stem: A 54-year-old two days after abdominal surgery asks why the nurses cluster their care at night and dim the lights, saying he would rather they just get on with it. His wound is healing slowly. Which response by the nurse is most accurate?

options.text: "Sleep helps the time pass more quickly during recovery."
options.rationale: Trivializes a physiological process with measurable clinical effects.

options.text: "Growth hormone is released during sleep, which supports tissue repair and wound healing."
options.rationale: A direct mechanism. Poor sleep also impairs immune function, wound healing, and pain tolerance.

options.text: "Sleep prevents you from needing pain medication."
options.rationale: Sleep improves pain tolerance; it does not remove the need for analgesia.

options.text: "It reduces the number of times we need to check on you."
options.rationale: Describes a staffing convenience rather than the patient's benefit.

questions.takeaway: Growth hormone releases during sleep, driving tissue repair and wound healing.
