questions.strategy: Sleep protection is a clinical intervention with a mechanism, not a comfort measure. Answer with the mechanism.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Why sleep is protected after surgery.
No mechanism.
Overstates the effect on pain.
A convenience, not a benefit.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B. REM sleep also supports memory consolidation and emotional processing.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old admitted for elective surgery has a bed partner who reports loud snoring with pauses in breathing most nights. He falls asleep during meetings and once while stopped in traffic, though he believes he sleeps enough. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Report the findings and discuss evaluation for obstructive sleep apnea
options.rationale: Snoring with apneic episodes plus daytime sleepiness is the described pattern, and it warrants evaluation rather than hygiene teaching alone.

options.text: Teach sleep hygiene and reassess in one month
options.rationale: Hygiene will not resolve airway obstruction, and delay allows the cardiovascular consequences to continue.

options.text: Advise the patient to sleep alone so the partner is not disturbed
options.rationale: Addresses the partner's sleep and ignores the patient's airway.

options.text: Reassure the patient that snoring is common and not concerning
options.rationale: Snoring with witnessed apnea and daytime sleepiness is not a benign finding.

questions.takeaway: Snoring plus witnessed apnea plus daytime sleepiness is a pattern to report, not a hygiene problem.
questions.strategy: The bed partner's report is valuable here precisely because the patient cannot observe their own breathing during sleep.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Snoring, apneic pauses, daytime sleepiness.
Hygiene does not address obstruction.
Addresses the wrong person.
Dismisses a significant pattern.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A: snoring with apneic episodes plus daytime sleepiness is the described pattern, and it warrants evaluation rather than hygiene teaching alone.

questions.stem: An 80-year-old in long-term care reports poor sleep. She takes a diuretic and four other medications, has osteoarthritis with night-time pain, wears hearing aids she removes at bedtime, and gets up several times to void. Which factors contribute to sleep problems in older adults? Select all that apply.

options.text: Nocturia
options.rationale: Named risk factor, and it fragments sleep through repeated waking.

options.text: Polypharmacy
options.rationale: Named risk factor, and several drug classes affect sleep directly.

options.text: Pain
options.rationale: Pain both delays sleep onset and wakes the person repeatedly, and it is frequently under-treated at night.

options.text: Comorbidities
options.rationale: Chronic conditions disrupt sleep through their own symptoms, and most older adults have more than one.

options.text: Increased total sleep requirement with age
options.rationale: Reversed. Older adults require less sleep, typically under 7 hours, and it is more fragmented.

options.text: Sensory impairment
options.rationale: Reduced hearing and vision weaken the cues that anchor the sleep-wake cycle, particularly in unfamiliar settings.

questions.takeaway: Nocturia, polypharmacy, pain, comorbidities, and sensory impairment.
questions.strategy: One option reverses the direction of an age-related change. That is the standard distractor pattern in lifespan items.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Factors contributing to sleep problems.
Sleep requirement decreases with age rather than increasing.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D, and F are selected.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old with heart failure tells the nurse he wakes most nights with chest pain that eases when he sits up. He has not reported it before because he assumed it was part of not sleeping well. Which term describes this?

options.text: Nocturnal angina
options.rationale: Chest pain from the heart occurring at night, and it is named alongside heart failure-related apnea as a cardiac cause of disrupted sleep.

options.text: A parasomnia
options.rationale: Undesirable physical events during sleep such as sleepwalking.

options.text: Obstructive sleep apnea
options.rationale: Airway obstruction producing snoring and apneic episodes, which is a different mechanism.

options.text: Sleep latency
options.rationale: The time it takes to fall asleep.

questions.takeaway: Cardiac disease disrupts sleep through nocturnal angina and heart failure-related apnea.
questions.strategy: Chest pain waking a patient at night is a finding to report, not a sleep complaint to manage with hygiene teaching.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Chest pain occurring at night in heart failure.
A behavioural event, not pain.
Obstruction rather than cardiac pain.
A measure of time to fall asleep.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A: chest pain from the heart occurring at night, and it is named alongside heart failure-related apnea as a cardiac cause of disrupted sleep.

questions.stem: A nurse manager reviews patient complaints about sleep on a busy medical unit. Staff enter rooms separately for vital signs, medications, and blood draws through the night, and alarms and hallway conversation continue after 2300. Which action has the greatest effect on nighttime interruptions?

options.text: Cluster nursing care so assessments and medications are grouped
options.rationale: Reduces the number of separate entries into the room, which is the largest controllable cause of hospital sleep loss.

options.text: Offer a sleep medication to every patient at bedtime
options.rationale: Medicates a problem the environment is causing, and it adds risk in older adults.

options.text: Keep hallway lights bright so staff can work without entering rooms
options.rationale: Light suppresses melatonin, and hallway light reaches patient rooms.

options.text: Complete all documentation at the bedside overnight
options.rationale: Increases presence in the room during sleeping hours.

questions.takeaway: Cluster care, dim lights, control noise, and position for comfort. Sleep bundles combine these.
questions.strategy: The pattern across all four options is whether the action reduces or increases stimulation in the room at night.

strategies: Priority key word

steps.detail: Greatest effect on nighttime interruptions.
Medicates an environmental problem.
Light suppresses melatonin.
Increases presence in the room.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A: reduces the number of separate entries into the room, which is the largest controllable cause of hospital sleep loss.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old on a medical unit reports he has not slept since admission four nights ago. The nurse reviews his medications, pain, the ward environment, his intake, and his age and medical history. Highlight the findings that represent modifiable causes the nurse can address.

segments.text: Receives a diuretic at 2000 and wakes three to four times to void
segments.rationale: Diuretic timing affects nocturia and night-time awakenings, and the timing can be changed.

segments.text: Rates his pain as 6 out of 10 at night
segments.rationale: Unrelieved pain is a named cause of disrupted sleep and is treatable.

segments.text: Reports the overhead light is switched on whenever staff enter
segments.rationale: Light suppresses melatonin, and dimming lights during evening hours is a named intervention.

segments.text: Is 68 years old
segments.rationale: Age is not modifiable, and reduced sleep in older adults is expected rather than correctable.

segments.text: Has a history of hypertension managed with medication
segments.rationale: Not itself a sleep disruptor in this scenario.

segments.text: Reports staff enter the room separately for vital signs, medications, and blood draws
segments.rationale: Clustering nursing care reduces interruptions, which is the largest controllable cause of hospital sleep loss.

segments.text: Drinks two cups of coffee with his evening meal
segments.rationale: Caffeine close to bedtime is a named disruptor and is straightforward to change.

questions.takeaway: Find the treatable causes before reaching for a sleeping tablet.
questions.strategy: Ask of each finding whether a nurse could change it this week. Age and a chronic diagnosis are context; timing, light, noise, and caffeine are levers.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Read for what can be changed
steps.detail: Timing, pain control, light, clustering, and caffeine all can.
Age and an existing diagnosis are not modifiable.
Five modifiable causes appear in this passage.

elimination.verdict: Highlight s1, s2, s3, s6, and s7.

questions.note: Two findings are relevant background rather than modifiable causes.

questions.stem: A client taking an opioid for chronic pain reports that although he sleeps eight hours, he feels mentally foggy and more emotionally reactive than before. The nurse recalls that opioids suppress one specific stage of sleep. Which function is supported specifically by REM sleep?

options.text: Memory consolidation and emotional processing
options.rationale: The named functions of REM, which is why REM suppression by medications has cognitive and mood consequences.

options.text: Tissue repair through growth hormone release
options.rationale: A function of sleep, and growth hormone release is not specific to REM.

options.text: Regulation of body temperature during the night
options.rationale: Not the named REM function.

options.text: Clearance of respiratory secretions
options.rationale: Unrelated to REM.

questions.takeaway: REM supports memory consolidation and emotional processing.
questions.strategy: This explains why antidepressants, opiates, and anticonvulsants, which suppress REM, affect mood and cognition beyond their sedating effects.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A function specific to REM.
Growth hormone belongs to sleep generally.
Neither is a named REM function.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A: the named functions of REM, which is why REM suppression by medications has cognitive and mood consequences.

questions.scenario: The nurse reviews the home substance and medication history of a client reporting poor sleep.
questions.stem: For each item, click to specify which effects apply. Each item may have more than one effect.
columns: Raises fall risk in older adults

rows.text: Caffeine
rows.rationale: A common and underreported disruptor, alongside nicotine and alcohol.

rows.text: Alcohol
rows.rationale: It shortens sleep latency and then fragments the night, and it reduces REM.

rows.text: Benzodiazepines
answer: Raises fall risk in older adults
rows.rationale: Short-term use only, with a specific risk of falls and confusion in older adults.

rows.text: Opiates
answer: Raises fall risk in older adults
rows.rationale: Named as a REM suppressant causing daytime drowsiness, and sedation raises fall risk.

rows.text: Nicotine
rows.rationale: A stimulant, and the most commonly overlooked of the three disruptors.

rows.text: Antidepressants
rows.rationale: Named alongside opiates and anticonvulsants, with daytime drowsiness as a consequence.

questions.constraint: Each column must have at least one response selected.
questions.takeaway: Caffeine, nicotine, and alcohol disrupt. Antidepressants, opiates, and anticonvulsants suppress REM. Sedating agents raise fall risk.
questions.strategy: Two items belong in more than one column. Alcohol both disrupts and suppresses REM, and opiates both suppress REM and sedate.
questions.note: Each column must have at least one response selected, and some items belong in more than one.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Caffeine, alcohol, nicotine.
Alcohol, opiates, antidepressants.
Anything sedating in an older adult.

elimination.verdict: Four rows map to one column and two map to two.

chapters.title: The Endocrine System and Diabetes Mellitus

questions.stem: A 66-year-old with a fifteen-year history of type 2 diabetes reports tingling and numbness in both feet that has developed gradually over the past year. He mentions he no longer feels the water temperature clearly when he bathes. Which complication does the nurse recognize?

options.text: A macrovascular complication
options.rationale: Macrovascular complications involve large vessels: coronary artery disease, myocardial infarction, and stroke.

options.text: A microvascular complication
options.rationale: Neuropathy is microvascular, alongside retinopathy and nephropathy. Small vessels supply the nerves, the eye, and the kidney.

options.text: An expected change of aging
options.rationale: A specific bilateral sensory change in a client with diabetes warrants assessment, not attribution to age.

options.text: An early sign of hypoglycemia
options.rationale: Hypoglycemia produces shakiness, diaphoresis, tachycardia, and confusion, not a chronic bilateral sensory loss.

questions.takeaway: Micro is small vessels: eyes, kidneys, nerves. Macro is large vessels: heart and brain.
questions.strategy: The prefix tells you which organs are involved. Sorting by vessel size answers most complication items without further recall.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Bilateral sensory change in the feet in long-standing diabetes.
Large-vessel disease affects the heart and brain.
A change from baseline is assessed, not attributed to aging.
Wrong symptom cluster and wrong time course.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B. Neuropathy plus poor circulation is why diabetic feet lose limbs.

questions.stem: A 20-year-old with type 1 diabetes is admitted after two days of vomiting. His glucose is 468 mg/dL, serum ketones are positive, and his pH is 7.19. The nurse completes a focused assessment as the insulin infusion is prepared. Which finding does the nurse expect?

options.text: Shallow, slow respirations
options.rationale: The opposite. Respirations are deep and rapid because the lungs are compensating for acidosis.

options.text: Deep, rapid respirations with a fruity breath odor
options.rationale: Kussmaul respirations blow off carbon dioxide to raise the pH, and the fruity odor is exhaled ketones.

options.text: Serum pH of 7.46
options.rationale: That is alkalosis. DKA produces a pH below 7.3.

options.text: Absent ketones in the urine
options.rationale: Ketones are the defining feature of DKA and appear in both urine and serum.

questions.takeaway: Kussmaul respirations are compensation for acidosis, not an airway problem. Treat with insulin and fluids.
questions.strategy: Do not reach for oxygen or suctioning when you see deep rapid breathing in DKA. Correcting the acidosis is what stops it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The question asks for an expected finding in DKA.
Respirations are deep and rapid, not shallow and slow.
7.46 is alkalotic; DKA is acidotic.
Ketones define the condition.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B, which pairs the respiratory pattern with the exhaled ketones.

questions.scenario: A client with type 1 diabetes calls the clinic with vomiting and a fever of 38.6 C. She has not eaten since yesterday and has held her insulin because she is not eating.
questions.stem: Which instructions does the nurse give? Select all that apply.

options.text: Resume the insulin as prescribed
options.rationale: Illness raises glucose through stress hormones whether or not the client eats. Holding insulin in type 1 leads to DKA.

options.text: Check the blood glucose every 3 to 4 hours
options.rationale: Checking every 3 to 4 hours catches the rise that illness produces, which is faster than a once-daily check would detect.

options.text: Continue to hold the insulin until eating resumes
options.rationale: The misconception that caused the problem, and the most dangerous option here.

options.text: Drink fluids every half hour to an hour
options.rationale: Vomiting and fever both drive dehydration, which is the immediate risk.

options.text: Substitute soft foods across 6 to 8 small meals if unable to follow the usual plan
options.rationale: Smaller, softer, more frequent meals maintain carbohydrate intake when a normal meal cannot be tolerated, which prevents the swing in both directions.

options.text: Report the vomiting and fever to the health care provider
options.rationale: Named, so that treatment can be prescribed to prevent dehydration.

options.text: Restrict all oral fluids until the vomiting settles
options.rationale: Reversed. Fluids are encouraged, and if they cannot be tolerated the provider is contacted for possible intravenous hydration.

questions.takeaway: During illness the insulin continues, monitoring increases, and fluids are encouraged.
questions.strategy: Extended response items score plus and minus, so a wrong selection subtracts. Select only what you can justify from a named rule.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The client has already made one error by holding insulin.
Holding insulin during illness in type 1 causes DKA.
Fluids are encouraged, not restricted.

elimination.verdict: A, B, D, E, and F are selected.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old with type 2 diabetes is brought in after four days of increasing confusion. Blood glucose is 640 mg/dL, serum ketones are negative, and the pH is normal. His mucous membranes are dry and his heart rate is 108. Which condition does the nurse suspect?

options.text: Diabetic ketoacidosis
options.rationale: DKA requires ketones and acidosis, and it occurs typically in type 1.

options.text: Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state
options.rationale: Extreme hyperglycemia without significant ketones, occurring more often in type 2.

options.text: Hypoglycemia
options.rationale: The glucose is 640 mg/dL.

options.text: An expected postprandial rise
options.rationale: No meal produces a glucose of 640 in any patient.

questions.takeaway: The dividing line between DKA and HHS is ketones, not the glucose number.
questions.strategy: Students sort by how high the sugar is and get it backwards, because HHS runs higher than DKA.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: No ketones, normal pH, type 2.
Ketones and acidosis are absent.
Glucose 640 is not low.
Not a postprandial value.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B: extreme hyperglycemia without significant ketones, occurring more often in type 2.

questions.scenario: A 19-year-old with type 1 diabetes presents with nausea and vomiting for one day. Glucose 412 mg/dL, serum ketones positive, pH 7.21, respirations 32 and deep, breath has a fruity odor.
questions.stem: Complete the diagram by selecting from the choices below.

options.text: Administer intravenous isotonic fluids
options.rationale: Dehydration from osmotic diuresis and vomiting is immediately life-threatening.

options.text: Administer a continuous intravenous insulin infusion
options.rationale: Insulin stops fat breakdown, which is what is generating the ketones and the acidosis.

options.text: Administer oxygen by non-rebreather mask
options.rationale: The deep rapid breathing is compensation for acidosis, not hypoxia. Oxygen does not treat it.

options.text: Encourage oral fluids only
options.rationale: The client is vomiting and cannot replace the deficit orally.

options.text: Prepare for intubation to control the respiratory rate
options.rationale: Suppressing the compensation would worsen the acidosis.

options.text: Diabetic ketoacidosis
options.rationale: Type 1, rapid onset, ketones present, pH under 7.3, and Kussmaul respirations with fruity breath.

options.text: Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state
options.rationale: HHS has no significant ketones and a normal pH, and develops over days to weeks.

options.text: Hypoglycemia
options.rationale: The glucose is 412 mg/dL.

options.text: An expected postprandial rise in glucose
options.rationale: No meal produces this picture, and a postprandial rise does not generate ketones or acidosis.

options.text: Serum potassium
options.rationale: Insulin and correction of the acidosis both shift potassium into cells, so the serum level can fall fast.

options.text: Serum pH and anion gap
options.rationale: These show whether the ketone production is actually stopping.

options.text: Serum calcium
options.rationale: Not a monitoring priority in DKA.

options.text: Deep tendon reflexes
options.rationale: Not the parameter that tracks this client's status.

options.text: Urine specific gravity
options.rationale: Volume status is followed through intake, output, and vital signs rather than this value.

questions.takeaway: DKA is treated with fluids, insulin, and potassium monitoring. The breathing pattern is compensation and is not treated directly.
questions.strategy: In a bow-tie, name the condition first. Once you have it, the actions and parameters follow from the pathophysiology rather than from recall.

strategies: Priority key word
Apply the ABCs

steps.detail: Ketones, pH under 7.3, and rapid onset in type 1 means DKA.
Kussmaul respirations are compensating; suppressing them worsens the pH.
The client is vomiting.

elimination.verdict: Actions A and B, condition A, parameters A and B.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old with type 2 diabetes on a sulfonylurea becomes shaky, diaphoretic, and confused at 1500 after eating little at lunch. The glucose reads 58 mg/dL. He is alert, follows commands, and is swallowing safely. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Administer intramuscular glucagon
options.rationale: Reserved for a client who cannot swallow safely. This client can take oral carbohydrate, which is faster and less invasive.

options.text: Give 15 g of a fast-acting carbohydrate
options.rationale: The Rule of 15. Below 70 mg/dL with intact swallowing, give 15 g of fast-acting carbohydrate, wait 15 minutes, and retest.

options.text: Start an intravenous dextrose infusion
options.rationale: Also reserved for unsafe swallowing, and it requires access this client does not need.

options.text: Recheck the glucose in 30 minutes
options.rationale: Delays treatment of a symptomatic low that can progress to seizures and loss of consciousness.

questions.takeaway: Conscious and swallowing safely means oral carbohydrate. Unsafe swallowing means glucagon or intravenous dextrose.
questions.strategy: The route is decided by swallowing, not by how low the number is. Check the stem for whether the client can protect the airway.

strategies: Priority key word

steps.detail: Key word first, and the stem states the client is alert and swallowing safely.
Glucagon is for the client who cannot swallow.
Intravenous dextrose is for the same situation.
Waiting is not a treatment for symptomatic hypoglycemia.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B. Then wait 15 minutes and retest, because one dose is often not enough.

questions.stem: A parent brings a 9-year-old to the clinic reporting that she has started wetting the bed again after years of being dry, seems tired all the time, and is drinking constantly. She has lost weight over the past month. Which findings support a possible new diagnosis of type 1 diabetes? Select all that apply.

options.text: New bedwetting after years of being dry at night
options.rationale: Enuresis is polyuria in a child, and it is often what brings the family in.

options.text: Excessive thirst
options.rationale: Polydipsia, the body's response to fluid lost through osmotic diuresis.

options.text: Weight gain over the past month
options.rationale: Weight loss, not gain, accompanies new type 1 diabetes. Without insulin the body breaks down fat and muscle.

options.text: Unusual fatigue and irritability
options.rationale: Both are named presenting features in children.

options.text: Excessive hunger
options.rationale: Polyphagia. The cells are starved of glucose even though the blood is full of it.

options.text: Dark velvety patches on the neck
options.rationale: Acanthosis nigricans is a sign of insulin resistance and points to type 2, not type 1.

questions.takeaway: In children, look for enuresis, irritability, unusual fatigue, and weight loss alongside the three Ps.
questions.strategy: Two distractors here are correct diabetes findings attached to the wrong type or the wrong direction. Check each against type 1 specifically.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Type 1 in a child, so the paediatric presentation applies.
Type 1 causes weight loss.
Acanthosis nigricans indicates insulin resistance, meaning type 2.

elimination.verdict: A, B, D, and E remain: the three Ps in paediatric form plus fatigue and irritability.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old with type 2 diabetes on a sulfonylurea becomes shaky, diaphoretic, and confused at 1500. He ate very little at lunch. His last recorded glucose was four hours ago and was within range. Which action does the nurse take FIRST?

options.text: Check the blood glucose
options.rationale: These findings fit hypoglycemia and several other causes. The glucose confirms it before you treat.

options.text: Administer the next scheduled insulin dose
options.rationale: Would drive the glucose lower and is the most dangerous option here.

options.text: Document the findings and continue monitoring
options.rationale: Delays action in a patient who may deteriorate quickly.

options.text: Encourage the patient to rest until symptoms pass
options.rationale: Hypoglycemia does not resolve with rest and can progress to seizures.

questions.takeaway: Confirm the glucose before treating, unless the patient is unable to wait.
questions.strategy: Point-of-care glucose monitoring exists so this takes under a minute. Assessment before intervention holds even when the picture looks obvious.

strategies: Assessment before intervention

steps.detail: Key word FIRST, with symptoms consistent with hypoglycemia.
Insulin would worsen a low.
Both delay treatment.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A: these findings fit hypoglycemia and several other causes.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old is admitted in diabetic ketoacidosis with a glucose of 512 mg/dL and a pH of 7.18. The serum potassium is 5.1 mEq/L and an insulin infusion has just been started. The nurse reviews the orders before continuing. Which action is the priority?

options.text: Withhold all potassium replacement because the level is elevated
options.rationale: The level is misleading. Acidosis has pushed potassium out of cells while days of osmotic diuresis depleted the total body store.

options.text: Monitor the serum potassium frequently during the insulin infusion
options.rationale: Insulin drives potassium into cells and correcting the acidosis reverses the shift, so the serum level can fall quickly and cause dysrhythmias.

options.text: Administer sodium bicarbonate to correct the acidosis rapidly
options.rationale: Not a routine intervention, and correcting the pH quickly would accelerate the potassium shift the nurse is trying to control.

options.text: Restrict all intravenous fluids until the potassium normalizes
options.rationale: Fluid resuscitation is a priority in DKA. Withholding it worsens the dehydration.

questions.takeaway: A normal or high potassium in DKA hides a real deficit that treatment is about to expose.
questions.strategy: When a stem gives a lab value that looks reassuring in a client whose physiology is shifting, ask what the treatment will do to that value.

strategies: Priority key word

steps.detail: Key word priority. Insulin has just been started.
Treats the number as if it reflected total body potassium.
Not routine, and it accelerates the shift.
Fluids are central to DKA management.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B. Potassium replacement runs alongside the insulin, not after it.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old newly diagnosed with type 2 diabetes tells the nurse his uncle lost a foot to the disease and asks what he can do to avoid the same outcome. He works long hours on his feet and has never seen a podiatrist. Which teaching points does the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: Inspect your feet daily
options.rationale: Neuropathy means injury is not felt, so it must be seen.

options.text: Attend regular eye examinations
options.rationale: Retinopathy can progress to irreversible blindness and is detectable before symptoms appear.

options.text: Keep blood pressure and lipid levels within target ranges
options.rationale: A stated goal of diabetes management, because macrovascular complications are driven by the same vascular damage.

options.text: Go barefoot indoors so the feet can breathe
options.rationale: Never barefoot. An unfelt injury on an insensate foot is how ulcers begin.

options.text: Trim toenails straight across
options.rationale: Reduces ingrown nails, and a podiatrist should do it if neuropathy or thick nails are present.

options.text: Use a heating pad on the feet in cold weather
options.rationale: Explicitly avoided. Neuropathy means the client may not feel a burn.

options.text: Report any wound that is not healing
options.rationale: Impaired healing and immune response turn minor injuries into serious infections.

questions.takeaway: Every foot-care rule traces to one of two deficits: the client cannot feel injury, or the injury will not heal.
questions.strategy: The two false options both involve exposing the foot to something it cannot feel. Once you see the pattern the item resolves quickly.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Prevention of complications in a new diagnosis.
Barefoot exposes an insensate foot to injury.
Heating pads risk burns the client will not feel.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, E, and G remain, covering feet, eyes, vascular targets, and wound reporting.

questions.stem: A nurse reviews the results of four clients seen in a screening clinic this morning. Each was tested differently: one fasting, one after a glucose load, one at random with no symptoms, and one with a glycosylated hemoglobin. Which result is diagnostic of diabetes mellitus?

options.text: Fasting glucose 112 mg/dL
options.rationale: Prediabetes. The fasting range for prediabetes is 100 to 125; diabetes begins at 126.

options.text: Glucose tolerance test 168 mg/dL
options.rationale: Prediabetes. The GTT range for prediabetes is 140 to 199; diabetes begins at 200.

options.text: Hemoglobin A1C of 7.2%
options.rationale: Diabetes is diagnosed above 6.5%. This value reflects roughly three months of average control.

options.text: Random glucose 154 mg/dL in an asymptomatic client
options.rationale: A random value is diagnostic at 200 or higher and only with symptoms present.

questions.takeaway: Fasting 126, GTT 200, random 200 with symptoms, A1C above 6.5%.
questions.strategy: Two of the four thresholds are fasting values and two are post-load or random. Decide which kind of value the option is before comparing it to a cut-off.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Only one option needs to cross a diagnostic threshold.
112 falls in the prediabetes range of 100 to 125.
168 falls in the prediabetes range of 140 to 199.
Random values need 200 and symptoms.

elimination.verdict: That leaves C. A1C above 6.5% is diagnostic on its own.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old with type 2 diabetes on insulin arrives for a supervised exercise session and is about to use the treadmill for thirty minutes. His blood glucose reads 88 mg/dL and he last ate three hours ago. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Proceed with the exercise as planned
options.rationale: 88 is normal at rest and too low to start activity. Exercise drives glucose down further.

options.text: Provide a carbohydrate snack before the activity
options.rationale: The teaching point is explicit: check the glucose before activity, and if it is below 100 mg/dL take a carbohydrate snack to prevent exercise-induced hypoglycemia.

options.text: Hold the activity and notify the provider
options.rationale: Over-cautious. Exercise is part of the treatment plan; it needs a snack, not cancellation.

options.text: Administer the scheduled rapid-acting insulin first
options.rationale: Would lower the glucose further just as activity lowers it again.

questions.takeaway: Glucose below 100 before exercise means a carbohydrate snack first.
questions.strategy: A normal-looking number can still be unsafe for what is about to happen. Read the number against the activity, not against the reference range.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 88 mg/dL is within normal limits but the client is about to exercise.
Ignores the threshold of 100 before activity.
Cancels an intervention that only needed preparation.
Compounds the fall in glucose.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B. The rule is under 100, snack first.

questions.stem: A client with type 2 diabetes has just been started on insulin after eight years on oral agents. He tells the nurse this must mean he now has type 1, or that he has failed at managing his condition. Which response by the nurse is most accurate?

options.text: Type 2 diabetes eventually becomes type 1 diabetes
options.rationale: They are separate conditions. Type 2 does not convert to type 1.

options.text: Needing insulin in type 2 means the client failed to follow the treatment plan
options.rationale: A harmful misconception. Insulin use reflects the natural course of the disease, not the client's effort.

options.text: In type 1 there is no insulin from the start, and in type 2 the pancreas may eventually fail to keep up with the resistance
options.rationale: Type 1 is autoimmune destruction of beta cells. Type 2 begins as resistance, and over time the beta cells become exhausted so production declines as well.

options.text: Insulin in type 2 is used only during hospitalization
options.rationale: Many clients with type 2 use insulin long term at home.

questions.takeaway: Type 1 has no insulin. Type 2 begins with resistance and adds declining production over time.
questions.strategy: Watch for options that blame the client. They are almost always wrong and they are written to feel plausible.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The client is asking about mechanism, so the answer should explain one.
The two types do not convert.
Blames the client and is factually wrong.
Insulin is widely used at home in type 2.

elimination.verdict: That leaves C. Declining production is also why a client with type 2 can develop DKA under enough stress.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old with type 1 diabetes was found drowsy at her desk after skipping lunch and taking her usual rapid-acting insulin. The nurse assesses her and must distinguish a low glucose from a high one before treating. Which findings should the nurse recognize as signs of hypoglycemia? Select all that apply.

options.text: Diaphoresis
options.rationale: A sympathetic response to falling glucose and one of the earliest signs.

options.text: Shakiness
options.rationale: Also sympathetic, and often the first thing the client notices.

options.text: Deep, rapid respirations with fruity breath
options.rationale: Kussmaul respirations and exhaled ketones belong to DKA, which is hyperglycemia.

options.text: Confusion
options.rationale: The brain depends on a continuous glucose supply, so cognition changes early.

options.text: Tachycardia
options.rationale: Part of the same sympathetic response.

options.text: Polyuria and polydipsia
options.rationale: Osmotic diuresis requires high glucose. These are hyperglycemic findings.

questions.takeaway: Hypoglycemia is sympathetic activation plus altered cognition. Hyperglycemia is fluid loss plus, in DKA, acidosis.
questions.strategy: Sorting findings by which state produces them prevents the most common error in diabetes items, which is treating one emergency as the other.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Signs of hypoglycemia specifically.
Kussmaul respirations and fruity breath are DKA findings.
The three Ps require hyperglycemia.

elimination.verdict: A, B, D, and E remain. Severe hypoglycemia progresses to seizures and loss of consciousness.

questions.stem: A nurse teaches a 26-year-old with type 1 diabetes what to do when she is unwell, since she recently held her insulin during a stomach upset because she was not eating. The nurse asks her to explain the plan back. Which statement indicates the teaching has been effective?

options.text: If I am not eating, I should hold my insulin until I can eat again
options.rationale: The most dangerous misconception in diabetes self-management. Illness raises glucose through stress hormones whether or not the client eats, and withholding insulin in type 1 leads to DKA.

options.text: I will take my insulin as prescribed and check my glucose every 3 to 4 hours
options.rationale: Both sick day rules. Insulin continues and monitoring becomes more frequent, because illness is when control is hardest.

options.text: I will check my glucose once daily until I feel better
options.rationale: Less monitoring at the moment more is needed.

options.text: I should avoid all fluids until the vomiting stops
options.rationale: Reversed. With vomiting, diarrhea, or fever the client drinks fluids every half hour to an hour and reports it, because dehydration is the immediate threat.

questions.takeaway: Illness raises glucose even when the client is not eating. Insulin continues and monitoring increases.
questions.strategy: Sick day items reward the answer that sounds like more work. Holding medication and reducing monitoring both feel intuitive and are both wrong.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Positive polarity: find the correct statement.
Holding insulin in type 1 during illness causes DKA.
Monitoring should increase, not decrease.
Fluids are encouraged during vomiting, not withheld.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B, which pairs continued insulin with 3 to 4 hourly glucose checks.

questions.stem: A 47-year-old newly diagnosed with type 2 diabetes tells the nurse he has been getting up four or five times a night to pass urine and cannot stop drinking water. He asks whether his kidneys are failing. Which explanation by the nurse is correct?

options.text: High glucose damages the kidneys, causing them to leak fluid
options.rationale: Describes nephropathy, which is a chronic complication developing over years. It does not explain polyuria at the onset of illness.

options.text: Glucose spills into the urine and draws water with it
options.rationale: Osmotic diuresis. Above roughly 180 mg/dL the kidney's reabsorption capacity is exceeded, glucose enters the urine, and being osmotically active it pulls water and electrolytes along.

options.text: Insulin deficiency directly stimulates the bladder
options.rationale: Insulin has no direct action on the bladder.

options.text: Ketones irritate the urinary tract, increasing urgency
options.rationale: Ketones appear in urine but do not cause the polyuria, which occurs in hyperglycemia with or without ketones.

questions.takeaway: Polyuria is osmotic diuresis. It drives the dehydration, which drives the polydipsia.
questions.strategy: The three Ps come from one process. Understanding it means you can reason to any of them rather than memorizing all three.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The question asks for the mechanism, not the consequence.
Nephropathy is a late complication, not the cause of new polyuria.
No such mechanism exists.
Polyuria occurs in HHS, where ketones are absent.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B. Glucose is osmotically active and takes water with it.

questions.scenario: A 74-year-old with type 2 diabetes is admitted after four days of increasing confusion. Blood glucose 618 mg/dL, serum ketones negative, serum pH 7.37, dry mucous membranes, poor skin turgor, heart rate 112, blood pressure 96/58.
questions.stem: For each nursing action, indicate whether it is indicated or not indicated for this client.

rows.text: Establish intravenous access for fluid resuscitation
rows.rationale: Severe dehydration is the immediate threat in HHS, and fluid replacement is the priority.

rows.text: Monitor serum potassium during insulin administration
rows.rationale: Insulin drives potassium into cells, so the serum level can fall quickly and cause dysrhythmias.

rows.text: Administer sodium bicarbonate to correct acidosis
rows.rationale: There is no acidosis. The pH is 7.37 and ketones are negative.

rows.text: Perform frequent neurological assessment
rows.rationale: Altered mental status is the hallmark of HHS and the marker of whether treatment is working.

rows.text: Encourage independent ambulation to the bathroom
rows.rationale: A confused, hypotensive, dehydrated older adult is a fall risk and needs assistance.

rows.text: Monitor intake and output
rows.rationale: Osmotic diuresis is driving the fluid loss, so output guides replacement.

questions.takeaway: In HHS the priority is fluid, not insulin alone, and there is no acidosis to correct.
questions.strategy: Work matrix rows against the data given. Two rows here are wrong because the client has no acidosis and is unsafe to mobilize alone.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Glucose over 600, no ketones, normal pH, and signs of volume depletion.
There is no acidosis to correct.
Confusion plus hypotension is a fall risk.

elimination.verdict: The four remaining rows are indicated: fluids, potassium monitoring, neurological checks, and intake and output.

questions.stem: A nurse observes a student teaching a 70-year-old with diabetes and peripheral neuropathy about foot care before discharge. The client has reduced sensation in both feet and has had one previous ulcer. The nurse intervenes if the student makes which statement?

options.text: Inspect your feet and the soles daily for blisters, redness, or drainage
options.rationale: Correct. Daily inspection catches injury the client cannot feel because of neuropathy.

options.text: Apply moisturizer to the tops and bottoms of your feet, and between your toes
options.rationale: Moisturizer goes on the tops and bottoms but never between the toes. Trapped moisture in a warm dark space grows fungus.

options.text: Buy new shoes at the end of the day
options.rationale: Correct. Feet swell through the day, so shoes fitted in the morning are too tight by evening.

options.text: Check the water temperature before bathing
options.rationale: Correct. Neuropathy means the client may not feel a scald until the burn has happened.

questions.takeaway: Moisturize the tops and bottoms, never between the toes.
questions.strategy: In a spot-the-error item, three options are correct practice. Verify each against a rule you can name; the one you cannot justify is the answer.

strategies: Negative polarity

steps.detail: Intervenes means find the error. Three statements will be correct.
Daily inspection is standard teaching.
End-of-day shoe fitting accounts for swelling.
Water temperature checking addresses neuropathy.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B. Every foot-care rule traces to neuropathy or to poor circulation and infection risk; moisture between the toes belongs to the second.
